Subhi J. Al'Aref, MD: First and foremost, I would like to dedicate this textbook to my wife Nadia who is my soulmate, love of my life, and my better half. I would like to thank my parents, Jamal and Nisreen, and my parents-in-law, Dr. Samir Darwish and Ms. Sahar Darwish, for being my backbone in life and providing limitless love, support, and care. I would also like to dedicate this textbook to my family, especially Omar, Jumana, Samik, Zeid, Reem, Rami & Hussein, Mustafa, Yasmine, Hassan, Sarah, and Sareen. Words can never express how much I love you.

Gurpreet Singh, PhD: I would like to dedicate this book to my wife Simran for being a constant source of love, my mentor Prof. Lakshminarayana Samavedham for his encouragement, and my parents and parents-in-law, S. Tarlochan Singh, Sdn. Narinder Kaur, S. Visheshver Singh Narula, and Late Sdn. Harmit Kaur Bajaj, for their support. Also, to my friends and siblings, you all have been a source of inspiration that has always instilled confidence in myself and has kept me motivated. Thank you.

Lohendran Baskaran, MBBS: To my family, thank you for your support, and for letting me chart my own journey. To friends, colleagues and collaborators, thank you for your support, past, present and future.

Dimitris Metaxas, PhD: I would like to dedicate this book to my wife Geanne for her continuous love and support and my two daughters Ada and Christina. To my late parents Nickolas and Ada for teaching me how to lead, excel, inspire, and help others. To my colleagues and collaborators, especially Dr. Leon Axel for the close to 30 years of excellence in collaborative cardiac research and results. To my students for their hard work, innovation, perseverance, and support resulting in many awards and publications in prestigious conferences and journals.

# Preface

The field of cardiovascular medicine has undergone tremendous evolution over the last number of decades. From reliance on auscultation and clinical examination to now, a deluge of diagnostic information that has aided more informed treatment decision making and improved clinical outcomes. To date, the clinician has managed to integrate the ever-growing information into practice but in the last number of years, data are outstripping the capacity of a physician to process it. In addition, there is an increasing awareness of the richness of information that is embedded within imaging data, which extends beyond what the human eye can process and extract. Artificial intelligence and machine learning have rapidly transformed every aspect of our lives and are now being explored and implemented in a number of aspects of cardiovascular medicine. Machine Learning in Cardiovascular Medicine is one of the first textbooks to highlight the ever-expanding applications of machine and deep learning within cardiovascular medicine. In this book, the editors have compiled an excellent overview of the current applications of machine learning for clinical data analysis, as well as highlighted the recent advances in deep learning for cardiovascular image analysis. From traditional to state-of-the-art algorithms, the first few chapters set the technical foundation for understanding the inner workings of these algorithms as well as appreciating available metrics for the evaluation of their performance for a specific clinical task. The book then delves into current applications of machine learning: from its role in natural language processing to various imaging modalities such as CT, MRI, and Echocardiography. The editors have provided a tour de force go to reference for all those in the field. Importantly, the editors seek to also expose the many limitations in the space and also the ethical challenges that we will all be facing as we seek to implement and refine these tools in our clinical practice. To do so, they have assembled an incredible group of authors with expertise in every aspect of artificial intelligence and cardiovascular medicine. As Andrew Ng famously stated: “As leaders, it is incumbent on all of us to make sure we are building a world in which every individual has an opportunity to thrive. Understanding what AI can do and how it fits into your strategy is the beginning, not the end, of that process,” this book is a perfect fit to educate the clinical and research communities regarding current, and potential, future applications of artificial intelligence within cardiovascular medicine. Jonathon A. Leipsic, M.D., F.R.C.P.C., F.S.C.C.T.

# Introduction

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a topic for discussion within various medical domains, and especially within the cardiovascular community. The availability of large multidimensional datasets within medicine offers a framework for significant advances with the appropriate harnessing of AI. The integration of AI can occur throughout the continuum of medicine; from basic laboratory discovery to clinical application and healthcare delivery. Yet, integrating AI within medicine has been met with both excitement and skepticism. By understanding how AI works and developing an appreciation for both its limitations and strengths, clinicians can harness its power to streamline workflow and improve patient care. AI provides an opportunity to improve upon research methodologies, beyond what are currently available using traditional statistical approaches. Further, computers scientists and data analysts can provide solutions, but often lack easy access to clinical insight that may help focus their efforts. This textbook provides the platform to bring these two disciplines together. Machine Learning in Cardiovascular Medicine addresses the ever-expanding applications of AI, and specifically machine learning (ML), in healthcare and within cardiovascular medicine. AI was initially born out of the need to solve nonlinear and combinatorially complex tasks. Over time, AI has transformed innumerable aspects of human life; the development of augmented reality, autonomous driving, robotics, as well as sophisticated predictive modeling are just a few examples of how AI has sparked the current innovative climate within the industry sector. While the industrial applications of ML are nearly ubiquitous, its introduction into the medical field has been much more gradual. The landscape, however, is rapidly changing as a result of the availability of computational power as well as the creation of large repositories of datasets. The computer science and medical communities are increasingly streamlining efforts at harnessing the potential of ML in order to solve complex tasks and optimize day-to-day workflow in the healthcare sector. This book is focused on emphasizing ML for biomedical applications and aims at providing a comprehensive summary of the past and present of AI, basics of ML as well as clinical applications of ML within cardiovascular medicine for predictive analytics and precision medicine. Subhi J. Al'Aref, M.D., F.A.C.C. 

 

# Chapter 1: Technological advances within digital medicine

Ahmed M. Altibi[¹](#B9780128202739000014.xhtml#aff1), Subhi J. Al’Aref[²](#B9780128202739000014.xhtml#aff2), and Pegah Khosravi[³](#B9780128202739000014.xhtml#aff3)     ¹Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Harvard University, Boston, MA, United States     ²Division of Cardiology, Department of Medicine, University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences, Little Rock, AR, United States     ³Computational Oncology, Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, NY, United States  

## Abstract

Contemporary advances within digital medicine have gradually changed the landscape of healthcare and biomedical research. Over decades, significant innovations have been witnessed in various aspects of digital medicine, including mobile health (mHealth) applications, telehealth, wearable healthcare technologies, and robotics. mHealth technology utilized artificial intelligence to mitigate the two major barriers for cardiac health promotion: (i) global deficit of healthcare professionals and (ii) ever-growing cost of healthcare services. mHealth applications have been used in preventative, diagnostic, and therapeutic aspects of medicine. Smartphone-based EKG and “pocket” echocardiography are two pioneering examples in diagnostic cardiology. Wearable technologies rely on implemented sensors to monitor for an array of physiologic parameters, such as vital signs, cardiac electrical activity, and physical activity metrics (e.g., steps count and energy expenditure). Fitness trackers and smartwatches, the most popular and commercially available wearable devices, solely play preventative role via self-quantifying of health metrics. To the contrary, other wearables are enabled to deploy therapeutic interventions—such as the wearable cardioverter defibrillator which can provide a life-saving shock in cases of dysrhythmias. Finally, advances in robotics and robotic-assisted interventions (e.g., percutaneous coronary interventions, peripheral vascular interventions, and catheter-based ablation of arrhythmias) have enhanced procedural accuracy, improved quality of clinical outcomes, and minimized occupational hazards associated with interventional cardiology.

### Keywords

Artificial intelligence; Digital medicine; Fitness trackers; Mobile health (mHealth); Pocket echocardiography; Robotic technology; Smartwatches; Telemedicine; Wearable cardioverter defibrillator; Wearable sensors

## Introduction

Technological advances within digital medicine have been gradually changing the landscape of healthcare and biomedical research. Since William Withering utilized digitalis 250 years ago, from Foxglove plant, to treat “dropsy” (congestive heart failure) ( In this chapter, we provide an overview of the key advances in digital technologies impacting healthcare in cardiovascular medicine, including: (i) wearable healthcare technology, (ii) mobile health and telehealth, and (iii) robotic technology. A plethora of wearable technologies currently exists and can be broadly classified into diagnostic versus therapeutic devices. Diagnostic wearables rely on digitized data acquisition for monitoring (e.g., smartwatches and fitness trackers). On the other hand, therapeutic devices have instrumental components enabling them to intervene to prevent, mitigate, or treat certain medical conditions (e.g., wearable cardioverter defibrillators).  

## Wearable sensing devices

### Fitness trackers and smartwatches

#### Introduction

  With the recent technological revolution involving nanocomputers, AI, big data, wireless networks, and cellular networks, the past decade has witnessed an explosion in the utility of wearable optic sensors technologies worldwide (  

#### Devices and sensors

Fitness trackers and Smartwatches are equipped with a multitude of sensors (accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, altimeter, barometers, and GPS) that function to record fitness-related metrics such as movement acceleration, steps count, energy expenditure, and physical location for the individual ( In addition to accelerometers, some wearables utilize additional sensors to increase the accuracy of the device, such as gyroscopes, magnetometers, barometers, and altimeters. Gyroscope sensor, or angular rate sensor, functions via sensing the angular velocity (change in rotational angle per unit of time), and hence, provides information on both orientation and rotation ( Finally, photoplethysmogram (PPG) is a noninvasive optical sensing technology that utilizes an infrared light to detect any minor volumetric changes in blood of the peripheral circulation ( Ultimately, the quality of a wearable device depends on the accuracy of its sensors and the algorithms utilized to operate data collected from these sensors. This explains the increased focus in revolutionizing sensory technologies in healthcare wearable devices (  

#### Clinical applications

The ability of optical sensors to detect abnormal heart rhythms has been a topic of interest in healthcare. The Apple Heart Study was designed to evaluate the Apple Watch irregular rhythm notification’s ability to accurately identify atrial fibrillation (AF) – the most common clinically significant arrhythmia ([Fig. 1.1](#B9780128202739000014.xhtml#f0010)) ( In addition to diagnostic and therapeutic applications, wearable devices can be implemented to collect aggregated data as part of large-scale public health research studies (

#### How does the WCD function?

The WCD device consists of two main components—a garment and a monitor. The garment is worn under clothing and functions to detect arrhythmias and to deliver life-saving shock when an abnormal heart rhythm is detected—via four sensing and three defibrillating electrodes (  

#### What are the indications for WCD?

Thus far, WCDs are used as bridging/temporizing interventions rather than destination measures substituting for ICDs. Clinical indications for WCDs were initially coined by American Heart Association (AHA) science advisory in 2016. Later, further endorsement was publicized by other scientific bodies (e.g., Heart Rhythm Society) ( 

1.  • Bridging for interrupted ICD or “pending” ICD implant.
2.  • Following myocardial infarction (MI) or coronary revascularization—with severely reduced ejection fraction (EF) (<35%).
3.  • Following new diagnosis of nonischemic cardiomyopathy—with severely reduced EF (<35%).

ICD “interruption” refers to the state where an implanted ICD system is extracted for a compelling reason such as device infection or endocarditis—to achieve proper source control (  

#### Does the WCD technology save lives?

WCD therapy has been proven to be highly effective in terminating VT/VF rhythms when worn properly. Studies have shown the first-shock termination rate to be comparable with that for ICDs, ranging between 95% and 100% ( WCD has been shown to be highly efficient in terminating abnormal rhythms. However, many experts have raised concerns that the device is increasingly presumed to be the “de facto” standard of care in certain subsets of patients, despite the inconclusive evidence. The evidence to support an overall mortality benefit and cost-effectiveness is still limited. This becomes important knowing that leasing a LifeVest costs ≥ $3000 per month (  

## Mobile health in cardiovascular medicine

### Introduction

 Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death globally among all ethnic and racial groups and is responsible for one in every four deaths in the United States (<miss\_match refids="bib1" ref\_cout="1"/>A nationwide framework for surveillance of cardiovascular and chronic lung diseases, 2011; mHealth incorporates all medical services and public health activities enabled via mobile devices. It is estimated that there are more than 300,000 mobile health applications available in the market—the majority are not FDA approved. Strikingly, more than 600 of these commercially available smartphone applications are specifically designed to improve adherence to therapy ( In the era of miniaturization, great strides have also been made to revolutionize current diagnostic and imaging modalities by integrating AI systems in the vicinity of mobile health technologies. Smartphone-based electrocardiogram (EKG) and “pocket” echocardiography are two pioneering examples for this integration in diagnostic cardiology (  

### Smartphone-based electrocardiogram (EKG)

Over the past decade, mHealth technologies have witnessed a tremendous leap in the applicability of mHealth in the monitoring of chronic diseases ( The use of smartphones for cardiac rhythm monitoring is another leap for EKG development and utilization. Currently, there are two types of smartphone technologies used to detect and monitor heart rhythms: (i) PPG, and (ii) Single-lead platform technology ( Over time, this technology has progressed to the more promising “single-lead” smartphone-based EKG—first FDA-approved in 2012. Single-lead technology combines an external EKG sensor with a smartphone application to generate a one lead rhythm strip (  ![Figure 1.3 Kardia single-lead mobile EKG.A single-lead mobile EKG utilizes two metal electrodes to generate a bipolar lead electric signal when pressure is applied by the patient’s digits.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000014/main.assets/f01-03-9780128202739.jpg)

Figure 1.3 Kardia single-lead mobile EKG.A single-lead mobile EKG utilizes two metal electrodes to generate a bipolar lead electric signal when pressure is applied by the patient’s digits.

 AliveCor Kardia is currently the most clinically validated mobile-based EKG technology. Studies have shown AliveCor to be highly sensitive (98%) and specific (97%) in capturing abnormal heart rhythms, such as AF ( Interestingly, the world’s first six-lead smartphone-enabled EKG was pioneered by Kardia in 2019. This functions via incorporating an innovative third electrode to allow visibility into certain arrhythmias that were previously undetected with single-lead EKG ([Fig. 1.4](#B9780128202739000014.xhtml#f0025)). (<miss\_match refids="bib41" ref\_cout="1"/>  ![Figure 1.4 Kardia six-lead mobile EKG.The world’s first six-lead smartphone-enabled EKG was FDA approved in 2019. The device incorporates two electrodes on the top for fingers, and one on the bottom to contact the skin of the left leg. This Kardia EKG delivers leads I, II, III, aVL, aVR, and aVF.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000014/main.assets/f01-04-9780128202739.jpg)

Figure 1.4 Kardia six-lead mobile EKG.The world’s first six-lead smartphone-enabled EKG was FDA approved in 2019. The device incorporates two electrodes on the top for fingers, and one on the bottom to contact the skin of the left leg. This Kardia EKG delivers leads I, II, III, aVL, aVR, and aVF.

  

### Pocket-echocardiography

Echocardiography is the primary imaging modality to assess cardiac function and to diagnose a multitude of cardiac conditions. The fundamental concept of “portable” echocardiography goes back to the 1970s when the “ultrasonic” stethoscope first appeared (<miss\_match refids="bib107" ref\_cout="1"/> “Pocket” echocardiography machines are smartphone-sized devices that provide diagnostic quality 2D with or without color Doppler imaging in real-time ( The introduction of pocket echocardiography devices in clinical practice has raised questions over the diagnostic capacity of these devices when compared to the standard transthoracic echocardiography (sTTE) ( In view of the increased evidence to support the valuable diagnostic utility of pocket echocardiography, the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) released special recommendations for healthcare providers on the use of pocket-size imaging devices ( ![Figure 1.5 Philips Lumify pocket ultrasound.A pocket echocardiography device consisting of a broad-bandwidth ultrasound probe that performs image acquisition, it is attached via a USB-probe to a smartphone that functions to display and archive echocardiographic images.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000014/main.assets/f01-05-9780128202739.jpg)

Figure 1.5 Philips Lumify pocket ultrasound.A pocket echocardiography device consisting of a broad-bandwidth ultrasound probe that performs image acquisition, it is attached via a USB-probe to a smartphone that functions to display and archive echocardiographic images.

 

## Robotic technology in cardiology

Robotic technology has been used in medicine for several decades, primarily in surgical ( The past few years have witnessed advances in robotic technology within cardiovascular medicine; leading to a wider utilization in both investigative and therapeutic domains (  

### Robotics in PCI

When Andreas Gruntzig performed the first-in-human coronary angioplasty in 1977 in Zurich, Switzerland, the landscape of cardiovascular medicine was transformed forever ( ![Figure 1.6 The CorPath 200 Robotic PCI System.(Left) The operator sits in a remote radiation-shielded interventional cockpit to perform the procedure. A console joystick is used to advance, retract, and rotate the catheter. (Right) Articulating robotic arm translates operator’s commands into precise movements and manipulations of guidewires and balloon/stent catheters.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000014/main.assets/f01-06-9780128202739.jpg)

Figure 1.6 The CorPath 200 Robotic PCI System.(Left) The operator sits in a remote radiation-shielded interventional cockpit to perform the procedure. A console joystick is used to advance, retract, and rotate the catheter. (Right) Articulating robotic arm translates operator’s commands into precise movements and manipulations of guidewires and balloon/stent catheters.

However, technical hurdles remain to deem certain complex coronary lesions ineligible for robotic interventions (e.g., bifurcated coronary lesions, severely calcified lesions, and chronic total occlusions), hampering global implementation of robotics in catheterization laboratories (  

### Robotics in PVI

Similar to PCI, peripheral vascular interventions (PVIs) have also been associated with increased risk for hazardous radiation exposure and orthopedic injuries. In fact, PVIs had been associated with a significantly greater (1.4 folds) radiation risk for operator as compared to PCI. Currently, two robotic systems are FDA-approved for PVIs: (i) CorPath 200 system (Corindus Vascular Robotics, MA, USA), and (ii) Magellan System (Auris Surgical Robotics Inc., CA, USA). The RAPID (Robotic-Assisted Peripheral Intervention for Peripheral Artery Disease) trial was a prospective single-arm trial to assess the feasibility and safety of CorPath robotic technology in femoropopliteal PVIs (  ![Figure 1.7 Magellan Robotic System.Magellan Robotic system is used in the treatment of peripheral vascular disease and a multitude of endovascular procedures. The figure depicts experimental setup for the robotic catheter (A), console joystick used to control catheter (B), view of the force measurement platform (C and D), fluoroscopic imaging for guidance (E), and phases of the procedure (F).](IMAGES/B9780128202739000014/main.assets/f01-07-9780128202739.jpg)

Figure 1.7 Magellan Robotic System.Magellan Robotic system is used in the treatment of peripheral vascular disease and a multitude of endovascular procedures. The figure depicts experimental setup for the robotic catheter (A), console joystick used to control catheter (B), view of the force measurement platform (C and D), fluoroscopic imaging for guidance (E), and phases of the procedure (F).

  

### Robotics in electrophysiology

Catheter-based ablation has become one of the preferred treatment modalities for sustained arrhythmias (i.e., atrial fibrillation) (  

### Future perspectives

Contemporary robotic-assisted cardiovascular interventions have enhanced procedural accuracy/precision, improved quality of clinical outcomes, and minimized occupational hazards (i.e., radiation exposure). Future iterations for robotic-assisted devices should take into consideration the technical challenges associated with more complex scenarios (e.g., robotic PCI for bifurcated or severely calcified coronary lesions). Further studies assessing cost-effectiveness of robotics for coronary and peripheral interventions are also warranted.  

## Conclusions

Innovations in digital cardiovascular technology continue to evolve with recent and ongoing advances in robotic technology, wearable technology, mobile health, telehealth, and others. Digitization of cardiovascular care holds promise to revolutionize diagnostic and imaging modalities, improve precision of therapeutic interventions, and mitigate occupational hazards on healthcare workers. With the powerful AI methods and ML algorithms, digital health technologies have the potential to transform the practice of cardiology. To outdistance the rapidly burgeoning digital medicine, development of ethical and regulatory frameworks ensuring appropriate implementation becomes a necessity (Chapter 18).

# Chapter 2: An overview of artificial intelligence: basics and state-of-the-art algorithms

Qi Chang[¹](#B9780128202739000026.xhtml#aff1), Leon Axel[²](#B9780128202739000026.xhtml#aff2), and Dimitris N. Metaxas[¹](#B9780128202739000026.xhtml#aff1)     ¹Department of Computer Science, Rutgers The State University of New Jersey, Piscataway, NJ, United States     ²Department of Radiology, New York University School of Medicine, New York, NY, United States  

## Abstract

Recently, deep convolutional neural networks have been successfully applied to medical image tasks by taking advantage of a large amount of training data with gold standard annotations. The first part of this chapter introduces several basic, yet critical, concepts regarding machine learning and deep learning, which provide a foundation for understanding of both the development of these algorithms as well as appreciating their current cardiovascular applications. Thereafter, this chapter provides an overview of state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms including Bayesian, Decision Tree, Support Vector Machine, and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).

### Keywords

Classification; Convolutional neural network (CNN); Deep learning; Evaluation metric; Machine learning; Regression

## Introduction

In the early days of artificial intelligence (AI), the field rapidly tackled and solved problems that were intellectually difficult for humans but were relatively straightforward for computers— problems that could be described by a list of formal, mathematical rules ( The first part of Chapter 2 presents basic concepts within machine learning and AI. Specifically, this chapter will cover basic knowledge on the scope and approach of machine learning, with a focus on specific terms that are often misconstrued within the community. In the second part of this chapter, we will provide an overview of the state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms commonly used in academic research and the industry domain. By discussing various algorithms and approaches, we aim to provide the reader with a platform to navigate through different algorithms and select an approach that is best suited for a specific research or medical task.  

## Basic concepts

### What are AI, machine learning, and deep learning? And what is the difference between them?

 John McCarthy, widely recognized as one of the godfathers of AI, defined AI as “the science and engineering of making intelligent machines.” As the name suggests, AI can be loosely interpreted to refer to the incorporation of human intelligence into machines. In machine learning, machines can learn on their own without being explicitly programmed to do so. It also allows for self-modifications based on data in real-time scenarios. In other words, machine learning is the study of computer algorithms that allow computer programs to automatically improve through experience. Deep learning is one of many approaches to machine learning. Other approaches include decision tree learning, inductive logic programming, clustering, reinforcement learning, and Bayesian networks, among others. Deep learning was loosely inspired by the structure and function of the brain, namely the interconnection of many neurons. Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are algorithms that mimic the biological structure of the brain. In ANNs, there are “neurons” which have discrete layers and connections to other “neurons.” Each layer picks out a specific feature to learn, such as curves/edges in image recognition. It’s this layering that gives deep learning its name, depth is created by using multiple layers as opposed to a single layer. Analogies between human and machine learning (ML) naturally bring to mind the term “AI” and the obvious question: “What’s the difference between AI and machine learning?” There’s no clear consensus on this matter, but most (not all) agree that ML is one form of AI, and that AI is a far broader subject encompassing such areas as robotics, language processing, and computer vision systems. To increase the ambiguity even further, machine learning is being applied with increasing frequency to many of those aforementioned fields. As such, we can conclude by stating that the discipline of ML refers to a specific body of knowledge and an associated set of techniques. It’s fairly clear what is, and what isn’t, machine learning, whereas the same can’t always be said of artificial intelligence. Paraphrasing Tom Mitchell’s often-cited definition, a computer program is said to learn if its performance of a certain task, as measured by a computable score, improves with experience (  

### Types of machine learning

There are some variations in the available definitions of machine learning algorithms. However, such algorithms are commonly divided into categories according to their purpose, with the main categories being: 

1.  • Supervised Learning
2.      Supervised learning algorithms try to model relationships and dependencies between the target prediction output and the input features, such that one can predict the output values for new data based on those relationships learned from the previous datasets. Here, human experts act as teachers where one feeds the computer with training data containing the input/predictors while providing the correct answers (output); using which the computer should be able to learn underlying patterns. The process of learning from data, and subsequently using the acquired knowledge to inform future decisions, is extremely powerful. Indeed, machine learning is rapidly becoming the engine that powers the modern data-driven economy. Widely used supervised machine learning techniques include Classification and Regression algorithms.
3.  *   Classification: It is a Supervised Learning task where the output is having defined labels (discrete value). It can be either binary or multiclass classification. In binary classification, the model predicts either 0 or 1; yes or no, but in case of multiclass classification, a model predicts more than one class. As an example: Gmail classifies mail in more than one class like social, promotions, updates, and forums. It can either classify one class or multi classes per input or, as in image segmentation, classify classes over each pixel.
    *   Regression: It is a Supervised Learning task where the output has a continuous value. The goal here is to predict a value as close as possible to an actual output value, with subsequent model evaluation by calculating an error value. As expected, the smaller the error the greater is the accuracy of a regression model.
4.  • Unsupervised Learning
5.      In this paradigm, a machine learning model is trained with unlabeled data and without any explicit target output. The computer might be able to discover new knowledge regarding patterns within datasets that humans might have previously neglected. However, these models are particularly useful in cases where the human expert doesn’t know what to look for within the dataset. Such algorithms try to use techniques on the input data to mine for rules, detect patterns, summarize and group the data points, which ultimately helps derive meaningful insights while better describing the data to the end-users. Commonly used unsupervised learning algorithms include K-Means, Self-Organizing Maps (SOM), Autoencoder, and Generative adversarial network (GAN) (
6.  • Semi-supervised Learning
7.      In the previous two paradigms, either there were no labels for all observations or labels are present for all the observations. Semi-supervised learning falls in between these two methods. In many practical situations, the cost of performing expert labeling is significant. Hence, in the absence of output labels in the majority of observations, semi-supervised algorithms are best suited for model creation. These methods exploit the idea that even though the group memberships of the unlabeled data are unknown, such data carries important information about group parameters.
8.  • Reinforcement Learning
9.      Reinforcement learning aims at using observations gathered from the interaction with the computationally simulated environment to learn to perform actions that would maximize the reward or minimize the risk. Reinforcement learning algorithms (referred to as the agent) continuously learn from the environment in an iterative fashion ([Fig. 2.1](#B9780128202739000026.xhtml#f0010)). In the process, an agent learns from its experiences until it explores the full range of possible states. Reinforcement Learning allows machines and software agents to automatically determine the ideal behavior within a specific context, to maximize its performance. Simple reward feedback is required for the agent to learn its behavior; this is known as the reinforcement signal. Some applications of the reinforcement learning algorithms are computer played board games (Chess, Go), robotic hands, and self-driving cars.

Input state is observed by the agent. 2. Decision-making function is used to make the agent perform an action. 3. After the action is performed, the agent receives reward or reinforcement from the environment. 4. The state-action pair information about the reward is stored.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.assets/f02-01-9780128202739.jpg)
     
     Figure 2.1 Reinforcement learning training process.In order to produce intelligent programs (also called agents), reinforcement learning goes through the following steps: 1. Input state is observed by the agent. 2. Decision-making function is used to make the agent perform an action. 3. ## Machine learning in practice

In the following sections, we will mainly focus on supervised learning tasks, which constitute a majority of the current applications of machine learning, and are the most frequently used methods in the medical domain. A generalized outline for a step-by-step approach to machine learning has been depicted in [Fig. 2.2](#B9780128202739000026.xhtml#f0015). To have a better understanding of the training process, the following technical terms are explained.  

### Generalization in machine learning: overfitting versus underfitting

Generalization refers to how well the concepts learned by a machine learning model apply to specific examples not seen by the model when it was learning. The goal of a good machine learning model is to generalize well from the training data to any data from the problem domain. This allows for accurate predictions when applying the model to never seen scenarios/data/patients. The cause of poor performance in machine learning is usually a result of either overfitting or underfitting of the model on the data. Overfitting refers to a phenomenon when the model learns the training data. The model learns both, the information and random noise, in the training data to an extent that it negatively impacts the performance of the model on new data. This means that the noise or random fluctuations in the training data is picked up and learned as concepts by the model. This negatively impacts the model’s ability to generalize as noise being “random” is not replicated in the subsequent data. An overfitted model thus will not perform well on unseen new data. ![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.assets/f02-02-9780128202739.jpg)

Figure 2.2 A general outline for the creation of machine learning–based models within a cardiology workflow ( ![Figure 2.3 Underfitting versus Overfitting.When the model is underfitting, the training error is high, while the training error is close to the test error. On the other hand, an overfitting model fits the training data too well, where the training error is lower than the test error.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.assets/f02-03-9780128202739.jpg)

Figure 2.3 Underfitting versus Overfitting.When the model is underfitting, the training error is high, while the training error is close to the test error. On the other hand, an overfitting model fits the training data too well, where the training error is lower than the test error.

Underfitting refers to the phenomenon when the model can neither model the training data nor generalize to new data. An underfitted machine learning model is not a suitable model as a result of poor performance on training data. Underfitting is often not discussed as it is easy to detect given the availability of good performance metrics. The remedy is to try alternate machine learning algorithms. Nevertheless, it does provide a good contrast to the problem of overfitting. Both overfitting and underfitting can lead to poor model performance. But by far the most common problem in applied machine learning is overfitting. Overfitting is a significant issue since evaluation of model performance on training data is different from model performance on unseen data, which in principle is the reason for model creation to begin with ([Fig. 2.3](#B9780128202739000026.xhtml#f0020)).  

### Dataset split: training versus validation versus testing

Training dataset is the sample of data used to fit/train the model. The validation dataset is used to evaluate a given model. By using this data to fine-tune the model hyperparameters, one could identify the best-fit model. Hence the model occasionally sees this data, but never does it “Learn” from it. The test dataset provides the gold standard which is used to evaluate the trained model. It’s only used once a model is completely trained (using the train and validation sets). The test set is generally what is used to evaluate competing models. This is done to perform an independent validation of the model’s performance. In addition to this, several sampling can be used to prevent model overfitting. Cross-validation is one of the most commonly used resampling techniques wherein the entire dataset is split into two parts: train and test. Thereafter, the test set is kept aside, while a randomly chosen X% of the train dataset is used as the actual train set while the remaining (100-X)% is used as the validation set (X is a fixed number (typically 80%). The model is then iteratively trained and validated on these different sets. The use of cross-validation avoids overfitting, with K-fold cross-validation being the most popular method, where k-refers to the number of iterations.  

### Basic evaluation metrics

Evaluation metrics measure the performance of a particular model, which helps with optimal model selection in the testing phase. Different metrics may reflect the different goals when designing the task at hand. For instance, there are different metrics for the tasks of classification, regression, ranking, clustering, topic modeling, etc. Some metrics, such as precision-recall, are useful for multiple tasks. Classification, regression, and ranking are examples of supervised learning, which constitute a majority of machine learning applications. The choice of evaluation metrics heavily impacts the ability of the model to learn from the data. Hence, depending upon the characteristics of the dataset and the problem statement, the choice of an evaluation metric is made ([Table 2.1](#B9780128202739000026.xhtml#t0010)). 

1.  • Model Accuracy
2.      Model accuracy in terms of classification models can be defined as the ratio of correctly classified samples to the total number of samples:

    | *   
    *       Or for binary classification models, the accuracy can be defined as:
    *   <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Accuracy</mml:mtext><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mspace/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>TP</mml:mtext><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mtext>TN</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>TP</mml:mtext><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mtext>TN</mml:mtext><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mtext>FP</mml:mtext><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mtext>FN</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:math> ![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si2.png)
    *       The use of the accuracy metric is justified when the number of examples for each class is somewhat balanced. However, when the dataset is imbalanced, accuracy should not be relied upon as it can be misleading. In those cases, metrics such as precision, recall, or F1 should be used.
    *   • Precision and Recall
    *       In a classification task, the precision for a class is the number of true positives divided by the total number of elements “labeled by the model” as belonging to the positive class:

    *       Recall is defined as the number of true positives divided by the total number of elements that actually belong to the positive class:
    *   <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Recall</mml:mtext><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>TP</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>TP</mml:mtext><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mtext>FN</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:math> ![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si4.png)
    *       In simple terms, high precision means that an algorithm returned substantially more relevant results than irrelevant ones, while high recall means that an algorithm returned most of the relevant results.
    *   • F1 Score
    *       The F1 score is the harmonic mean of the precision and recall, where an F1 score reaches its best value at 1 and worst at 0.
    *   <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>F</mml:mtext><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Precision</mml:mtext><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mtext>Recall</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Precision</mml:mtext><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mtext>Recall</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:math> ![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si5.png)
    *       In segmentation tasks, F1 score is also referred to as the Dice Coefficient.
    *   • ROC Curve and AUC (Area under the ROC Curve)
    *       A receiver operating characteristic curve, or ROC curve, is a graphical plot that illustrates the diagnostic ability of a binary classifier system as its discrimination threshold is varied. The ROC curve is created by plotting the true positive rate (TPR) against the false positive rate (FPR) at various threshold settings. The ROC curve is a two-dimensional depiction of classifier performance. To compare classifiers, we may want to reduce ROC performance to a single scalar value representing an expected performance. A common method is to calculate the area under the ROC curve, abbreviated as AUC ([Fig. 2.4](#B9780128202739000026.xhtml#f0025)). An excellent model has AUC close to 1 which means it has good measure of separability. A poor model has AUC close to 0 which means it has a poor measure of separability. In fact, an AUC of zero means that a specific model is reciprocating the result: it is predicting 0s as 1s and 1s as 0s. Finally, when AUC is equal to 0.5, it means the model has no class separation capacity at all.

    ## State-of-the-art algorithms
    
    ### Bayesian machine learning
    
     Bayesian machine learning allows for the influence of prior knowledge and experience regarding the format and structure of a constructed model, independent of what the data tells us. This is especially useful when a particular dataset is too small to confidently train a particular model on probability theory. Bayes’ theorem describes the probability of an event, based on prior knowledge of conditions that might be related to the event. <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>P</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>A|B</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>P</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>B|A</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mtext>P</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>A</mml:mtext><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>P</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>B</mml:mtext><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:math> ![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si6.png)Here, P(A) and P(B) are independent probabilities of event A and B, respectively. P(A|B) means probability of observing A, given that event B has happened. In Bayesian machine learning, we use the Bayes’ theorem to infer model parameters (theta) from data (D): <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mtext>|</mml:mtext><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:math> ![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si7.png)<mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math>![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si8.png) is a term that generally cannot be computed, but since it is just a normalizing constant, it doesn’t matter that much. When comparing models, one is mainly interested in expressions containing theta, because <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math>![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si8.png) stays the same for each model. <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math>![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si9.png) is an estimation of model parameters based on expert opinion or previous experience. Most often, expert opinion is inconclusive and in the setting of ample data this expert opinion has minimal influence on model parameters. Inference should converge to probable theta as long as its not zero. <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math>![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si10.png) is called the likelihood of data given model parameters. The formula for likelihood is model-specific. Scientists often use likelihood for evaluation of models: a model that gives higher likelihood to real data is better. Finally, <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math>![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si11.png) is a probability distribution over model parameters obtained from prior beliefs and data.  
    
    ### Decision tree
    
    Decision Trees are a type of Supervised Machine Learning where the data is continuously split according to a certain parameter. The tree can be explained by two entities, namely decision nodes and leaves. The leaves are the decisions or the final outcomes. And the decision nodes are where the data is split. A single decision tree is often not as performant as linear regression, logistic regression, etc. However, by introducing random forests and boosting, it can result in dramatic improvements in prediction accuracy at the expense of some loss in interpretation. Among decision support tools, decision trees have several advantages. Decision trees ( 
    
    1.  • Are simple to understand and interpret. People can intuitively understand decision tree models after a brief explanation.
    2.  • Have value even with relatively smaller datasets. Important insights can be generated based on experts describing a situation (its alternatives, probabilities, and costs) and their preference for outcomes.
    3.  • Help determine worst, best, and expected values for different scenarios.
    4.  • Use a white box model, if a given result is provided by a model.
    5.  • Can be combined with other decision techniques.
    
     
    
    ### Decision tree versus random forest
    
    If there was a way to generate a very large number of trees, averaging out their solutions, then one would likely get an answer that is going to be very close to the true answer. Enter the random forest—a collection of decision trees with a single, aggregated result. Random forests are commonly reported as the most accurate learning algorithm. Random forests reduce the variance seen in decision trees by: 
    
    1.  • Using different samples for training,
    2.  • Specifying random feature subsets,
    3.  • Building and combining small (shallow) trees.
    
     
    
    ### Random forest versus boosting
    
    Like random forests, gradient boosting is a set of decision trees. The two main differences are: 
    
    1.  • How trees are built: random forests build each tree independently while gradient boosting builds one tree at a time. This additive model (ensemble) works in a forward, stagewise manner, introducing a weak learner to improve the shortcomings of existing weak learners.
    2.  • Combining results: random forests combine results at the end of the process (by averaging or “majority rules”), while gradient boosting combines results along the way.
    
     
    
    ### Regression
    
    Regression is based on a hypothesis that can be linear, quadratic, polynomial, nonlinear, etc. The hypothesis is a function based on some hidden parameters and input values. In the training phase, the hidden parameters are optimized while the input values are presented in the training. The process that does the optimization is the gradient descent algorithm. If one is using neural networks, then there is an additional need for a back-propagation algorithm to compute gradient at each layer. Once the hypothesis parameters are trained (when they gave least error during the training), then the same hypothesis with the trained parameters is used with new input values to predict outcomes that will again be real values.  
    
    ### Linear regression versus logistic regression
    
    1.  • In case of Linear Regression, the outcome is continuous while in the case of Logistic Regression the outcome is discrete (not continuous).
    2.  • Linear Regression is a regression algorithm for Machine Learning while Logistic Regression is a classification algorithm for machine learning.
    
     
    
    ### Support vector machine
    
    Support Vector Machine, abbreviated as SVM, can be used for both regression and classification tasks. The objective of the support vector machine algorithm is to find a hyperplane in an N-dimensional space that distinctly classifies the data points. To separate the two classes of data points, there are many possible hyperplanes that could be chosen. The objective is to find a plane that has the maximum margin, i.e., the maximum distance between data points of both classes. Maximizing the margin distance provides some reinforcement, so that future data points can be classified with more confidence. The loss function that helps maximize the margin is the hinge loss: <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace/><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi>max</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mi>w</mml:mi><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mspace/><mml:msub><mml:mi>w</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math> ![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si12.png)where t the target label, <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>w</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math>![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si13.png)and <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>w</mml:mi><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math>![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si14.png) the model parameters.   
    
    ## Deep learning and neural networks
    
    ### Why neural networks work?
    
     Since the inception of deep learning, few ideas have generated as much impact as convolutional neural networks (CNNs or ConvNets). Inspired by the experiments of David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel on the visual cortex ( The Neural Network layers are inspired by the basic structure of the brain. The computational unit of the brain is a neuron. Approximately 86 billion neurons can be found in the human nervous system, and they are connected with approximately 10^(14)–10^(15) synapses ( ![Figure 2.5 The basic structure of a neuron versus the structure of a neural network.  Image reproduced with permission from https://thenounproject.com/term/neuron/214105/.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.assets/f02-05-9780128202739.jpg)
    
    Figure 2.5 The basic structure of a neuron versus the structure of a neural network.   
    Image reproduced with permission from [https://thenounproject.com/term/neuron/214105/](https://thenounproject.com/term/neuron/214105/).
    
     
    
    ### Typical deep learning pipeline
    
    The training of a deep learning task is similar to that of ML tasks, like classification, segmentation, or clustering. All pipeline steps are built upon a general framework, for instance, Tensorflow ( In the data preprocessing stage, the input data are collected and cleaned, while at this stage the ground truth is also defined and the quality of the data is validated. During the training stage, the prepared images and labels (if exist) are sent into a predefined convolutional neural network. Based on the output of the network, it calculates the loss function while the backpropagation will send the loss back to achieve optimal weights for each of the network layers. One Epoch is when an entire dataset is passed forward and backward through the neural network only once. Iterations are the number of batches needed to complete one epoch. During the testing stage, the platform should verify the test dataset, and decide which model is the best.  
    
    ### Neural network versus convolutional neural network
    
    Convolutional Neural Networks are very similar to ordinary Neural Networks: they are made up of neurons that have learnable weights and biases. Each neuron receives some input, performs a dot product, and optionally follows it with a nonlinearity. The whole network still expresses a single differentiable score function: from the raw image pixels on one end to class scores at the other end. In addition, CNNs still have a loss function (e.g., SVM/Softmax) on the last (fully connected) layer, and all the tips/tricks that have been developed for learning regular Neural Networks still apply. Convolutional Neural Network architectures make the explicit assumption that the inputs are images, which allows us to encode certain properties into the architecture. Such a step allows efficient implementation of the forward function, as a result of vastly reduced parameters in the network.   
    
    ### Convolutional neural network layers
    
    1.  • Convolutional Layer
    2.      The convolutional (conv) layer is the core building block of a Convolutional Network (ConvNet) that does most of the computational heavy lifting. The conv layer’s parameters consist of a set of learnable filters. Every filter is spatially small (in terms of width and height) but extends through the full depth of the input volume. For example, a typical filter on a first layer of a ConvNet might have a size of 5 × 5 × 3 (i.e., 5-pixel width and height, and 3 because images have a depth of 3, which are the color channels). During the forward pass, one slides (more precisely, convolves) each filter across the width and height of the input volume and computes dot products between the entries of the filter and the input at any position. As one slides the filter over the width and height of the input volume, a 2-dimensional activation map is produced that gives the responses of that filter at every spatial position. Intuitively, the network will learn filters that activate when they see some type of visual feature such as an edge of some orientation or a blotch of some color on the first layer, or eventually entire honeycomb or wheellike patterns on higher layers of the network. Now, there will be an entire set of filters in each conv layer (e.g., 12 filters), and each of them will produce a separate two-dimensional activation map. Finally, these activation maps are stacked along the depth dimension thereby producing the output volume.
    3.  • Pooling Layer
    4.      It is common to periodically insert a pooling layer in-between successive conv layers in a ConvNet architecture. Its function is to progressively reduce the spatial size of the representation to reduce the number of parameters and computation in the network, and hence to also control for overfitting. The Pooling Layer operates independently on every depth slice of the input and resizes it spatially, using the MAX operation. The most common form is a pooling layer with filters of size 2 × 2 applied with a stride of 2 downsamples every depth slice in the input, and by 2 along both width and height, discarding 75% of the activations. Every MAX operation would, in this scenario, be taking a max over 4 numbers (little 2 × 2 region in some depth slice).
    5.  • Normalization Layer
    6.      Many types of normalization layers have been proposed for use in ConvNet architectures, sometimes with the intention of implementing inhibition schemes observed in the biological brain.
    7.  • Fully connected layer
    8.      Neurons in a fully connected layer have full connections to all activations in the previous layer, as seen in regular neural networks. Their activations can hence be computed with a matrix multiplication followed by a bias offset.
    9.  • Activation layer
    10.      Every activation function (or nonlinearity) takes a single number and performs a certain fixed mathematical operation on it. There are several activation functions one may encounter in practice:
    11.  *   Sigmoid Activation Layer: It takes a real-valued number and “squashes” it into a range between 0 and 1. In particular, large negative numbers become 0 and large positive numbers become 1. The mathematical form is: <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>/</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math>![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si15.png).
         *   Tanh Activation Layer: It squashes a real-valued number to the range \[-1, 1\]. Like the sigmoid neuron, its activations saturate, but unlike the sigmoid neuron its output is zero-centered. Therefore, in practice the tanh nonlinearity is always preferred to the sigmoid nonlinearity. The mathematical form is: <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>tanh</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math>![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si16.png).
         *   ReLU Activation Layer: The Rectified Linear Unit has become very popular in the last few years. It computes the function <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>max</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math>![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si17.png). In other words, the activation is simply thresholded at zero.
         *   Leaky ReLU Activation Layer: Instead of the function being zero when x < 0, a leaky ReLU will instead have a small negative slope (of 0.01, or so). That is, the function computes <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math>![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si18.png), where <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:math>![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000026/main.stripin/si19.png) is a small constant.
    
     
    
    ### Convolutional neural network architectures
    
    The machine learning community has persisted in its effort at innovating a variety of neural network layers to achieve higher performance. Different settings and combination of layers significantly affect accuracy and performance. In this section, we discuss how these are commonly stacked together to form entire ConvNets. 
    
    1.  • LeNet 
    2.      The first successful applications of Convolutional Networks were developed by Yann LeCun in the 1990s. Of these, the best known is the LeNet architecture that was used to read zip codes, digits, etc. 
    3.  • AlexNet 
    4.      The first work that popularized Convolutional Networks in Computer Vision was the AlexNet, developed by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoff Hinton. The AlexNet was submitted to the ImageNet ILSVRC challenge in 2012 and significantly outperformed the second runner-up (top five error of 16% compared to the runner-up with 26% error). AlexNet had a very similar architecture to LeNet, but was deeper, bigger, and featured Convolutional Layers stacked on top of each other (previously it was common to only have a single Conv layer always immediately followed by a POOL layer). 
    5.  • ZF Net 
    6.      The ILSVRC 2013 winner was a Convolutional Network from Matthew Zeiler and Rob Fergus. It became known as the ZFNet (short for Zeiler and Fergus Net). It was an improvement on AlexNet by tweaking the architecture hyperparameters, in particular by expanding the size of the middle convolutional layers and making the stride and filter size on the first layer smaller. 
    7.   
    8.  • GoogLeNet 
    9.      The ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) 2014 winner was a Convolutional Network from Szegedy et al. from Google. Its main contribution was the development of an Inception Module that dramatically reduced the number of parameters in the network (4M, compared to AlexNet with 60M). Additionally, it used Average Pooling instead of Fully Connected layers at the top of the ConvNet, eliminating a large amount of parameters that do not seem to matter much. There are also several follow-up versions to the GoogLeNet, most recently Inception-v4. 
    10.  • VGGNet 
    11.      The runner-up in ILSVRC 2014 was the network from Karen Simonyan and Andrew Zisserman that became known as the VGGNet. Its main contribution was in showing that the depth of the network is a critical component of good performance. Their best network contained 16 CONV/FC layers and, appealingly, featured an extremely homogeneous architecture that only performed 3 × 3 convolutions and 2 × 2 pooling from the beginning to the end. Their pretrained model is available for plug and play use in Caffe. A downside of the VGGNet is that it is more expensive to evaluate and uses a lot more memory and parameters (140M). Most of these parameters are in the first fully connected layer, and it was since found that these FC layers can be removed with no performance downgrade, significantly reducing the number of necessary parameters. 
    12.  • ResNet 
    13.      Residual Network developed by (

         ## Conclusions
         
         The application of traditional and advanced machine learning methods to solve cardiovascular tasks has witnessed significant strides over the past few years. This chapter covers the basic knowledge on the scope and approach of machine learning algorithms, specifically the utilization of convolutional neural networks to medical image tasks. Deep learning promises to revolutionize cardiovascular image analysis, and current efforts are focused at providing tools for interpretation of neural network output, as well as optimization for clinical applications.

    # Chapter 3: Machine learning for predictive analytics
    
    Sehj Kashyap, Kristin M. Corey, Aman Kansal, and Mark Sendak     Duke Institute for Health Innovation, Durham, NC, United States  
    
    ## Abstract
    
    Advances in the field of machine learning are enabling the development of new predictive models in the field of cardiovascular medicine. In this chapter, we cover how predictive machine learning models are developed, their recent use-cases in cardiovascular medicine, and limitations for their expanded use in healthcare. Predictive modeling has long been used in medicine, but recently, machine learning methods offer the ability to learn patterns in large and heterogeneous health data for improved predictive modeling. In addition to describing the general methods by which machine learning models are developed, we share their recent applications in electrophysiology, interventional cardiology, heart failure, and preventive cardiovascular care. We conclude with a discussion about issues regarding data quality, generalizability, bias, and interpretability, and how these influence model development and clinical integration.
    
    ### Keywords
    
    Artificial intelligence; Cardiovascular medicine; Clinical decision support; Machine learning; Predictive models

    ## Introduction
    
    Predictive models have long been used in medicine for clinical tasks such as risk-stratification, patient prognostication, and treatment planning. The Framingham risk score, ASCVD risk score, and NEWS score are examples of predictive models that use logistic regression and scoring-based methods, and have already been integrated into routine clinical care (  What is unique about machine learning methods for predictive analytics as compared to traditional methods like statistical modeling and rules-based systems? It is important to acknowledge that there is no well-defined line separating machine learning methods from statistical and rule-based methods (  
    
    ## Developing a predictive model
    
    In this section, we highlight four key steps in developing ML predictive models: (1) defining the opportunity, (2) creating the dataset, (3) developing the model, and (4) evaluating model performance. For more detailed outlines for developing machine learning models, we refer readers to the following reviews (  
    
    ### Defining the opportunity
    
    The first critical step in developing a machine learning model is to clarify whether there is an opportunity for the intended clinical benefit. As pointed out by several researchers (   
    
    Table 3.1
    
    A summary of key questions that should be asked at the outset of model development to clarify the opportunity of a model-integrated workflow.
    
      
    | Defining the opportunity |
    | --- |
    | 
    
    • What action(s) will be triggered or changed as a result of the model prediction? Can these actions be taken?
    
    • How much lead time is needed between the prediction time and the window of time over which an outcome is predicted to occur?
    
    • How will workflows be affected or need to change to utilize the model predictions?
    
    • Will the benefits realized exceed the costs of taking action?
    
     |
    
    Often, a predictive model triggers an action or a series of actions to realize these benefit(s). Identifying what action would be triggered or if those actions could be taken is the first important step. The second step is to determine the minimum lead time required between when the prediction is made and when the outcome occurs to take the identified steps. The range for clinically useful lead times can vary between close to zero, to months or years. For example, predicting an incident episode of atrial fibrillation right before onset could still be useful as an intervention can be rapidly deployed. Third, it is important to consider how workflows may be affected by clinical and operational constraints; what can be done to make taking the desired action as easy as possible in the real-world setting? Finally, will the benefits be realized in the true positive cases identified by the model exceed the costs of taking action on the false-positive cases? How does the model performance compare with and without deployment of the model? If a model predicts cardiac decompensation and triggers intensive care unit (ICU) admission, is the escalation of care for that particular patient the most beneficial use of an ICU bed? These are some of the considerations that need to be thought through before beginning model development work and several authors have proposed doing utility assessments before and during model development (  
    
    ### Creating the dataset
    
    After the opportunity has been defined, a dataset is prepared to train a model. Health data can come in many forms or modalities, for example, clinical registry data, medical device data, imaging data, and lab results data ( Besides mathematically representing health data, it is also useful to organize the data onto a patient timeline. This has been proposed by multiple authors and most recently used in the paper by Rajkomar et al. for scalable deep learning in health ( Once the data have been gathered, organized, and represented mathematically, data quality checks must be done. These checks can reveal unusual entries in the data that need to be corrected or discarded before model training ( An important but subtle point is the validity of the labels. Labels are the clinical endpoints that a model is built to predict. If each patient record is converted into a mathematically represented input, the label is the output that the model must learn to map to from the input. If a model is built to detect hyperkalemia from electrocardiograph (ECG) recordings, the input is the ECG recordings and the label is whether that particular ECG reading was taken from a patient with hyperkalemia or not. In clinical medicine, nearly all endpoints to be predicted may have an element of subjective interpretation. For example, cardiac decompensation may be hard to define ( ![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000038/main.assets/f03-01-9780128202739.jpg)
    
    Figure 3.1 Patient timeline view of health data.Patient health data can be organized into a timeline. Different health data streams may update at different times on the timeline (as indicated by the gray circles). When developing a predictive model, it is important to identify what is the observation window, the prediction time, and the prediction window. Only data within the observation window (before the prediction) should be used to train a model. Accidently including data from beyond the prediction time can cause information leakage and inappropriately overoptimistic model performance on prediction tasks.   
    The figure adapted from Rajkomar, A. et al. (2018b). Ensuring fairness in machine learning to advance health equity, Annals of Internal Medicine, 169(12), pp. 866–872. doi: 10.7326/M18-1990;   
    
    ### Developing a model
    
    Developing a model entails selecting a model type and learning the model parameters. Many model types exist and often many models are developed and evaluated before selecting a model to implement. One of the first steps is usually understanding whether the model will be predicting a real number (a regression problem) or probability of the patient data belonging to a certain class (a classification problem). Several different models are available to handle these problems. Further, the selection of a model for implementation depends on various considerations ( In learning the model parameters, the key goal is to learn, from the data, a mathematical function that maps inputs to outputs and can generalize to unseen inputs in the future. To enable this, the data are divided into two main parts: a development set and a validation set. The validation set is intended to act as unseen data; therefore, it should not be explored in any way until the final model has been selected and trained. The development set on the other hand is where model exploration can occur; different models can be tried, trained, and compared to select the best performing models. To ensure that the development data are not simply memorized, the development set is further subdivided into a training and tuning set. The model is trained on the training set and simultaneously, as the model parameters are being learned, the tuning set is used to check if the performance is generalizable to the patient population being studied. Model generalizability is directly linked to the clinical usability of these models. A model that does not generalize well is seldom of any use because, as powerful as these models are at recognizing patterns, the model would have only “memorized” the presented datapoints but would not have “learned” the actual problem at hand. Some of the most popular sampling techniques for model evaluation include K-Fold, Leave-one-out, and others. Different parameters and models can be tested for performance using the development set, but the validation set can only be tested once. The way in which development and validation splits are made can also be important. Ken et al. and others have found that splits on patients and time can improve the robustness of fitted models to nonstationarity of health data (  
    
    ### Evaluating model performance
    
    Once a model has been learned, its performance is evaluated. The most common metric on which a model is evaluated is its ability to discriminate between patients who have an outcome and patients who do not. Discrimination performance is measured by metrics such as the area under the receiver operating curve (AUROC), which summarizes discriminative performance across thresholds, and area under the precision-recall curve, sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score. No one metric is considered sufficient for evaluating a model; for example, the AUROC has limitations both in interpretation and its equal weighting of false positives and false negatives. Furthermore, the results of a prediction model often trigger binary choices, and the selection of a threshold and performance of a model at a clinical threshold is important to examine. In addition, most of the clinical datasets have a class imbalance, that is, the number of examples of one class is far more in number than the other class or classes. In this instance, it is important to implement techniques such as undersampling or oversampling before training a model. Further, depending upon these attributes of a dataset, the choice of which performance parameter to look at while evaluating a model performance becomes very important as well. For example, a hypothetical dataset with two classes may have the number of examples for each class in the ratio of 99:1. A model trained and evaluated based on “classification accuracy” could be misleading as most of the time the goal to develop a model that is good at predicting the outcome for the minority class. For such datasets, the metrics should be carefully chosen, for example, the choice of Mathew’s correlation coefficient might have been a better evaluation metric in the above-stated problem. ![Figure 3.2 Data representation and model development.This figure shows the data preparation and model development phase of predictive model development. Health data are first represented mathematically, each ECG is represented as a fixed-length vector of length 3000. As there are 5920 ECGs in this example, the input is a matrix of 5920 × 3000. Each ECG has a label indicating whether it belongs to a patient with hyperkalemia or not. This data is then split into the development and validation set. The development set is used to train a model by being further split into a training and tuning set. The validation set is used for evaluating the final model that is performant in the development set; it gives an estimate of the model's performance on unseen data. The process of validation, as well as the test set, may be repeated with different data splits to get confidence intervals for the performance metrics.  ECG example images from Galloway, C. D. et al.
