    Another set of metrics tests the calibration of the trained model: how accurate are the estimated probability outputs by the model? If cases are prioritized by predicted probabilities, it is important to ensure that the probabilities correlate strongly to outcome incidence rates. Beyond the above metrics, other evaluations stress-test the reliability of the model: robustness checks, fragility checks, and differential performance ( Model evaluations are iterative and may depend on the context in which they are deployed. Furthermore, ongoing monitoring after integrating the model into clinical workflow is important for ensuring continued performance and safety. Changes in the data generating process may negatively affect the model performance and corrective steps like model retraining may need to be taken periodically (  
    
    ## Machine learning applications in cardiovascular medicine
    
    The applications of machine learning in cardiology span across a diverse set of specialties and tasks ([Fig. 3.3](#B9780128202739000038.xhtml#f0020)). Although cardiology has made significant strides in assessing individual patient risk and establishing evidence-directed guidelines, there is still tremendous opportunity for machine learning to improve both patient outcomes and quality of life. In this section, we highlight recent innovations integrating machine learning across four subspecialties within cardiology: preventive care, heart failure, interventional cardiology, and electrophysiology.  
    
    ### Preventive care
    
    Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality. Multiple CVD risk prediction tools have been constructed ( ![Figure 3.3 Examples of predictive modeling in cardiovascular medicine.Predictive models in cardiovascular medicine have been developed using hundreds to millions of data points and techniques spanning traditional statistical modeling to deep learning approaches. Traditional risk calculators entail significant prespecification of the model structure. Machine learning approaches enable empirical learning of the structure and parameters of functions through a minimally guided learning process. Deep neural networks and other deep learning models have significantly more trainable parameters than other ML approaches like random forests and ensemble methods. Generative adversarial networks: Neural networks that learn everything from data with no human input. These networks learn complex statistical patterns in the data that can be used to generate new synthetic data points that look like real data. Convolutional neural networks: Neural networks that learn directly from raw images, which allows for the discovery of complex and nuanced relationships not known beforehand. Random forests: A collection of “if-then-else” statements learned from data; allows for nonlinear variable interactions to be automatically discovered. Regression analysis: A statistical model that assumes a specified relationship between the dependent and independent variables. Popular choices include linear and logistic regression models. Human decision making: Decisions that are made without formal analyses of data, such as wisdom, experience, intuition, and heuristics. Abbreviations: ML, machine learning.  This figure is adapted from and the following definitions of prototypical algorithms are laid out from Rajkomar, A., Dean, J., & Kohane, I. (2019) Machine learning in medicine, New England Journal of Medicine, pp. 1347–1358. doi: 10.1056/NEJMra1814259.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000038/main.assets/f03-03-9780128202739.jpg)
    
    Figure 3.3 Examples of predictive modeling in cardiovascular medicine.Predictive models in cardiovascular medicine have been developed using hundreds to millions of data points and techniques spanning traditional statistical modeling to deep learning approaches. Traditional risk calculators entail significant prespecification of the model structure. Machine learning approaches enable empirical learning of the structure and parameters of functions through a minimally guided learning process. Deep neural networks and other deep learning models have significantly more trainable parameters than other ML approaches like random forests and ensemble methods. Generative adversarial networks: Neural networks that learn everything from data with no human input. These networks learn complex statistical patterns in the data that can be used to generate new synthetic data points that look like real data. Convolutional neural networks: Neural networks that learn directly from raw images, which allows for the discovery of complex and nuanced relationships not known beforehand. Random forests: A collection of “if-then-else” statements learned from data; allows for nonlinear variable interactions to be automatically discovered. Regression analysis: A statistical model that assumes a specified relationship between the dependent and independent variables. Popular choices include linear and logistic regression models. Human decision making: Decisions that are made without formal analyses of data, such as wisdom, experience, intuition, and heuristics. Abbreviations: ML, machine learning.   
    This figure is adapted from and the following definitions of prototypical algorithms are laid out from Rajkomar, A., Dean, J., & Kohane, I. (2019) Machine learning in medicine, New England Journal of Medicine, pp. 1347–1358. doi: 10.1056/NEJMra1814259.
    
    Weng et al. used electronic health record data of 370,000 patients receiving care in the United Kingdom to build machine learning models for predicting incident CVD ( Additional studies have supplemented the clinical data with biological data. Halim et al. investigated which of 53 previously reported protein biomarkers were most predictive of CVD ( Another application of machine learning in the detection of CAD has been in aiding selection of patients for noninvasive diagnostic imaging. Al’Aref et al. explored whether a machine learning model can improve the estimation of a patient’s pretest probability for obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD) and therefore increase the diagnostic yield of noninvasive imaging modalities like coronary computed tomography angiography (  
    
    ### Heart failure
    
    In recent years, machine learning has been leveraged to better diagnose and prognose heart failure (HF). Choi et al. explored whether the use of deep learning to model temporal relations among events in EHRs could improve the prediction of incident diagnosis of HF ( Beyond diagnosis, Mortazavi et al. and Frizzel et al. studied whether machine learning models could be used to accurately prognosticate HF-related sequelae in HF patients, specifically HF-related and all-cause readmissions (  
    
    ### Interventional cardiology
    
    Machine learning in interventional cardiology (IC) has been limited thus far and has been largely focused on assessing the risk of complications and outcomes following procedures ( An area of IC that has attracted increasing attention is the diagnosis and management of cardiogenic shock (CS). CS is a state of cellular and tissue hypoxia due to cardiac dysfunction. The causes of CS are diverse and include myocardial infarction, postoperative low cardiac output syndrome, and decompensated chronic HF ( Future research applying machine learning to CS is attractive for multiple reasons. First, mortality is high and outcomes have not appreciably changed. CS entails a state of rapid decline and anticipating CS is difficult and not well studied. Second, current clinical assessment often integrates data across multiple datasets including EHR, continuous hemodynamics, angiography, and imaging that can often be difficult even for the most seasoned clinicians. Finally, with improved diagnosis and management, it will be important to design workflows that maximize efficiency and enhance communication among interdisciplinary teams.  
    
    ### Electrophysiology
    
    Machine learning has been instrumental in advancing the interpretation of ECGs. Precise classification of ECGs is crucial in detecting life-threatening arrhythmias and electrolyte imbalances. Recent work has focused on developing algorithms for feature extraction and ECG classification using wavelet transform methods ( In another example, Attia et al. sought to develop an algorithm for identifying patients with atrial fibrillation from normal sinus rhythm ECG strips. Atrial fibrillation is common, underdiagnosed, and associated with an increased risk of stroke and mortality ( In addition to arrhythmia detection, recent work has also been focused on developing deep learning models to screen for life-threatening electrolyte abnormalities from ECG. A study by Galloway et al. used a deep CNN to detect hyperkalemia from ECGs of patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Hyperkalemia, especially in this patient population, can be life-threatening and screening is severely underperformed (  
    
    ## Challenges and opportunities
    
    Despite the potential impact machine learning may have on the field of cardiovascular medicine, there remain important challenges and opportunities to build and implement these types of models into everyday practice (  
    
    ### Data quality
    
    A model is only as good as the data from which it is derived. Data quality can be defined in terms of breadth, completeness, conformance, and plausibility and can drive a large portion of the quality of the model itself ( Apart from having the type of data needed for a prediction task, data quality also extends to the type of features engineered for a specific task. In developing HF prediction models, Choi et al. used EHR features such as orders, medications, and Common Procedural Terminology codes along with their corresponding timestamps to incorporate temporality into the development of the model ( Additionally, inadequate outcome prevalence can compromise supervised model development just as much as inadequate input features. Unfortunately, it is challenging to ascertain the amount of data required to train a performant model before developing and evaluating machine learning models. Models trained on data that lack appropriate amounts of the outcome prevalence or labeled events may experience overfitting, causing underestimation of risk in low-risk populations and overestimation of risk in high-risk populations (  
    
    ### Generalizability
    
    Generalizability has been a challenge in model dissemination and it is important for end-users to understand appropriate scenarios where models should and should not be used ( Apart from the challenge of demonstrating model generalizability to external sites, models are rarely validated over different time periods. The majority of model validation techniques perform validation of models using a held-out test set that is randomly selected from the source dataset. Very rarely are models tested on data outside the window time frame of the data source cohort due to difficulties in obtaining additional data. One way to estimate a model’s performance over time is by holding-out a subset of data that belongs to the most recent time in the data period as a validation set. [Fig. 3.4](#B9780128202739000038.xhtml#f0025) demonstrates a type of temporal validation where prediction trends are displayed over time on a held-out validation set of the most recent data. These are then compared to trends of the actual outcomes within the same dataset ( ![Figure 3.4 Assessing temporal stability of predictive model.January 2014–September 2016 shows model predicted complication rates of training data and October 2016–January 2017 displays projected complication rates based on nonrandom, an out-of-sample test set from a different time period. This is an example of an analysis displaying temporal stability.  The figure is originally published in Corey, K. M. et al. (2018). Development and validation of machine learning models to identify high-risk surgical patients using automatically curated electronic health record data (Pythia): A retrospective, single-site study, PLoS Medicine, 15(11). doi: 10.1371/journal.pmed.1002701.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000038/main.assets/f03-04-9780128202739.jpg)
    
    Figure 3.4 Assessing temporal stability of predictive model.January 2014–September 2016 shows model predicted complication rates of training data and October 2016–January 2017 displays projected complication rates based on nonrandom, an out-of-sample test set from a different time period. This is an example of an analysis displaying temporal stability.   
    The figure is originally published in Corey, K. M. et al. (2018). Development and validation of machine learning models to identify high-risk surgical patients using automatically curated electronic health record data (Pythia): A retrospective, single-site study, PLoS Medicine, 15(11). doi: 10.1371/journal.pmed.1002701.
    
    Furthermore, models have been shown to exhibit calibration drift over time. Davis et al. demonstrated that despite proper model calibration, over time calibration declined causing overpredicted risk. These drifts can be due to changing disease prevalence or phenotype as well as changes in systematic data capture (  
    
    ### Bias
    
    Eloquently stated by Rajkomar et al. “All human activity is marred by unwanted and unconscious bias” ( Data collection biases come from an overrepresentation of a certain population within the data. Unbalanced training cohorts can lead to algorithmic biases when models are used on populations that are underrepresented in the training data. For example, Tomasev et al. developed a model to predict acute kidney injury using patients from the US Department of Veterans Affairs Healthcare system, where 6.38% of the population were female (  
    
    ### Interpretability
    
    As machine learning in healthcare continues to grow, the role of model interpretability is evolving. Often called as the “black box,” machine learning algorithms (classically deep learning) have been criticized for their lack of “explain-ability” in their decision-making process. Some see a lack of model interpretability as a safety concern (  
    
    ## Conclusions
    
    In this chapter, we have covered methods for developing machine learning models for prediction, their applications in cardiovascular methods, and the main challenges and opportunities for their expanded use. As is evident from the examples shared, machine learning methods offer applications to an array of existing and new problems in cardiovascular medicine. These methods could significantly improve prediction and prognosis as well as offer new methods for diagnosis. However, the vast majority of models that have been described in the literature have not been implemented into clinical practice let alone become integrated into routine clinical practice. No one pathway exists for translating machine learning models into healthcare delivery (

    # Chapter 4: Deep learning for biomedical applications
    
    Jessica De Freitas[¹](#B978012820273900004X.xhtml#aff1)^,[²](#B978012820273900004X.xhtml#aff2), Benjamin S. Glicksberg[¹](#B978012820273900004X.xhtml#aff1)^,[²](#B978012820273900004X.xhtml#aff2), Kipp W. Johnson[²](#B978012820273900004X.xhtml#aff2), and Riccardo Miotto[¹](#B978012820273900004X.xhtml#aff1)^,[²](#B978012820273900004X.xhtml#aff2)     ¹Hasso Plattner Institute for Digital Health at Mount Sinai, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, United States     ²Department of Genetics and Genomic Sciences, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, United States  
    
    ## Abstract
    
    The types of data most commonly used for machine learning in biomedical research, including electronic health records, imaging, -omics, sensor data, and medical text, are complex, heterogeneous, poorly annotated, and generally unstructured. However, gaining knowledge and actionable insights from all these data sources is a key challenge in implementing personalized medicine and next-generation healthcare. Deep learning, which describes a class of machine learning algorithms based on neural networks, provides effective opportunities to model, represent, and learn from such complex and heterogeneous sources. Here, we review how this paradigm has already affected healthcare, we note limitations and needs for improved methods and applications, and we discuss the challenges to implement and deploy augmented human intelligence based on deep learning in the clinical domain.
    
    ### Keywords
    
    Augmented human intelligence; Biomedical applications; Biomedical informatics; Deep learning; Digital health; Electronic health records; Genomics; Health monitoring; Neural networks; Personalized healthcare

    ## Introduction
    
    Healthcare is approaching a new era where clinical decisions and patient behaviors will be influenced by the analysis of large quantities of biomedical data. On one side, physicians are capturing the status of their treated patients, their thoughts, orders, and outcomes in electronic health records (EHRs), -omics biobanks, and images. On the other side, patients are becoming more aware of the importance of prevention and keeping continuous track of their health status using wearable devices and preventative visits. Advances in machine learning (ML) are then taking advantage of this data in an attempt to supplement clinical medicine. However, there are many challenges in making full use of biomedical data, owing to their high-dimensionality, heterogeneity, temporal dependency, sparsity, and irregularity ( A common approach in biomedical research is to have a domain expert specifying the phenotypes to use in an ad hoc manner. However, the supervised definition of the feature space scales poorly and misses the opportunity to discover novel patterns. Alternatively, representation learning methods allow automatic discovery of representations needed for prediction from the raw data ( DL, a subfield of ML, has seen a dramatic resurgence in the past 6 years, largely driven by increases in computational power and the availability of massive new datasets. The field has witnessed striking advances in the ability of machines to manipulate data, including images ( This chapter discusses recent and forthcoming applications of DL in medicine highlighting the key aspects to significantly impact healthcare. We do not aim to provide a comprehensive background on technical details or general application of deep learning (see, e.g.,  
    
    ## A brief overview on deep learning
    
    ML is a general-purpose paradigm of artificial intelligence that can learn relationships from the data without the need to define them a priori (  In contrast, DL is a form of representation learning, that is, a machine is fed with raw data and develops its own representations needed for pattern recognition, which is composed of multiple layers of representations, usually derived with neural networks. These layers are typically arranged sequentially and composed of a large number of basic, nonlinear operations, such that the representation of one layer (beginning with the raw data input) is fed into the next layer and transformed into a more abstract representation ( Different important advances established DL as the state-of-the-art solution for several tasks. These models can scale to large datasets, mostly because of their ability to run on specialized computing hardware, and continue to improve with more data, enabling them to outperform many classical ML approaches. Easy-to-use software packages have brought these techniques to a broad community of computational scientists. Additionally, recent improvements for regularizations, strategies that aim to reduce generalization error, have made networks more robust, even when the number of parameters is very large. The larger datasets now available are also sufficient for fitting the many parameters characterizing deep neural networks. The convergence of all these factors currently makes DL extremely adaptable and capable of addressing the differences of each domain to which it is applied. Moreover, DL systems can accept multiple data types as input, which is of particular relevance for heterogeneous healthcare data. The most common models are trained using supervised learning, in which datasets are composed of input data points (e.g., a brain MRI scan, lab results) and corresponding output data labels (e.g., disease diagnosis, “abnormal” vs. “normal”). Unsupervised (or self-supervised) learning is usually used to draw inferences from datasets consisting of input data without labeled responses and to derive robust representations of the input space. Reinforcement learning, on the other hand, relies on computational agents that learn by trial and error or by expert demonstration and has recently been applied in medicine to learn wound suture for robotic-assisted surgery ( ![Figure 4.1 Schema of the most common neural networks shaping deep learning architectures.](IMAGES/B978012820273900004X/main.assets/f04-01-9780128202739.jpg)
    
    Figure 4.1 Schema of the most common neural networks shaping deep learning architectures.
    
     
    
    ## Deep learning for healthcare
    
    The application of DL in medicine has been constantly increasing since 2012. Although initial publications only reported pilot studies and proof of concepts, more recent works are considering all the processes leading up to clinical deployment ( The literature of this growing field is summarized in different excellent review papers and books (e.g., In the following sections, we review a few relevant applications of DL in medicine, in particular related to medical imaging, EHRs, biomedical data, and health monitoring data. For each data type, we provide a comprehensive description of at least one study from the literature and briefly overview other relevant work. To the best of our knowledge, there are only a few applications that harness the ability of DL to combine various data sources or a part of them in a joint representation for medical analysis and prediction. We address this point in the discussion section. ![Figure 4.2 A timeline of FDA approvals for the clinical use of artificial intelligence-based technologies updated to mid-2019.](IMAGES/B978012820273900004X/main.assets/f04-02-9780128202739.jpg)

Deep learning algorithms can then be implemented to learn from such data to answer clinically relevant questions.](IMAGES/B978012820273900004X/main.assets/f04-03-9780128202739.jpg)

Here, patient data stemming from hospital-linked electronic health records can be integrated together with other sources of data including genomics, environmental exposures, and elements captured from smartphones and other devices, such as activity logs and geocoding information. Deep learning algorithms can then be implemented to learn from such data to answer clinically relevant questions.
    
     
    
    ## Clinical imaging
    
    Some of the greatest success of DL has been in the field of computer vision, which focuses on deriving insight from images and videos, and deals with tasks such as object classification, detection, and segmentation. In the medical domain, computer vision can be used to determine, for example, if a patient’s MRI scan contains an abnormal lesion. CNNs have grown to be central in this field, as they are good in modeling data with natural spatial invariance (i.e., images do not change if rotated or shifted). There are several examples of powerful applications of DL and CNNs in medical image analysis and computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) ( CNNs were used to create an algorithm for automated detection of diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema in retinal fundus photographs ( Skin cancer is primarily diagnosed visually, beginning with an initial screening and followed potentially by dermoscopic analysis, a biopsy, and histopathological examination. Automated classification of skin lesions using images promises to accelerate this process and to reduce subjectivity biases. Esteva et al. used a single CNN, trained end to end from images directly, using only pixels and disease labels as inputs to classify skin lesions (  Zech and Badgeley et al. built deep neural networks to automatically detect pneumonia in chest radiographs ( In addition to discovery, ML with images can be integrated as part of a “learning healthcare system” to facilitate hospital processes ( DL has also been used to facilitate the analysis of cell images and tissue samples, where finding a trade-off between imaging quality, speed, noise reduction, and consistency in the analysis is difficult and often is a cause of missed opportunities and biased analysis. Lee et al. used CycleGAN (  
    
    ## Electronic health records
    
    EHRs from millions of patients are routinely collected across diverse healthcare institutions. They consist of heterogeneous data elements, including demographic information, diagnosis, laboratory results, medication prescriptions, and free text clinical notes ( A common approach of ML with EHRs is to have a domain expert designate the patterns to look for (i.e., the learning task and the targets) and to specify clinical variables in an ad hoc manner. Although appropriate in some situations, defining the feature space in a supervised manner does not scale or generalize well and does not allow for the discovery of novel patterns and features. DL can mitigate these limitations by reducing the need of manual feature engineering. In particular, deep neural networks are generally used to process aggregated EHRs, including both structured (e.g., diagnosis, medications, laboratory tests/results, procedures) and unstructured (e.g., free-text clinical notes) data, to obtain vector-based representations that are used for specific clinical inferences. In one of the first applications of DL to EHRs, Miotto et al. presented “Deep Patient,” an unsupervised deep feature learning framework to derive a general-purpose patient representation from EHR data that facilitates clinical predictive modeling ( [Fig. 4.4](#B978012820273900004X.xhtml#f0025) includes high-level conceptual architecture to derive deep patient representations. All EHRs are first extracted from the clinical data warehouse, preprocessed to identify and normalize clinically relevant phenotypes, and grouped in patient vectors. Each patient can be described by just a single vector or by a sequence of vectors computed in, for example, predefined temporal windows. The collection of vectors obtained from all the patients is used as input of the deep unsupervised neural network to discover a set of high-level general descriptors. Every patient in the data warehouse is then represented using these features and such deep representations can be efficiently and effectively applied to different clinical tasks (  ![image](IMAGES/B978012820273900004X/main.assets/f04-04-9780128202739.jpg)
    
    Figure 4.4 Conceptual framework used to derive the deep patient representations through unsupervised deep learning of a large EHR data warehouse (1). Experimental results on determining the probability of patients to develop various diseases within different time windows showed significant improvements over raw EHR data and alternative representation learning models in terms of AUC-ROC, that is, area under the ROC curve (2) and R-precision (3) (  To prove the effectiveness of the idea, Deep Patient was used to capture hierarchical regularities and dependencies in the aggregated EHRs of about 700,000 patients from Mount Sinai Hospital. Patient data included some general demographic details (e.g., age, gender, and race), and common clinical descriptors available in a structured format such as diagnoses (ICD-9 codes), medications, procedures, and lab tests, as well as preprocessed clinical notes. The authors evaluated this representation as broadly predictive of health states by assessing the probability of patients to develop various diseases within different time windows. The evaluation included 76,214 test patients comprising 78 diseases from diverse clinical domains and temporal windows. Results significantly outperformed those achieved using representations based on raw EHR data and alternative feature learning strategies (see [Fig. 4.4](#B978012820273900004X.xhtml#f0025)). Interestingly, prediction performance for severe diabetes, schizophrenia, and various cancers obtained the largest improvements compared to other algorithms. This is likely related to the chronic nature of these diseases, which lead to a larger and more consistent quantity of data. These findings showed that the deep learned features describe patients in a way that is general and conducive to processing by automated methods in different domains and for different applications, such as therapy recommendation, disease subtyping, clinical trial recruitment, patient similarity, and readmission risks. This work represented a first step toward the next generation of clinical systems that can (1) scale to include many millions to billions of patient records and (2) use a single, distributed patient representation to effectively support clinicians in their daily activities—rather than multiple systems working with different patient representations derived for different tasks. A large number of studies built upon this idea and addressed some of the limitations of Deep Patient (i.e., no explicit modeling of time, difficult interpretability of the predictions). Doctor AI uses patient history to predict diagnosis and medications for subsequent encounters using RNNs ( All these works focus on modeling patients to leverage clinical decision systems. In a separate but related research direction, DL has been used to derive EHR-based disease definitions (i.e., phenotypes) to facilitate cohort definitions. Similar to prospective study designs, high-quality EHR-based research requires rigorous selection criteria to designate case/control status particular to each disease. However, using a single clinical concept, such as a disease ICD code, often is not sufficient to produce reliable distinctions. Advanced EHR phenotyping of diseases is best understood as an “expert system,” where researchers with advanced knowledge of a particular disease phenotype design a list of criteria that may be used to identify affected (i.e., cases) and sometimes assuredly nonaffected (i.e., controls) individuals by excluding those with ambiguous clinical status or insufficient data. This typically takes the form of intricate rule-based algorithms specifying the presence and/or absence of particular billing codes, predefined ranges for laboratory tests, prescription of characteristic medications and processing of clinical notes, among others ( ![image](IMAGES/B978012820273900004X/main.assets/f04-05-9780128202739.jpg)
    
    Figure 4.5 Disease phenotype for schizophrenic disorders derived using medical concepts embeddings ( An important issue of EHRs is that a wealth of relevant clinical information is locked behind free-text clinical notes, requiring time-consuming chart review to obtain the complete clinical status of patients. Natural Language Processing (NLP), a branch of computer science that enables machines to understand and process human language for applications like machine translation (  Other promising applications of deep learning to EHRs include generation of synthetic clinical data using GANs (  
    
    ## Biological data
    
    DL in high-throughput biology is used to capture the internal structure of increasingly larger and high-dimensional datasets (e.g., DNA sequencing, RNA measurements). DL has been successfully applied in functional genomics, a field that tries to understand the relationship between genotype and phenotype by studying processes such as transcription, translation, and epigenetic regulation. The development of high throughput sequencing assays has provided massive amounts of -omics data, on the scale that DL requires for optimal performance. Databases like the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) contain a wealth of knowledge on functional elements related to DNA binding, DNA accessibility, DNA methylation, 3D chromatin structure, transcription, and RNA binding ( DNA-binding proteins modulate DNA’s function in many ways such as controlling transcription, regulating cell growth and division, and modifying 3D structure. CNNs have been used to predict DNA-binding protein sites ( Although there are about 20,000 known genes, the number of proteins is much higher due to alternative splicing, rearrangements in the pattern of introns and exons when they are joined together to become mRNA. SpliceAI is a deep neural network that predicts splicing from pre-mRNA sequence ( One of the first applications of CNNs to genomics data, DeepSEA, is a model trained to predict the effects of noncoding variants solely on genomic sequence ( DL has also been used in more technical tasks such as calling genetic variants. Functional genomic assays rely on accurate base calling from next-generation sequencing data but this remains a challenge because of the error-prone process. Instrumentation, data processing tools, and even the genomic sequence itself introduce difficulties in establishing a ground truth. A majority of widely used base calling tools assume that read errors are independent, even though this is known to be an invalid assumption. DeepVariant is a CNN that has approximated the true but unknown interdependent relationship between read errors, thereby avoiding the independent read error assumption in variant calling ( In cases where datasets are not sufficiently large enough to train a model on, transfer learning is an approach that incorporates the parameters from another model that was trained on a similar task. Transfer learning has been applied to predictive models of chromatin accessibility trained on DNA sequence data. Researchers trained the multitask model Basset on 149 cell types and then using these parameters for initialization, trained single-task models of chromatin accessibility in 15 other cell types. The performance of the models with transferred parameters performed better than models with randomly initialized parameters ( Differing data modalities can be used together as inputs in DL models to make use of complementary information. Features can be concatenated if raw data are not very different (early integration). Otherwise, if data modalities are very different, each can be first processed with separate layers, then the outputs can be concatenated, with subsequent layers integrating the features from each data modality (intermediate integration). Information on DNA sequences, gene expression, and chromatin accessibility were integrated to predict transcription factor binding in various cell types ( Unsupervised DL aims to characterize unlabeled data by extracting meaningful patterns from the data. These methods have been used to impute missing data (  
    
    ## Digital health monitoring devices
    
    Sensor-equipped smartphones, wearables, inexpensive embedded computing, and the related Internet-of-Things technologies are transforming health monitoring ( ML is considered to be a key element in analyzing this type of data, leveraging other fields such as time series modeling and computer vision (  However, there are just a few preliminary studies applying DL on commercial wearable devices for health monitoring. This is likely due to hardware limitations and difficulties in collecting large quantities of data that can benefit from DL methodologies. Most of the work in the field is on human activity recognition. Deep stacked autoencoders, for example, were used to correlate smartphone sensor data and personal health ( DL, specifically computer vision, promises to leverage all digital health monitoring applications involving cameras, especially in passive environments. As an example, an emerging intelligent house device with potentially wide-ranging applications for healthcare outside of traditional medical settings is the smart mirror.  
    
    ## Discussion
    
    In this chapter, we have discussed several important applications for DL in biomedicine across many clinical domains and data types. Further, we have provided some key examples of innovative studies that utilize DL effectively for biomedical research. It is clear that the trend will continue for many more studies utilizing such approaches. With the expected excitement and buzz around this field, it is important to consider how these types of work can have real-world impact. Here, we will discuss some high priority topics of DL in biomedicine that must be addressed going forward.  To effectively personalize medicine to the individual, it is important to characterize all the various states that make us unique. This involves information from our genetic makeup to our environmental exposures all the way to social graphs and networks ( Although it is clear that DL represents a new frontier in biomedicine to enable more nuanced discoveries, one of the most important issues will be how these findings can be utilized. This will be critical for ML models that seek to augment the healthcare process. For these models to be integrated into practice, several barriers must be addressed. First and foremost, the results of these models must be robust and extensible to all populations. As we have seen, ML models of EHR data can learn factors that are unrelated to phenotype studied, such as healthcare process variables that are specific to the hospital setting. In such cases, this overfitting could result in suboptimal performance when applied to other populations ( Once a robust model is built and sufficiently replicated, the next challenge is to convince those involved in the healthcare process to utilize it. It is imperative that practitioners (e.g., nurses, clinicians), hospital administration, and the patients themselves all be involved in this decision and that all of these individuals are properly trained on how to best utilize the output from DL algorithms (

    # Chapter 5: Generative adversarial network for cardiovascular imaging
    
    Mina Rezaei     Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States  
    
    ## Abstract
    
    Analysis of cardiac function plays an important role in clinical cardiology for patient management, disease diagnosis, risk evaluation, and treatment decision. Delineation of right- and left-sided cavities, as well as major vessels, is an important step in clinical cardiology for cardiac disease diagnosis. Medical imaging provides a noninvasive diagnostic tool to study cardiac anatomy and detect pathological changes that occur in disease states such as dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and right ventricular dysfunction. The accurate automation of the corresponding task can accelerate the diagnostic part and assist in therapy decisions. In this chapter, we overview recent machine learning approaches that have been applied for automatic cardiac diagnosis based on deep learning and generative adversarial networks and explain the recent application of generative adversarial networks (GANs) for classification, detection, segmentation, registration, image reconstruction, and synthetization mostly in cardiovascular imaging. In continuum, we review the public cardiac dataset with open challenges and conclude the chapter with GAN limitations and future research directions.
    
    ### Keywords
    
    Cardiovascular imaging; Deep probabilistic models; Discriminator model; Generative adversarial networks; Generator model; Neural network

    ## Introduction
    
    Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death in the United States, being responsible for 840,768 deaths (635,260 cardiac) in 2016 as reported by the American College of Cardiology ( Cardiac image analysis plays an important role in cardiovascular disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and clinical monitoring. Cardiac imaging can provide useful information for the detection of different pathological conditions such as valvular disease, coronary artery disease, and myocardial disease. Further, imaging is often essential for the evaluation of therapy success. However, it is often difficult to interpret the raw data extracted from images due to the high variability in image quality and structure appearance among various individuals. [Fig. 5.1](#B9780128202739000051.xhtml#f0010) illustrates the diversity of myocardial tissue, vessels, and atrial/ventricular cavities in the systolic and diastolic phases on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). ![Figure 5.1 Short-axis MRI images from patient 35 in the ACDC dataset \[20\] shown as 2D.The top row shows sequential systolic phase, with the last sub-figure in the top row showing the end of systole (myocardial contraction).     Machine learning has been applied to cardiac images and clinical data to improve prediction accuracy and efficiency, which could result in more precise and targeted therapy while streamlining the diagnostic process. For instance, the number of investigations that have utilized machine learning approaches for automating medical image segmentation, for example, cardiac MRI segmentation ( Generative approaches build models based on prior domain knowledge regarding the appearance and spatial distribution of the different tissue types. In the scenario of supervised learning, a generative model estimates the joint probability distribution of data P(X,Y) between the observed image X and the corresponding segmentation mask or label Y. Examples of popular generative models are Naive Bayes, Hidden Markov Models, Latent Dirichlet Allocation, and Boltzmann Machines. Traditionally, generative probabilistic models have been popular where simple conditionally independent Gaussian models ( On the contrary, discriminative models directly learn the relationship between the local features of images to specific labels without any domain knowledge. Examples are logistic regression, scalar vector machine, neural networks, nearest neighbor, and conditional random fields.     The remainder of the chapter is structured as follows: We begin with a brief introduction of the principles of GANs, overview the challenges associated with conventional GANs, and discuss the motivation behind some GAN variants in [Research background](#B9780128202739000051.xhtml#s0015) section. This is followed by a comprehensive review of medical image analysis tasks using GANs in [Deep learning in cardiac medical imaging](#B9780128202739000051.xhtml#s0045) section. We categorize all the work according to machine learning canonical tasks such as reconstruction, image synthesis, segmentation, classification, detection, registration, and multitask learning and highlight recent work on cardiac imaging. Section [GAN application in medical imaging](#B9780128202739000051.xhtml#s0050) is a summary section followed by a discussion of prospective applications and forthcoming challenges.

![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000051/main.stripin/si6.png)5.3 The generator G implicitly defines a probability distribution P[z] as the distribution of the samples (G) obtained by z. Therefore, we would like [Eq. (5.3)](#B9780128202739000051.xhtml#fd3) to converge to a good estimator of P[data], if given enough capacity and training time. If the discriminator D is trained to optimality before the next generator G updates, then minimizing L[G] is proven to be equivalent to minimizing the Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) between P[data](x) and P[g](z) as mentioned by Goodfellow et al. The desired outcome after training is that samples formed by <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mover><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow></mml:math>![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000051/main.stripin/si2.png) should approximate the real data distribution P[data](x).  
    
    ### Challenges for GAN optimization
    
    The training procedure by GAN is hard and different from neural networks because we simultaneously optimize the generator and the discriminator for opposing objectives. Therefore, many methods address this problem by proposing variant losses, training with different architecture, or even different optimization algorithm. Another problem by classical GAN is nonconvergence where the model parameters oscillate, destabilize, and never converge. There has been nontrivial progress on how and when one can prove that GANs are globally convergent such as (1) game theory, (2) simplifying assumption, and (3) using normal neural network techniques. 
    
    *   (1) Game theory: These techniques try to model GAN training process using notions from game theory. Current studies ( 
    *   (2) Simplifying assumptions: Some studies have shown that by simplifying assumptions of the generator and discriminator, one can move away the nonconvergence problem. For example, the simplified LGQ GAN ( 
    *   (3) Using techniques from normal neural networks: Other studies have shown the success of convergence by applying normal and nonconvex neural networks. Mode collapse is one of the hardest problems to solve in GAN. Here, the generator collapses, which produces limited varieties of samples. For example, in ACDC dataset ( The nonconvergence and mode collapse are often explained as an imbalance between the discriminator and the generator. The obvious solution is to balance their training to avoid overfitting. However, little progress has been made but not due to a lack of effort. Some researchers even believe that this is not a feasible or a desirable goal because a good discriminator gives good feedback. Some of the attention is, therefore, shifted for cost functions with nonvanishing gradients instead. In a discriminative model, loss measures the accuracy of the prediction, which is then used to monitor the progress of the training. However, the adversarial loss in GAN measures how well the discriminator is performing compared to the generator. Often, the generator cost increases but the image quality is improving. The next step is to examine the generated images manually to verify the progress. This makes model comparison harder, which in turn leads to difficulties in picking the best model in a single run. It also complicates the tuning process. Therefore, the next sections aim to cover investigations that have aimed at solving this issue.  
        
        ### Loss-variant GANs
        
        Another design decision in GANs that significantly impacts performance is the choice of loss function in [Eq. (5.3)](#B9780128202739000051.xhtml#fd3), which is an essential step to match the generated distribution to real data distribution. The objective function of original GAN is to minimize the JSD, wherein the JSD is derived from the Kullback–Liebler divergence (KLD). Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) ( Relaxed Wasserstein GAN (RWGAN) ( Cramer GAN ( The Fisher GAN ( Energy-based GAN (EBGAN) (

        ### Architecture-variant GANs
        
        Motivated by different challenges in GAN training procedure described in [Generative adversarial networks](#B9780128202739000051.xhtml#s0020) section, there have been several types of architecture variants proposed in the literature ( DCGAN ( Conditional GAN ( Recurrent GAN (  Pix2Pix ( CycleGAN ( SRGAN ( BigGAN ( Scalability: As the authors discovered that GANs benefit dramatically from scaling, they introduced two architectural changes to improve scalability (described in detail in the paper’s Appendix B), while at the same time improved conditioning by applying orthogonal regularization to the generator. Robustness: The orthogonal regularization applied to the generator makes the model amenable to the “truncation trick” so that fine control of the trade-offs between fidelity and variety is possible by truncating the latent space. Stability: The authors discovered and characterized instabilities specific to large-scale GANs and devised solutions to minimize the instabilities, although these involve a relatively high trade-off on performance. In addition to its performance boost at 128×128 resolution, BigGAN also outperformed the previous state of the art at 256×256 and 512×512 resolution on ImageNet. The model was also tested on the larger image dataset, JFT-300M, to demonstrate its transferability.   
        
        ### GAN evaluation
        
        When it comes to evaluating GANs, there are several methods that can be divided into quantitative or qualitative measures ([Table 5.2](#B9780128202739000051.xhtml#t0015)). In continuum, we briefly overview some of these measurements: Inception score: The inception score (IS) measures the quality of the generated samples.         ## GAN application in medical imaging
        
        In this section, we provide an overview of the current state of the art in the application of deep learning algorithms to medical imaging. We cover details of GANs application for cardiovascular imaging. This section focuses on GAN application for canonical tasks such as image synthetization, reconstruction, classification, detection, segmentation, and registration.  
        
        ### Medical image synthesis
        
        GANs have been widely proposed for image generation. We can group the GAN-based approaches into two categories: unsupervised generative framework and conditional GANs. Unsupervised GAN maps random noise to synthetic, realistically looking images following the training data distribution while the conditional GAN framework has a condition on prior knowledge for both the generator and the discriminator rather than solely utilizing noise. [Fig. 5.6](#B9780128202739000051.xhtml#f0035) shows the difference between unsupervised GAN and conditional GAN framework. Unsupervised GAN has been widely used to synthesize certain types of medical images either from noise alone or from prior knowledge by setting the conditions of image data for handling imbalanced classes ( In an unsupervised setting, different GAN frameworks have been implemented for 2D or 3D synthetic image generation. Thereafter, the generated images in addition to the training samples are fed to the deep learning models with the goal of providing balanced, augmented, and diverse data. Hence, the diversity gained from synthesized images can introduce more variability into the training set and considerably improve classification results. In continuum, we describe the GAN framework used for generating minority class examples. For instance, Rezaei et al. proposed different 2D and 3D conditional and unsupervised DCGAN for MRI image synthesis to mitigate imbalanced class problem. The researchers then provided different experiments on balanced datasets with GAN generated samples, classical data augmentation, and imbalanced dataset. As expected, the diversity gained from synthesized images introduced more variability into the training set and considerably improved classification results. Figs. [5.7](#B9780128202739000051.xhtml#f0040) and [5.8](#B9780128202739000051.xhtml#f0045) show different settings by unsupervised and conditional configuration for image synthetization, respectively.  ![Figure 5.6 Comparision of unsupervised GAN and semisupervised or conditional GAN.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000051/main.assets/f05-06-9780128202739.jpg)

Positron emission tomography (PET) images are frequently used for diagnosis and staging in oncology, and the combined acquisition of PET and CT images is a standard procedure in clinical practice. Furthermore, PET/CT imaging is becoming an important evaluation tool for new drug therapies. However, PET studies are expensive and lead to radiation exposure, which carries an increased risk of future malignancy. Consequently, the imaging community has been working on synthesizing PET images directly from CT data. In this context, GANs have also shown outstanding performance. Initial promising results for synthesizing liver PET images from CT data with conditional GANs have been obtained by MRI. PET from MRI has been used for monitoring disease of progression, understanding the physiopathology while evaluating treatment efficacy in multiple sclerosis (MS). In addition, the measurement of myelin content in PET images of the human brain has recently been shown to be clinically useful ( Ultrasound. X-ray. Microscopy.  
        
        ### Classification and detection
        
        Classification is one of the most successful applications of deep neural networks and generative adversarial networks that have been applied to various medical imaging benchmarks. Hierarchical image features can be extracted from a deep neural network and trained with imagewise class labels. GANs have been used for classification problems as well, either using part of the generator and/or discriminator as a feature extractor or directly using the discriminator as a classifier. Examples of classification by conditional GAN on cardiac images are included ( Computational detection of anomalies from images using supervised algorithms require a large amount of annotated training data—extremely difficult and time consuming to be provided by experts. Unsupervised algorithms, such as GANs, have the potential to be effective in such a setting. The main driving idea of anomaly detection is to train GAN on normal images, so that inference on diseased images would lead to incomplete reconstructions. Such incompleteness is typically associated with the regions of an anomaly.  
        
        ### Segmentation
        
        Conditional GANs (cGANs) have the advantage of being able to provide better representations for multimodal data generation because there is a control on the modes of the data being generated. This makes cGANs suitable for image semantic segmentation task, where we condition on an observed image and generate a corresponding output image. Cascade-GANs (

        ## Challenges, limitations, and future perspectives
        
        It is clear that deep learning and generative adversarial neural networks are very useful when one is tasked with producing accurate decisions based on complicated datasets. However, there are some major challenges and limitations of GANs that were discussed in [Research background](#B9780128202739000051.xhtml#s0015) section. Emphasis should be placed on technical challenges such as mode collapse, none convergence, lack of interpretability and theoretical underpinnings of many GAN models and techniques, and the resulting difficulty in deciding exactly what it is that makes one model better than another, specifically in medical datasets. Other challenges are a result of difficulties in evaluation and assessment of performance. The progress of the GANs model in medical imaging and the clinical dataset is not quite as settled. One issue is that medical images are often three-dimensional, and three-dimensional convolutional neural networks are not as well developed as their 2D counterparts. A significant challenge relates to memory and compute consumption when using CNNs with higher-dimensional imaging data; challenges that researchers are trying various approaches to deal with (treating 3D as stacks of 2Ds, patch- or segment-based training and inference, downscaling, etc.). Other important challenges are related to data, trust, interpretability, workflow integration, and regulations.

        # Chapter 6: Natural language processing
        
        Jake Vasilakes, Sicheng Zhou, and Rui Zhang     Institute for Health Informatics and College of Pharmacy, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, United States  
        
        ## Abstract
        
        Natural language processing (NLP) is a subfield of artificial intelligence that is concerned with the automatic understanding of human language by computers. NLP has seen much success in recent years due to increased computing power and the rise of deep learning, and this success has extended into the domains of biomedical and clinical text. NLP has contributed to tasks such as the discovery of drug interactions, the development of clinical decision support systems, and the facilitation of chart review. Part I of this chapter provides an introduction to NLP, some common tasks in the biomedical domain, and the methods for accomplishing these tasks. Part II gives a survey of recent applications of NLP in cardiovascular medicine.
        
        ### Keywords
        
        Artificial intelligence; Biomedical informatics; Clinical informatics; Information extraction; Machine learning; Natural language processing
