        ## Discussion and outlook
        
        Progress in applying ML to ultrasound has accelerated over the last few years, as part of an overall movement to increase automation for medical applications over at least the past decade. As is the case in other domains, DL algorithms and in particular, CNNs, have become the predominant classification methods, overtaking other classifiers operating on hand-crafted features. As in other types of biomedical image interpretation, U-Nets have been found to perform well for segmentation tasks. In TTE, most approaches have used variants of CNNs to segment the left ventricle and then measure volumes and ejection fraction from those boundaries. However, in a few cases, CNNs have been trained to operate directly on the US images to make measurements. Most approaches have trained CNNs in standard ways and do not make full use of transfer learning (  Progress has been made in accuracy, but there is much more to be done. Automated methods eliminate intra- and interobserver variability of the measurements themselves, although variability still exists due to variability in the imaging. Thus, automated methods have improved precision compared to manual interpretation. Automated methods have also been shown to have low biases when compared to manual measurements as the criterion standard. However, LoAs are large. Imagine telling a patient that they have an ejection fraction between 25% and 65% (due to a LoA of ±20% as reported in some results). That would not be helpful. Still, the large LoAs are partially a result of the fact that the criterion standard is manual measurement, which itself suffers from intra- and interobserver variability. In addition, much more work needs to be done to characterize and understand the outlier error cases. This has been done to some level in a couple of investigations, but needs to be performed systematically and routinely. That will lead to improved results. Most research has focused on the aspects of the TTE system flow depicted in [Fig. 8.3](#B9780128202739000087.xhtml#f0020), and in particular on view of classification and left ventricular measurements. The vast majority of published papers have focused on B-mode video processing, rather than the Doppler information that is also available from echocardiography examinations. Electrocardiogram (ECG) data are also collected during TTE, which is particularly useful for determining the underlying rhythm and correlating a particular image to the cardiac cycle. However, ECG data are also not typically used in research on ML for TTE, in some cases for convenience (it is simpler to just analyze US imagery) and in some cases because the focus is on point-of-care US where ECG may not be included. More broadly, there is a rich research space to fuse US information with other sensor modalities. Consideration of workflow of an ML system within a clinical environment is an important topic. Commercial products that incorporate some degree of artificial intelligence do address workflow and aspects of workflow, such as provision for manual editing as well as measuring time saved. However, workflow and human factors are typically not evaluated explicitly. In academic papers, the focus is on a particular subfunction, and workflow and the overall system that is needed are typically not considered. Published papers with more of a system view will be valuable. A critical aspect of automated echocardiography that has been typically neglected involves aiding nonexperts in acquiring the correct views (guiding probe position, orientation) and high-quality images. For example, it is well reported that automated algorithms are less accurate for poor quality images, even when acquired by trained sonographers. Improving image quality will lead to improved accuracy. Aiding image acquisition and identifying which images to process needs to become a significant topic in future research. Finally, approaches to explainable AI are notably missing from the literature. The AI community is increasingly giving attention on how humans gain trust in AI-enabled systems. As echocardiography is image-based, trust can be promoted as the human views segmentations or other annotations on images interpreted by the AI system. For example, the human will learn types of cases that the AI system can measure accurately, and which types of cases need to be scrutinized more closely. Still, trust is an important aspect of a human-machine system, and the research into explainable AI has much to contribute to echocardiography. Overall, we expect that the acceleration in ML applications to echocardiography will lead to the following: 
        
        1.  • improved accuracy and faster measurements for 2D echocardiography,
        2.  • increased adoption of 3D echocardiography (e.g., 3D TTE and 3D ICE),
        3.  • increased use of echocardiography for point of care applications by nonexperts (US at the bedside) and eventually even within the home environment,
        4.  • increased use of ML for cardiac procedure guidance,
        5.  • emerging use of ML for noninvasive, longitudinal monitoring of cardiovascular conditions with biofeedback.
        
        More broadly speaking, ML has the potential in improving accuracy, speed, and expanding the application of medical US to the nonexpert user. Many discussion points above can also be applied to other organs such as those covered in [Section 3](#B9780128202739000087.xhtml#s0010). In general, when compared to publicly available nonmedical datasets such as ImageNet ( Increased automation enabled by ML will free sonographers and clinicians from making low-level measurements, which will allow them to provide more individualized care for more patients and ultimately improve the overall patient outcome.

        # Chapter 9: Computed tomography and artificial intelligence
        
        Damini Dey[¹](#B9780128202739000099.xhtml#aff1), Andrew Lin[¹](#B9780128202739000099.xhtml#aff1), Donghee Han[²](#B9780128202739000099.xhtml#aff2), and Piotr J. Slomka[¹](#B9780128202739000099.xhtml#aff1)     ¹Biomedical Imaging Research Institute and Artificial Intelligence in Medicine, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, Los Angeles, CA, United States     ²Department of Imaging and the Smidt Heart Institute, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, Los Angeles, CA, United States  
        
        ## Abstract
        
        In the past 2 decades, significant advances in computed tomography (CT) hardware and software have expanded the clinical utility of CT imaging. Hardware improvements include faster gantry rotation with improved temporal resolution, improved spatial resolution, and greater coverage of the patient, enabling faster acquisition. Concurrently, there have been applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in all aspects of CT imaging—acquisition, reconstruction, analysis, and measurement of novel image features—which may further improve the value and reduce cost. Chapter 9 summarizes the recent advances in AI applied to several key aspects of CT imaging, interpretation, and analysis.
        
        ### Keywords
        
        Artificial intelligence; Computed tomography; Deep learning; Diagnosis; Machine learning; Prognosis

        ## Introduction
        
        In the past 2 decades, significant advances in computed tomography (CT) hardware and software have expanded the clinical utility of CT imaging. In the cardiovascular domain, imaging of the coronary arteries is technically challenging due to their small size and rapid constant motion. Cardiac CT requires high temporal resolution to “freeze” such motion and, therefore, has benefited from steadily increasing CT gantry rotation speeds. Imaging of the coronary arteries also requires high spatial resolution and reconstruction of submillimeter slices. Multiple CT slices need to be acquired simultaneously for complete coverage of the heart in one breath-hold. To meet these requirements, technical advances in CT hardware have focused on improved temporal and spatial resolution and more detectors for increased coverage (  
        
        ### Terminology
        
        In general, AI describes a computational program that can perform tasks that are associated with human intelligence, as such learning and problem-solving. Machine learning (ML) represents learning techniques that can give AI the ability to learn, typically progressively from large datasets, without making any prior assumptions. Finally, deep learning (DL) methods, a subset of ML, mimic human cognition by using multiple layers of convolutional neural networks (CNNs); in each layer, convolutional filters perform as feature extractors. In the past few years, the popularity and application of DL methods have expanded dramatically.  
        
        ## Artificial intelligence in CT image reconstruction
        
        Given the hardware developments in CT imaging, there is a demand for image reconstruction algorithms to be more accurate and computationally efficient. In addition to well-established analytic and iterative methods for CT image reconstruction, a new wave of data-driven and learning-based methods has emerged, which draw extensively from DL techniques.  
        
        ### Deep learning approaches
        
        The power of DL lies in the multilayer approach used to extract and identify important features from an input. CNNs are usually trained by first defining a loss function, which measures the discrepancy between the actual and desired outputs of the CNN for the training dataset. An optimized set of weights for the convolutional layers is then determined using an iterative optimization algorithm (  
        
        ### Denoising low-dose CT images
        
        DL approaches have the potential to help reduce CT radiation doses while speeding up reconstruction times. With an estimated 80 million CT scans performed in the United States each year ( Chen et al. first trained a CNN to reduce noise in CT images by learning a patch-based neural net (  
        
        ### Improving sparse-view CT reconstruction
        
        Low-dose CT can also be obtained by reducing the number of projections over the same acquisition arc, also known as a sparse-view protocol (   
        
        ### Removing image artifacts
        
        CNNs have also been used to reduce artifacts caused by metal or beam hardening. Metallic implants in patients are highly attenuated, leading to “hardening” of the polychromatic X-ray beams and resultant streak artifacts in reconstructed CT images ( In summary, the described AI techniques can optimize or even replace modern analytic and iterative reconstruction methods with algorithms learned from big data. They can improve the quality of images reconstructed from insufficient data, as occurring in low-dose or sparse-view CT, or overcome artifacts due to adverse object conditions such as metal in a patient. Although not yet ready for clinical implementation, these algorithms have the potential to enhance CT workflow by providing rapid and computationally efficient image reconstruction.  
        
        ## Artificial intelligence in cardiac CT image analysis
        
        The big data generated by precision cardiovascular imaging is heterogeneous and rapidly changing, requiring increasingly sophisticated and efficient computational models for their analysis and interpretation. Noninvasive imaging with coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring noncontrast cardiac CT and coronary CT angiography (CTA) plays a key role in the diagnosis, risk stratification, and management of patients with cardiovascular disease. By facilitating CT image segmentation, measurements, and subsequent clinical pathways, AI may assist physicians in delivering more efficient and personalized care with improved accuracy and reduced costs.  
        
        ### Image segmentation
        
        One of the first DL algorithms developed for cardiac CT used marginal space learning—which incrementally learns classifiers in marginal spaces of lower dimensions—to automatically segment all four heart chambers in 3D CT volumes. This method was tested on a large annotated dataset, achieving accurate boundary delineation with an average speed of 4 s per volume ( Coronary artery segmentation from coronary CTA enables luminal stenosis grading, plaque assessment, and blood flow simulation. The two major steps in this process are coronary centerline extraction and lumen segmentation. Centerline extraction has typically been performed using CNNs as a pre- or postprocessing step for traditional methods ( Automated segmentation of heart valves has been of recent interest due to the surge in transcatheter valve replacement procedures, which require valve modeling and precise sizing of the implants. Marginal space learning can provide patient-specific modeling and segmentation of all four valves from cardiac CT; this framework incorporates a constrained multilinear shape method to efficiently estimate the patient-specific valve parameters from cine images (  
        
        ### Semiautomated plaque analysis
        
        Beyond the detection of coronary stenosis, coronary CTA enables a comprehensive assessment of atherosclerotic plaque, with certain visually determined plaque characteristics conferring an increased risk of future cardiovascular events (

The hemodynamic significance of a given coronary stenosis can also be assessed using AI techniques.         ### Cardiac CT radiomics
        
        Radiomics is a new field of quantitative image analysis in which digital medical images are converted into mineable high-dimensional data ( ![Figure 9.6 Machine learning prediction of lesion-specific ischemia.The machine learning risk score (ML-combined) integrating clinical features and quantitative CTA measures had a significantly higher area under the curve (AUC) than quantitative percent stenosis and pretest likelihood of coronary artery disease for the prediction of lesion-specific ischemia by invasive fractional flow reserve.  Reproduced with permission from: Dey, D., Gaur, S., Ovrehus, K.A., Slomka, P.J., Betancur, J., & Goeller, M., et al.         Coronary atherosclerotic plaques consist of distinct histological components with different CT attenuation values; each voxel is a separate measurement of the amount of radiation absorbed in the given volume. This has enabled the noninvasive assessment of plaque characteristics in vivo with coronary CTA. However, as previously discussed, the visual interpretation of plaque features is subject to interobserver variability, and current plaque quantification methods are based on absolute voxel attenuation values without considering the relationship between voxels. Radiomics can provide an objective, mathematical, or AI-based description of plaque that incorporates the spatial distribution of voxels. This approach has been shown to outperform conventional qualitative and quantitative parameters for the detection of high-risk plaque ( In summary, AI applications have shown great promise in facilitating cardiac CT image analysis, by automating image segmentation and quantification and assisting physician interpretation. Furthermore, the integration of clinical and imaging data using AI models improves cardiovascular risk stratification over conventional methods. Radiomic analysis is a new field that quantifies spatial and textural features from images and utilizes AI approaches to identify novel imaging biomarkers from big data. In the foreseeable future, AI may work in the background of cardiac CT image analysis software and routine clinical reporting, automatically collecting data and enabling real-time diagnosis and risk stratification.  
        
        ## Artificial intelligence in CT brain for stroke
        
        Stroke is one of the major causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide (  
        
        ### Noncontrast CT
        
        The noncontrast CT scan is an effective and rapid method of CT examination without contrast injection. It is the current standard for the initial imaging of patients who are suspected of having a stroke. The two different types of stroke, hemorrhagic and ischemic, have different treatment strategies. The biggest advantage of noncontrast CT is its ability to detect an intracranial hemorrhage to discriminate hemorrhagic stroke. DL-based AI applications can improve the detection of intracranial hemorrhage. The largest contemporary study consisting of 313,318 noncontrast CT scans evaluated a fully automated (DL) algorithm designed to detect time-sensitive abnormal findings, including intracranial hemorrhage ( In the case of ischemic stroke, CT findings are often subtle compared to hemorrhagic stroke; thus, training and experience are required for accurate noncontrast CT evaluations. The Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score (ASPECTS) is a 10-point quantitative score that measures the extent of early ischemic changes in brain noncontrast CT images ( The hyperdense sign in noncontrast CT represents a marker of thromboembolus in patients with acute ischemic stroke. AI-based automated detection of the hyperdense vessel sign in emergency imaging may accelerate the identification of patients with ischemic stroke. This was demonstrated in a study that used an AI algorithm to detect the hyperdense middle cerebral artery (MCA) dot sign (  
        
        ### CT angiography
        
        CTA can effectively evaluate the presence and extent of intracranial vessel occlusion in patients with acute ischemic stroke. In addition, CTA enables the visualization of the anatomy of the proximal extracranial vessel and collateral flows, providing information to guide endovascular treatment. Although it is not challenging for expert readers to interpret CTA, the automated analysis of CTA imaging can be used to assist physicians by improving the accuracy and efficiency of their readings. In a study of 875 patients, where 46% of the subjects had large artery occlusions, automated CTA analysis based on a DL algorithm showed an accuracy of 86%, sensitivity of 90%, and specificity of 83% compared to the interpretations of experienced stroke neurologists ( Another application of AI algorithms to CTA images is to assess collateral flow. Collateral flow is defined as blood flow through a network of preexistent vascular anastomoses. Assessments of collateral flow based on CTA imaging can identify patients who may benefit from an endovascular thrombectomy (  
        
        ### CT perfusion
        
        CTP is a series of 3D CT scans acquired after intravenous contrast injection, which demonstrates blood perfusion in the brain. Compared to noncontrast CT, CTP can identify earlier ischemic changes. Prior research evaluated estimates of CTP postprocessing quantitative parameters including cerebral blood flow, cerebral blood volume, and mean transit time. These perfusion parameters help identify brain tissue characterizations in patients with acute ischemic stroke. Automated and operator-independent imaging processing tools have been used to quantify CTP parameters, providing rapid processing of quantitative CTP parameters within several minutes ( CTP enables the distinction of potentially salvageable ischemic tissue (penumbra) from irreversibly infarcted tissue (core). The accurate estimation of core and penumbra volume is an important point in CTP image analysis that helps determine the optimal treatment strategy. Core and penumbra volumes evolve over time: the core becomes larger, as the penumbral tissue becomes irreversibly damaged core. These changes depend on various clinical and imaging factors, such as the location of the infarct and the baseline size of the core and penumbral tissues. Prior research has demonstrated that ML algorithms can predict not only core and penumbra volumes, but also how the core volume changes over time ( In summary, AI applications for CT-based stroke evaluation have performed well in rapid, automated, and standardized analysis of noncontrast CT, CTA, and CTP scans. This information can provide real-time support for clinical decision-making and individualized treatment strategies for patients with acute ischemic stroke. Future studies will need to determine the feasibility and efficacy of integrating these AI algorithms into the clinical workflow of stroke management.  
        
        ## Artificial intelligence in CT for cancer screening
        
        Cancer is a group of diseases involving the uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells in the body. Cancer remains the most prominent cause of morbidity and mortality, accounting for approximately 1.8 million new cancer cases in 2019; a number that is projected to rise to more than 2.3 million by 2030 (  
        
        ### Lung nodule detection
        
        Early detection of malignant lung nodules improves prognosis, and CT is a useful modality for detecting lung nodules. Current guidelines suggest that a low-dose CT scan (LDCT) is an appropriate and effective screening tool for selected high-risk populations (  
        
        ### Identification of high-risk imaging features
        
        Pulmonary nodules are incidentally detected in more than 1.5 million adults in the United States each year ( Radiomics is the process of extracting a large number of quantitative features from medical images and can be used to identify subtle imaging features of malignant lung nodules that cannot be detected by visual interpretation. Once the features have been extracted using dedicated software, a potential challenge for radiomics is to identify and prioritize stable radiomics features. Traditional ML methods can be used for feature selection from a large radiomic dataset ( Recent advances in DL algorithms have demonstrated promising results for identifying, classifying, and quantifying patterns in medical imaging analysis ( To summarize, a variety of AI applications have been used to enhance accuracy and efficiency in lung cancer CT screening. The application of such algorithms can assist in the manual identification of pulmonary nodules and reduce physician interpretation time.  
        
        ## Summary
        
        In summary, with the increasing sophistication of ML and deep-learning techniques, AI-based algorithms can be utilized to improve medical imaging. When testing the performance of AI algorithms, the test data must be always kept separate from training data, to enable realistic estimates of performance. Further, external validation in data from unseen centers, not just hold-out data from the same center, can be expected to provide the most robust performance. Individualized risk prediction, which explains the AI findings for a specific patient, will be increasingly useful because they can personalize medical therapy. They will also be important for the acceptance of new AI approaches by physicians by overcoming the “black box” perception of AI. From the current data, AI-based algorithms can be expected to improve most aspects of CT imaging—personalized acquisition, reconstruction, image interpretation, and analysis and measurement of novel image features.

        # Chapter 10: Magnetic resonance imaging and artificial intelligence
        
        Giuseppe Muscogiuri[¹](#B9780128202739000105.xhtml#aff1), Marco Guglielmo[¹](#B9780128202739000105.xhtml#aff1), Andrea Baggiano[¹](#B9780128202739000105.xhtml#aff1), Laura Fusini[¹](#B9780128202739000105.xhtml#aff1), Francesca Ricci[²](#B9780128202739000105.xhtml#aff2), Gloria Cicala[³](#B9780128202739000105.xhtml#aff3), Mark G. Rabbat[⁴](#B9780128202739000105.xhtml#aff4)^,[⁵](#B9780128202739000105.xhtml#aff5), Andrea I. Guaricci[⁶](#B9780128202739000105.xhtml#aff6), and Gianluca Pontone[¹](#B9780128202739000105.xhtml#aff1)     ¹Centro Cardiologico Monzino, IRCCS, Milan, Italy     ²Department of Biomedicine and Prevention Division of Diagnostic Imaging, University of Rome “Tor Vergata,” Rome, Italy     ³Department of Medicine and Surgery, Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria di Parma, Università degli Studi, Parma, Italy     ⁴Loyola University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, United States     ⁵Edward Hines Jr. VA Hospital, Hines, IL, United States     ⁶Institute of Cardiovascular Disease, Department of Emergency and Organ Transplantation, University Hospital Policlinico of Bari, Bari, Italy  
        
        ## Abstract
        
        Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) is the best-suited cardiac imaging modality to provide reliable and reproducible information regarding cardiac volumes, function, and tissue characterization. In clinical practice, artificial intelligence (AI) in CMR can be applied to the whole process, ranging from sequence reconstruction, image analysis, and reporting of findings. In sequence reconstruction, the application of AI is mainly focused on the speed of reconstruction, while in image analysis and reporting AI is primarily aimed at automating the process of segmentation of both ventricles as well as fibrotic tissue. Within the realm of tissue characterization, AI can also be helpful in the depiction of tissue abnormalities from noncontrast images. Finally, AI can be useful for prognostic stratification.
        
        ### Keywords
        
        Artificial intelligence; Cardiac magnetic resonance; Diagnosis; Function; Myocardial tissue characterization; Prognosis

        ## Introduction
        
        The diagnostic and prognostic role of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly increasing in medicine ( The aforementioned applications of AI in CMR can be helpful from numerous aspects, especially in relation to workflow optimization by shortening acquisition periods, image analysis and reporting of findings that would help with the institution of patient-specific and disease-specific therapy. In the next section of this chapter, we will provide an overview of the application of AI in CMR.  
        
        ## Image reconstruction with AI
        
        In this era, CMR represents the most accurate and reproducible noninvasive cardiovascular imaging technique that allows for the evaluation of chamber volumes and function in addition to tissue characterization of ventricular walls ( To overcome such a limitation, several strategies have been developed by different vendors. In particular, new sequences have been used for different acquisition and reconstruction of the k-space (   ![Figure 10.1 Illustration to highlight the advantage of artificial intelligence for image reconstruction. The application of artificial intelligence reduces the time of reconstruction as demonstrated in the upper arrow. The second arrow represents a significantly longer time in the absence of an artificial intelligence algorithm used for image reconstruction.         ## Role of AI in cardiac MR analysis
        
        ### Left and right ventricular function
        
         Cine images represent an important aspect of CMR examinations. Acquiring cine images in long-axis and short-axis planes provides the ability to evaluate wall motion, chamber volumes and function, anatomy, and valvular disease with high reproducibility ( The neural networks used for CMR image analysis had been developed on small but heterogeneous populations and comparisons have often been performed to establish the network with the best performance ( The aforementioned limitation of a small sample size used for the development of a neural network for image analysis was outdated by Bai and colleagues, who used the UK-biobank as the source of data (

        ## AI for prognostic assessment
        
        CMR is a useful noninvasive imaging tool that provides valuable information for prognosis and risk stratification ( The application of ML algorithms for risk stratification has been seen in cohorts undergoing cardiac CT. Motwani and colleagues showed that an ML approach, built with a boosted ensemble algorithm and 10-fold stratified cross-validation, combining clinical data and quantitative atherosclerotic plaque measures, was able to better predict 5-year all-cause mortality compared to existing clinical or cardiac CT metrics alone ( Recently, an article by Chen et al. studied the role of ML in predicting 1-year cardiovascular events in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy ( However, randomized trials are the next logical step with this innovative approach that could prove the effectiveness of an AI-based method on risk assessment. The ideal workflow for establishing the prognostic trajectory of individuals using ML is summarized in [Fig. 10.4](#B9780128202739000105.xhtml#f0025).  ![Figure 10.4 Illustration of the application of artificial intelligence for risk assessment. Clinical data (upper box) can be combined with cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) findings to improve risk assessment.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000105/main.assets/f10-04-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 10.4 Illustration of the application of artificial intelligence for risk assessment. Clinical data (upper box) can be combined with cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) findings to improve risk assessment.
        
          
        
        ## Limitation and future directions
        
        The major limitation of AI in cardiac MR is represented by the limited insight that is offered to clinicians regarding the inner working of various AI models, traditionally called as the “black box” aspect of AI. Furthermore it is well known that the development of a powerful AI algorithm requires large datasets for training and validation purposes. This aspect is quite challenging as each institution, site, and/or company has its own regulations and policies on data sharing and privacy. Nevertheless, the potential implications for an expanded role for AI within healthcare in general, and cardiac magnetic resonance in particular, promises to revolutionize the field, and future multi-disciplinary collaborations are likely to focus efforts and attempt at reaching solutions for current existent limitations.  
        
        ## Conclusions
        
        The application of AI promises to revolutionize and advance the utility of CMR in clinical medicine and across healthcare systems. AI in CMR adds value in regards to image acquisition, reporting of findings, and contextualization of data ([Fig. 10.5](#B9780128202739000105.xhtml#f0030)). At the time being, the application of AI in CMR includes the following: ![Figure 10.5 Application of AI during the process of image acquisition and reporting of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR). The first application of AI could be observed between the CMR acquisition and postprocessing boxes; in this case, AI can be useful to speed up the time of image reconstruction. During image postprocessing AI can be useful for image analysis and in the evaluation of volumes and tissue characterization as can be observed in the middle box. Finally, the analysis of CMR findings with AI can be useful for prognostication of cardiovascular outcomes.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000105/main.assets/f10-05-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 10.5 Application of AI during the process of image acquisition and reporting of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR). The first application of AI could be observed between the CMR acquisition and postprocessing boxes; in this case, AI can be useful to speed up the time of image reconstruction. During image postprocessing AI can be useful for image analysis and in the evaluation of volumes and tissue characterization as can be observed in the middle box. Finally, the analysis of CMR findings with AI can be useful for prognostication of cardiovascular outcomes.
        
        *   (1) Optimization of the workflow involving CMR image reconstruction and reporting.
        *   (2) Extraction of tissue characteristics without the need for additional contrast agents.
        *   (3) Improvement in prognostication of outcomes in select high-risk cohorts.
        
        The ensuing few years promise to result in significant advances in the application of AI in the field of cardiac MR, with the ultimate goal of providing physicians with tools to optimize daily workflow while providing patients with specific and precise risk assessment.

        # Chapter 11: Nuclear imaging and artificial intelligence
        
        Benjamin C. Lee[¹](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#aff1), Felix Y.J. Keng[²](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#aff2), Subhi J. Al’Aref[³](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#aff3), and Lohendran Baskaran[¹](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#aff1)^,[²](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#aff2)     ¹Dalio Institute of Cardiovascular Imaging, Weill Cornell Medicine/NewYork-Presbyterian, New York, NY, United States     ²Department of Cardiovascular Medicine, National Heart Centre, Singapore     ³Division of Cardiology, Department of Medicine, University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences, Little Rock, AR, United States  
        
        ## Abstract
        
        Myocardial perfusion imaging with single-photon emission computed tomography and positron emission tomography has aided in diagnosing the severity of coronary artery disease. Artificial intelligence in cardiovascular nuclear medicine imaging includes various methods such as rule-based reasoning, artificial neural networks, structured machine learning, and deep convolutional neural networks. These artificial intelligence methods have been applied in detecting perfusion defects and other endpoints. Deep learning methods have been applied to nuclear medicine image formation to decrease computation time, improve image quality, and reduce radiation exposure to patients. This chapter summarizes AI methodologies applied to image analysis and image reconstruction for cardiovascular nuclear medicine imaging.
        
        ### Keywords
        
        AI; Artificial intelligence; Deep learning; Diagnosis; Image analysis; Image reconstruction; Machine learning; Nuclear medicine; PET; Positron emission tomography; Prognosis; Single photon emission computed tomography; SPECT

        Myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) has aided in diagnosing coronary artery disease (CAD) particularly in assessing its severity, manifest as ischemic heart disease (IHD). Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is the most widely available and validated nuclear medicine imaging modality ([Fig. 11.1D](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0010)). Positron emission tomography (PET) on the other hand produces higher resolution images ([Fig. 11.1E](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0010)) and has a higher diagnostic accuracy than SPECT and cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) ( Image reconstruction of nuclear medicine images was first performed by the filtered backprojection (FBP) algorithm, an analytical formulation of inverting the projection data in the camera-collected sinograms ([Fig. 11.1A and B](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0010)) to the original image. However, FBP does not account for the inherent Poisson noise model and therefore iterative reconstruction methods were developed to better model the physical process and camera system thus reducing noise and artifacts in the reconstructed image. ![Figure 11.1 Nuclear medicine imagesExample measurement data from a SPECT camera shows (A) a single angular projection of the torso and (B) a single slice sinogram through the heart showing the perfusion activity in the left ventricular (LV) myocardium. Filtered backprojection reconstructed 99mTc-sestamibi SPECT images of the LV are shown in (D) three multiplanar reformation cardiac views and (C) the LV myocardium segmented polar map representation with a 17-segment overlay. (E) 3D iterative reconstructed 13N-ammonia PET images also in 3 cardiac views show the LV myocardium at a higher resolution.  Images from each modality are not necessarily from the same patient.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000117/main.assets/f11-01-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 11.1 Nuclear medicine imagesExample measurement data from a SPECT camera shows (A) a single angular projection of the torso and (B) a single slice sinogram through the heart showing the perfusion activity in the left ventricular (LV) myocardium.         Image analysis begins with the segmentation of the left ventricular (LV) myocardium using polar sampling to get the maximum count circumferential profile of each short-axis slice ( Artificial intelligence in cardiovascular nuclear medicine imaging has been applied as early as 1985 using reason-based semantic nets and fuzzy logic ( Recent developments of deep learning algorithms such as the convolutional neural network (CNN) and availability of faster hardware such as graphics processing units have contributed to AI-based image reconstruction of nuclear medicine images, mostly for PET images due to it being a newer and higher resolution modality. These deep learning-based techniques aim to decrease reconstruction time, improve image quality, and reduce radiation dose to the patient.  
        
        ## Artificial intelligence in cardiac SPECT and PET image analysis
        
        Application of AI methods for cardiovascular SPECT and PET image analysis to diagnose IHD began with expert systems using a knowledge base and associated rules. Learning-based methods soon followed with artificial neural networks. Due to heavy computational requirements to train a neural network, other machine learning methods such as support vector machines and decision tree-based methods gained more popularity. Attention to neural networks was later renewed due to hardware improvements and new deep learning algorithms in the form of convolutional neural networks. As most of the research in AI for medical image analysis has been to diagnose or predict similar disease indicators or clinical endpoints, the following topics are organized by AI algorithms: nonlearning-based expert systems, structured traditional machine learning, shallow artificial neural networks, and deep convolutional neural networks. The methods reviewed focused on cardiovascular imaging, which were mostly from SPECT systems.  
        
        ### Nonlearning expert systems
        
        Expert systems are programmed with known facts and their inferences to emulate the decision-making process and performance of a human expert. The first type is case-based reasoning, which is a process of making decisions based on past experiences. It finds the most similar prior problem in the knowledge base, based on a similarity metric on relevant features, and applies that solution to the current problem. A more common type of expert system employs rule-based reasoning, which encodes knowledge from experts into “if-then” association rules. Although rule-based reasoning can be more difficult to implement compared to case-based reasoning, rule-based expert systems are typically more accurate. The earliest SPECT application of a rule-based expert system was introduced in 1985, where Later, To validate the association rules in PERFEX and discover new rules to predict heart disease,  
        
        ### Traditional machine learning
        
        In contrast to expert systems, learning-based systems, such as supervised machine learning, develop a model of the data only guided by the labeled output as ground truth. The learnable weights or coefficients of a model are iteratively updated in small steps that eventually reduce the error between the model’s prediction and the ground truth output. Any machine learning method that inputs features, hand-engineered by a domain expert from raw data, is considered traditional machine learning. As such, models that input structured or tabular data fall into this category. Specifically, models that are not deep neural networks also fall into this category, like support vector machines (SVMs), decision tree-based ensemble methods, and shallow artificial neural networks. Linear regression and logistic regression, borrowed from statistics, are also part of machine learning because they learn their coefficients from data. An SVM is a classifier that separates two classes with a linear boundary that maximizes the margin between the boundary line and the closest data points from each class, known as support vectors ([Fig. 11.2A](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0020)). SVMs can also generate nonlinear class boundaries by warping the feature space into higher dimensions to make the two classes separable by a linear boundary. An SVM with the kernel trick replaces the expensive coordinate transformation with a simpler distance computation to the decision boundary. Decision tree-based ensemble methods combine multiple decision trees and are categorized into either bagging or boosting ensembles. Bagging, a contraction of bootstrap aggregating, either averages or majority votes on the outputs of individual models that were trained in parallel on different subsets of the training data. Random Forest is an example that uses bagging on individual decision trees ([Fig. 11.2B](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0020)). Boosting is a method that sequences individual weak learning models that perform slightly better than random guessing, with increased weights iteratively placed on the previously incorrectly predicted training cases, thus converting the whole series of weak learning models to a stronger ensembled learning model. AdaBoost, short for adaptive boosting, was the first boosting algorithm to use weak learners like decision stumps, decision trees with a single split. LogitBoost reframed boosting probabilistically using the logistic loss function ([Fig. 11.2C](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0020)) instead of the exponential loss of AdaBoost. Therefore, LogitBoost is less sensitive to noisy data and outliers compared to AdaBoost. Gradient Boosting, also called gradient boosting machine or gradient tree boosting, is a generalization of AdaBoost, where each new weak learning model added reduces the overall model error using gradients to provide the next optimization direction. XGBoost, which stands for Extreme Gradient Boosting, is a gradient boosting algorithm with many algorithmic improvements that reduce overfitting, run an order of magnitude faster than its predecessors, and are well suited on large datasets. ![Figure 11.2 Nonnuclear medicine modality images(A) Computed tomography (CT) attenuation correction images (CTAC), shown in the 3 cardiac views, are lower resolution CT images used to correct attenuation artifacts during PET and some SPECT image reconstructions. Deep learning algorithms can generate synthetic CTAC images from (C) cardiac magnetic resonance images (MRIs) in PET/MR systems. Due to the higher resolution, anatomical structures measured from cardiovascular CT angiography (CCTA) images are used as the ground truth for machine learning-based basal valve plane placement in SPECT images.  Images from each modality are not necessarily from the same patient.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000117/main.assets/f11-02-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 11.2 Nonnuclear medicine modality images(A) Computed tomography (CT) attenuation correction images (CTAC), shown in the 3 cardiac views, are lower resolution CT images used to correct attenuation artifacts during PET and some SPECT image reconstructions. Deep learning algorithms can generate synthetic CTAC images from (C) cardiac magnetic resonance images (MRIs) in PET/MR systems. Due to the higher resolution, anatomical structures measured from cardiovascular CT angiography (CCTA) images are used as the ground truth for machine learning-based basal valve plane placement in SPECT images.   
        Images from each modality are not necessarily from the same patient.
        
        Both bagging and boosting reduce the variance of the output, producing more stable models. They differ in that bagging is better suited for reducing overfitting while boosting can reduce bias and increase accuracy. In the early 2010s, preliminary work on SPECT images used SVMs to detect abnormal perfusion (   ![Figure 11.3 Traditional machine learning algorithms used in SPECT(A) Support vector machines, (B) bagging ensemble learning, and (C) boosting ensemble learning are structured-data machine learning algorithms used for automated diagnosis of coronary artery disease using features derived from SPECT images. (A) Support vector machines using the kernel trick can convert a nonlinear decision boundary such as the circle shown to a linear hyper-plane by transforming the data in a higher dimension. Support vectors are the data points closest to the decision boundary with maximum margins. (B) Random Forest is a bagging method where multiple decision trees are trained on random subsets of the data and the output decision is a majority vote of each individual decision. (C) LogitBoost is a boosting method where multiple decision stumps, decision trees with a single spit, sequentially improve the accuracy of the prior decision stump by weighting the data according to the logistic loss function. The output decision is a vote of each model inversely weighted by the training error.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000117/main.assets/f11-03-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 11.3 Traditional machine learning algorithms used in SPECT(A) Support vector machines, (B) bagging ensemble learning, and (C) boosting ensemble learning are structured-data machine learning algorithms used for automated diagnosis of coronary artery disease using features derived from SPECT images. (A) Support vector machines using the kernel trick can convert a nonlinear decision boundary such as the circle shown to a linear hyper-plane by transforming the data in a higher dimension. Support vectors are the data points closest to the decision boundary with maximum margins. (B) Random Forest is a bagging method where multiple decision trees are trained on random subsets of the data and the output decision is a majority vote of each individual decision. (C) LogitBoost is a boosting method where multiple decision stumps, decision trees with a single spit, sequentially improve the accuracy of the prior decision stump by weighting the data according to the logistic loss function. The output decision is a vote of each model inversely weighted by the training error.

        ### Shallow artificial neural networks
        
        Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are learning algorithms with interconnected artificial neurons called perceptrons that are loosely based on biological neurons ([Fig. 11.4A](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0025)). Each perceptron or node sums multiple weighted input values and based on a threshold, outputs a single value between 0 and 1, called an activation. This nonlinear operation of limiting the output to a range is performed by a sigmoid or an S-shaped function and allows for input to output mappings that are more complicated than a simple linear combination. A feed-forward neural network propagates the weighted and combined activation signals from one layer of nodes to the next in one direction without cyclical connections. These are also called fully connected layers or multilayer perceptrons. The output at the last layer can output continuous-valued regression results or be binarized for classification. Although current deep artificial neural networks have up to hundreds of layers ([Fig. 11.4B](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0025)), the earliest artificial neural networks consisted of just an input layer, one hidden layer, and an output layer because a single hidden layer was found to be sufficient to approximate any continuous function ( ![Figure 11.4 Shallow and deep artificial neural networks(A) A shallow artificial neural network has only one hidden layer. Weighted feature inputs move from the input layer to the hidden layer to be summed with biases and sent through a nonlinear activation function that maps that sum to an activation value between 0 and 1. This activation is fed through another weighted sum in the output layer. In the output evaluation, the softmax function normalizes the unbounded logit outputs to class probabilities that sum to 1. The argmax function selects the most probable class as the final output of this binary classifier. Given the label outputs as ground truths, the confusion matrix and the area-under-the ROC curve evaluate the predictive performance. The derivative or gradient of the cross-entropy loss function is used in the backpropagation technique to update the two sets of weights during the training step. (B) A neural network is considered deep if there many layers and nodes, specifically if there are 2 or more hidden layers. This deep artificial neural network example has 10 trainable layers consisting of 9 hidden layers and 1 output layer, excluding the input layer, which has no weights.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000117/main.assets/f11-04-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 11.4 Shallow and deep artificial neural networks(A) A shallow artificial neural network has only one hidden layer. Weighted feature inputs move from the input layer to the hidden layer to be summed with biases and sent through a nonlinear activation function that maps that sum to an activation value between 0 and 1. This activation is fed through another weighted sum in the output layer. In the output evaluation, the softmax function normalizes the unbounded logit outputs to class probabilities that sum to 1. The argmax function selects the most probable class as the final output of this binary classifier. Given the label outputs as ground truths, the confusion matrix and the area-under-the ROC curve evaluate the predictive performance. The derivative or gradient of the cross-entropy loss function is used in the backpropagation technique to update the two sets of weights during the training step. (B) A neural network is considered deep if there many layers and nodes, specifically if there are 2 or more hidden layers. This deep artificial neural network example has 10 trainable layers consisting of 9 hidden layers and 1 output layer, excluding the input layer, which has no weights.
        
        The perceptron was introduced in the 1950s but an efficient algorithm for training neural networks called backpropagation was not developed until 1986. In backpropagation, the gradients of the output errors generated from a loss function propagate backwards through the layers correcting their weights iteratively ([Fig. 11.4A](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0025)). Shallow ANNs were the earliest traditional machine learning models studied on SPECT images, 2 decades earlier than SVMs and tree-based ensemble methods noted in the prior section.         ### Deep learning and convolutional neural networks
        
        Deep learning is a subset of machine learning in which raw data such as images or time sequences are inputted into a learning model instead of hand-engineered features. Precisely, a deep learning model is a neural network with more than one hidden layer and can be as deep as several hundred layers ([Fig. 11.4B](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0025)). The multiple hidden layers afford the neural network to automate the feature extraction process and create higher-order decision boundaries. Convolutional neural networks or CNNs ([Fig. 11.5A](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0030)) are deep learning models that automatically extract features from large 1D, 2D, 3D, or even 4D inputs in the first part of the network consisting of convolutional layers by compressing the data into a set of important features. This is performed by a mathematical operation called a convolution that involves sliding a filter across an image. A moving average filter or a smoothing filter is an example. Any kind of filter may be learned in the training process. Input images filtered over several convolutional layers are transformed into features and are then sent to the final part of the network consisting of fully connected layers like a regular ANN, for the classification or regression prediction step. The convolutional layers allow CNNs to be efficient because only spatially local network connections are considered. The unbiased nature of the CNN’s feature extraction step may lead to never-before-considered and better output-predictive features than hand-engineered ones. CNNs gained widespread popularity in the computer vision community starting in 2012 when the AlexNet CNN outperformed state-of-the-art image classification algorithms by wide margins (   ![Figure 11.5 Convolutional neural networks and variants(A) The convolutional neural network (CNN) in this example is the VGG16 network with a slight modification of a two-channel output layer for binary classification. The 2D input image is convolved with 64 filters with trainable weights to produce a 64-channel activation image in the first hidden layers. The successive hidden layers with half the image size but twice the channel depth progressively convert spatial information into more complex feature information. There are 16 total trainable layers consisting of a set of 13 convolutional layers and a set of 3 fully connected layers, with a flattening step in between to unravel 3D array of values to a long 1D array. (B) The convolutional encoder–decoder borrows the convolutional layers of a CNN to perform encoding of the input image into a compressed representation or set of features in the bottleneck layer, from which the decoder reconstructs an output image through a series of convolutions and upsampling. (C) A U-Net is an encoder–decoder used for image segmentation but with resolution-preserving skip connections that copy and concatenate activation images in the contraction path to similar-sized activation images in the expansion path.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000117/main.assets/f11-05-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 11.5 Convolutional neural networks and variants(A) The convolutional neural network (CNN) in this example is the VGG16 network with a slight modification of a two-channel output layer for binary classification. The 2D input image is convolved with 64 filters with trainable weights to produce a 64-channel activation image in the first hidden layers. The successive hidden layers with half the image size but twice the channel depth progressively convert spatial information into more complex feature information. There are 16 total trainable layers consisting of a set of 13 convolutional layers and a set of 3 fully connected layers, with a flattening step in between to unravel 3D array of values to a long 1D array. (B) The convolutional encoder–decoder borrows the convolutional layers of a CNN to perform encoding of the input image into a compressed representation or set of features in the bottleneck layer, from which the decoder reconstructs an output image through a series of convolutions and upsampling. (C) A U-Net is an encoder–decoder used for image segmentation but with resolution-preserving skip connections that copy and concatenate activation images in the contraction path to similar-sized activation images in the expansion path.
        
        CNNs have been applied to other conditions in nuclear medicine beyond coronary artery disease. Cardiac sarcoidosis (CS) is an inflammatory disease in which small clumps of white blood cells called granulomas form in the heart. One criticism of machine learning is that it is a “black box” where the nonlinearity of the machine learning algorithms makes it difficult to know how and why the algorithm arrived at its decision. It is desirable to understand the algorithm’s feature visualization and feature importance. In another study using PET images, CNNs were originally designed for inputting rectangular natural images of the outside world; however, changing the network architecture of CNNs to better adapt to the desired input data is possible. Projecting the capped cylindrically 3D shape of the LV myocardium to a 2D polar map to input into a CNN introduces spatial distortions where the apical region is compressed, and the basal regions are expanded. Additionally, a 2D polar map image leaves blank regions in the corner of the circumscribed square input image. To avoid these issues, CNNs have also been adapted to produce output images. This new architecture is called a fully convolutional network (FCN), which leaves out the fully connected layers of the second half of the CNN and consists of only convolutional layers. The U-Net is a special case of an FCN that mirrors the downsampling convolutional layers of a CNN with succeeding deconvolutional layers that upsample the compressed features to a segmented image of the original size ([Fig. 11.5C](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0030)) (  
        
        ## Artificial intelligence in cardiac SPECT and PET image reconstruction
        
        Artificial intelligence in image reconstruction for nuclear medicine has been a recent development due to the relatively recent advent of the convolutional neural network. As most image reconstruction deep learning methods are CNN based, the topics are organized by the goals of the reconstruction. Some of these objectives include directly reconstructing the image from the measurement data without an explicit image measurement model in an end-to-end approach, while others include using the traditional image reconstruction algorithms but generating attenuation maps from non-CT imaging modalities or correcting for motion artifacts. Deep learning has also been applied to the last step of the image reconstruction pipeline that includes noise reduction techniques that allow for either improving image quality or lowering the radiopharmaceutical dosage while retaining the same image quality. Although much of this research in nuclear medicine has been focused on brain imaging, the techniques described here are applicable to cardiovascular imaging.  
        
        ### End-to-end reconstruction
        
        In the machine learning context, end-to-end reconstruction refers to estimating an image directly from the raw measurement data of the imaging camera without using conventional filtered backprojection or iterative reconstruction methods like ordered subsets expectation-maximization (OSEM). The measurement data that SPECT and PET cameras ultimately produce are sinogram data ([Fig. 11.1B](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0010)), which are sets of angular projections ([Fig. 11.1A](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0010)). In 2018,  
        
        ### Attenuation correction
        
        For PET, varying radiopaque areas of the body can attenuate an emitted positron from reaching its intended sensor causing attenuation artifacts where some parts of the myocardium may incorrectly appear to have lower counts. Incorporating a CT attenuation correction (CTAC) map ([Fig. 11.2A](#B9780128202739000117.xhtml#f0015)) from a PET/CT imaging system into the reconstruction process can correct for this. For PET/MR imaging systems,  
        
        ### Motion correction
        
        Motion of the patient during imaging is unavoidable, whether it is cardiac, respiratory, or patient motion. The impact of motion is blurred imaging.  
        
        ### Denoising and image quality improvement
        
        Autoencoders are convolutional neural networks that extract the most important information in images by forcing the successive image activations of the network through a bottleneck. Autoencoders are special cases of encoder–decoder networks where the input and outputs are the same. The impact of the bottleneck retaining the most important information is a smoothing or denoising effect. Another wide area of deep learning reconstruction research is in denoising low-dose nuclear medicine scans. Many of these approaches generally train an encoder–decoder network with low-dose image inputs and standard-dose image outputs. During testing or running of the model, the low-dose images are transformed into ones with reduced noise. There are many examples of this using different networks.         ## Summary
        
        Artificial intelligence methods have had a long history in nuclear medicine imaging beginning with expert systems using mostly rule-based reasoning, next shallow artificial neural networks, and then traditional machine learning algorithms. Recent deep learning algorithms include convolutional neural networks for classification, U-Net and V-Net for segmentation, encoder–decoder networks for image reconstruction, and generative adversarial networks for image generation. One of the challenges that remain for machine learning in nuclear medicine imaging is training models with sufficiently large numbers of training images on the order of thousands to hundreds of thousands of images to avoid overfitting models. Some strategies to address the small data problem include: (1) data augmentation to increase the training set, (2) employing unsupervised, semisupervised or self-supervised learning to reduce the dependence on expensive manual data labeling, and (3) using a hybrid approach of rules and machine learning to extend the generalizability of these models. The other broader challenge is instilling confidence in machine-learned predictions by adding interpretability to address the “how” and explainability to address the “why.” These are yet unsolved but critical ongoing areas of machine learning research.

        # Chapter 12: Radiomics in cardiovascular imaging: principles and clinical implications
        
        Márton Tokodi[¹](#B9780128202739000129.xhtml#aff1), Attila Kovács[¹](#B9780128202739000129.xhtml#aff1), and Pál Maurovich-Horvat[²](#B9780128202739000129.xhtml#aff2)     ¹Heart and Vascular Center, Semmelweis University, Budapest, Hungary     ²Department of Radiology, Medical Imaging Center, Semmelweis University, Budapest, Hungary  
        
        ## Abstract
        
        The rapid technological advancements in noninvasive imaging, coupled with the increasing availability of large datasets and the expansion of computational power, have reformed every aspect of cardiovascular (CV) medicine. As a result, imaging has become an essential part of both clinical practice and research. Day by day, thousands of images are acquired in CV imaging laboratories and are interpreted using a wide range of qualitative and quantitative descriptors. However, radiologic images contain much more information than we can comprehend visually or quantify with simple manual measurements. Radiomics—the process of high-throughput extraction of quantitative features from imaging data—holds the key to unleash the untapped potential of information withheld in imaging datasets and to support personalized diagnostic and therapeutic decisions. In this chapter, we review the principles of radiomics, along with its potential role in CV imaging.
        
        ### Keywords
        
        Cardiovascular imaging; Machine learning; Precision medicine; Radiology; Radiomics; Texture analysis

        ## Introduction
        
        Over the past decades, the medical community has witnessed an unprecedented expansion in the arsenal of noninvasive imaging technologies ( Massive amounts of medical images are acquired along the diagnostic and therapeutic pathway that a CV patient follows. The conventional interpretation of these images is reliant on the compound of basic, guideline-defined geometric quantifiers and qualitative, often subjective, descriptors. Although this approach is sufficient for clinical judgment in most cases, it has substantial shortcomings, and there is much space to improve. Images encompass an abundance of meaningful information that is challenging to quantify, interpret, and link with diagnosis or prognosis using solely conventional metrics. Moreover, visually assessed qualitative characteristics rely on a priori knowledge, have limited capabilities to discern subtle differences, and are hard to reproduce. Therefore, medical professionals are in the pursuit of novel technologies that can augment the interpretation of images allowing more personalized patient management. Advanced data extraction and analytic tools might offer a panacea for the limitations above. One of these emerging technologies is radiomics, which can be defined as the high-throughput extraction of quantitative features enabling the conversion of images into structured, mineable datasets. These high-dimensional databases can be supplied to machine learning (ML) algorithms that are capable of simultaneously interpreting myriads of variables to generate and test hypotheses, and ultimately to support clinical decisions. Radiomic features can describe the texture and spatial complexity in detail through the uncovering of patterns that are invisible to the naked eye. Thus, it provides a nearly limitless supply of imaging biomarkers with potential incremental value over conventional descriptors. The utility of radiomics-based predictive models was first demonstrated in the field of oncology, where notable success was achieved in tumor classification, prediction of treatment response, and prognostication in multiple cohorts ( In this chapter, we provide an overview of basic radiomics concepts and workflow, along with its potential role in CV imaging. Besides its strength, we will also review some of the pitfalls that should be avoided while utilizing this state-of-the-art analytic approach.  
        
        ## Concept of radiomics
        
        Radiomics is a precision phenotyping toolbox designed to break down radiological images into a multitude of features (  
        
        ## Process of radiomics
        
        The practice of radiomics comprises discrete steps ([Fig. 12.1](#B9780128202739000129.xhtml#f0010)): (1) image acquisition, (2) identification of the region of interest (ROI) and segmentation, (3) extraction of descriptive features from segmented ROI, (4) generation of searchable databases, and (5) mining these databases to develop ML-based models.  
        
        ### Image acquisition
        
        Images suitable for radiomics analysis can be assessed using different imaging modalities such as cardiac ultrasound, CT, MRI, or nuclear medicine imaging techniques. It should be highlighted that radiomics can be applied on standard, routinely acquired clinical images without requiring dedicated acquisition protocols or additional imaging. Accordingly, radiomics has a real potential for being integrated into the routine clinical workflow as an adjunct to conventional measures. ![Figure 12.1 Pipeline of radiomics-based analysis. The radiomics workflow comprises five discrete steps: (1) image acquisition, (2) identification of the ROI and segmentation, (3) extraction of descriptive features from segmented ROI, (4) generation of searchable databases, and (5) mining these databases to develop machine learning–based models. Abbreviations: CT, computed tomography; LV, left ventricle; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; PVAT, perivascular adipose tissue; ROI, region of interest.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000129/main.assets/f12-01-9780128202739.jpg)

The radiomics workflow comprises five discrete steps: (1) image acquisition, (2) identification of the ROI and segmentation, (3) extraction of descriptive features from segmented ROI, (4) generation of searchable databases, and (5) mining these databases to develop machine learning–based models.         Nevertheless, the standardization of imaging protocols across different centers is still lacking. This usually does not hamper the identification and measurement of conventional features used in current clinical practice. However, when images are analyzed in-depth in order to extract pixel-based data, differences in image acquisition, reconstruction, and postprocessing parameters can introduce significant variability that is not caused by the underlying pathological conditions (  
        
        ### Identification of the region of interest and segmentation
        
        Following the selection of the images to be analyzed, the next critical and challenging step is the identification and segmentation of image regions (i.e., ROI) containing essential prognostic information. As the radiomic features are extracted from the delineated areas or volumes, variations in contouring that alter the ROI will modify the values of the radiomic features as well. Therefore, it is indispensable to have a consistent contouring technique defined through standard operating procedures. There are various contouring methods ranging from manual to fully automated techniques (  
        
        ### Extraction of radiomic features
        
        After the segmentation of the ROI, radiomic features can be extracted through dedicated pipelines developed by individual manufacturers or using open-source packages. Radiomic features can be categorized into four major groups ([Fig. 12.2](#B9780128202739000129.xhtml#f0015)): (1) intensity-based metrics, (2) texture-based metrics, (3) shape-based measures, and (4) transform-based features.  
        
        #### Intensity-based metrics
        
        Intensity-based metrics (or first-order statistics) are calculated from individual pixel values without considering any additional information that might be obtained from analyzing the spatial relationship between pixels. The pixel values can be analyzed using the tools of histogram analysis. These metrics are used to quantify different aspects of the distribution, such as central tendency, variation, shape, and diversity. The basic mathematical descriptors of central tendency and variation, such as mean, median, minimum, maximum, percentiles, and interquartile range are well known among medical professionals. Although these metrics are simple to calculate and interpret, they do not describe precisely the size and shape of the distribution. As several different distributions may exist with the same central tendency but different shapes, these statistics are not sufficient to characterize a given image. The shape of the distribution is most frequently described by variance— a measure of sample variation around the mean— and standard deviation (SD), which is the square root of variance. In normally distributed datasets, the SD quantifies the band around the mean where approximately 68% of the data points are located. Skewness and kurtosis are less frequently used by medical professionals; however, they capture other meaningful characteristics of the distribution. Skewness expresses how asymmetric the distribution is. Negative skewness indicates that the bulk of the data is located to the right of the mean, whereas positive skewness means the opposite. Kurtosis quantifies how close the data points are to the mean. Small values indicate that most values are situated within one SD of the mean, and the dataset contains only a few outliers, whereas higher values imply that a large proportion of data points can be found beyond one SD. In normally distributed datasets, the kurtosis is equal to 3. It is common to compare the kurtosis of a distribution to this value to assess how data points are dispersed around the mean. The statistics mentioned above provide information about the average, the variation, and the distribution of the sample but not about the diversity of pixel values. Concepts of information theory can be applied to quantify heterogeneity. Energy measures the overall magnitude of the values, and it is calculated by squaring and then summing them. Uniformity quantifies the similarity of the values, and it is computed by squaring the relative frequency of the given values and then summing them. Entropy measures the information content of the dataset ( ![Figure 12.2 Classes of radiomic features. Intensity-based metrics (or first-order statistics) are calculated by analyzing individual pixel values using the tools of histogram analysis. Texture-based features attempt to describe patterns using mathematical formulae based on the spatial arrangement of pixels. The texture analytic toolbar includes diverse approaches such as second- and higher-order metrics, and Laws’ texture energy approach, to name a few. Shape-based metrics aim to quantify the size, the localization, the spatial complexity, and the self-symmetry of the given lesion or abnormality. Transform-based methods convert the images into other domains, such as the frequency domain, to extract additional radiomic features. It is important to note that we are providing only a few examples of each feature class; however, thousands of other radiomic parameters can be extracted from radiological images.         #### Texture-based metrics
        
        The preceding parameters neglect all spatial information and use the absolute values of individual pixels solely. In order to consider spatial relationships, more sophisticated mathematical approaches are required. As a promising solution, the field of texture analysis was born in the 1970s, and it has been continuously evolving ever since (  
        
        ##### Second-order statistics
        
        In 1973, Haralick et al. proposed the idea of gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) for the classification of materials and terrains based on their texture ( Prior to matrix generation, pixels values are required to be discretized into a given number of bins, as pixels with exactly the same values occur very scarcely. The matrix will have the same number of rows as columns, which equals the number of bins. Next, a direction and a distance are needed to be defined to analyze the texture. The direction is usually described with an angle ([Fig. 12.4](#B9780128202739000129.xhtml#f0025)). Statistics are calculated in four directions only (0, 45, 90, 135 degrees), as the remaining directions are the exact counterparts of the above. As the next step, the transposed matrix is added to the original raw GLCM to receive a symmetrical matrix. Because relative frequencies are more informative than absolute numbers, the matrix should be normalized by dividing each of its elements by the sum of all values in the GLCM. Due to the fact that texture is an intrinsic property of an image, the same results should be obtained even if the image is rotated. Therefore, to achieve rotationally invariant results, statistics are calculated on the four GLCMs and then averaged.   ![Figure 12.3 Characterization of texture using second- and higher-order radiomic features. After the segmentation of the ROI, pixels are discretized into a given number of bins. GLCMs aim to quantify how frequently different combinations of gray levels occur in pairs of pixels that are separated by a predefined distance along a given direction. GLRLMs quantify how many consecutive pixels have the same value along a predefined direction. GLGLMs measure the distribution of gap lengths for each gray level in an image. To achieve rotationally invariant results, matrices (GLCM, GLRLM, GLGLM) and statistics should be calculated in all four directions (0, 45, 90, and 135 degrees) and then averaged. GLSZMs quantify the number of continuous pixels with the same gray level. NGTDMs are generated by the summation of differences between the gray level of each pixel and its neighborhood within a predefined distance. GLDMs determine the number of connected pixels within a given distance that are dependent on the center pixel. A neighboring pixel is considered dependent on the center pixel if the difference between their gray-level values does not exceed a predefined threshold. The GLSZM, the NGTDM, and the GLDM are rotation independent; thus, only one of each is calculated from the given ROI.         ##### Higher-order statistics
        
        Whereas second-order statistics examine the relationship between pairs of pixels, higher-order metrics attempt to describe the link between three or more pixels. Hereunder, we review some of the most widely used concepts ([Fig. 12.3](#B9780128202739000129.xhtml#f0020)). Gray-level run-length matrix (GLRLM) quantifies how many consecutive pixels have the same value along a predefined direction ( Gray-level gap-length matrix (GLGLM) measures the distribution of gap lengths for each gray level in an image ( Gray-level size zone matrix (GLSZM) quantifies the number of continuous pixels with the same gray level ( ![Figure 12.4 Schematic illustration of directions. To calculate some of the second- and higher-order radiomic features, a direction is required to be defined. By convention, the direction is described with an angle. Pixels to the east of the reference pixel are at 0 degrees, the ones to the northeast are at 45 degrees, the ones to the north are at 90 degrees, and the ones to the northwest are at 135 degrees. Statistics are calculated in four directions only (0, 45, 90, 135 degrees), as the remaining ones are the exact counterparts of the above.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000129/main.assets/f12-04-9780128202739.jpg)
