        #### Shape-based metrics
        
        Beyond its texture, the spatial distribution, localization, and size of a given abnormality carry additional information with potential diagnostic and prognostic value. Some of these metrics are simple and routinely assessed in clinical practice, whereas others are less known and more challenging to understand.  
        
        ##### One-, two-, and three-dimensional metrics
        
        One-dimensional (1D) metrics are based on measuring the distance between two points. These parameters are commonly used in daily clinical practice to describe the size of an abnormality. Diameters measured in different directions can be used to derive new statistics that can characterize additional properties (e.g., the ratio of the longest and the shortest diameters describes the roundness or ellipticity of a lesion). Two-dimensional (2D) metrics are calculated based on cross-sectional planes and are used to compute different parameters that are based on areas. These parameters are often used to approximate the three-dimensional (3D) properties of the abnormality (e.g., the 1D diameter and the 2D area are all considered approximations of the 3D volume). Three-dimensional metrics aim to quantify different aspects of a volumetric shape. The geometrical properties of 3D objects have been thoroughly examined in the field of rigid-body mechanics. All objects have so-called principal axes or eigenvectors. These mutually perpendicular axes intersect at the center of mass. The force applied to the principal axes acts independently, meaning that if we push or rotate the object along or around any of these axes, the object will not move or rotate in any other direction. These eigenvectors also have eigenvalues that can be interpreted as weights proportional to the amount of mass located along that given principal axis. The eigenvectors can be used to quantify different shape-based metrics— for example, roundness, which is the difference between the largest eigenvalues of the smallest enclosing and the largest enclosed ellipse.  
        
        ##### Fractal dimension
        
        Fractal dimension measures the spatial complexity of an object and quantifies self-symmetry by analyzing repeating patterns at different scales ( The most simplistic concept of quantifying fractal dimension is the box-counting method. In this analysis, the boxes of a grid occupied by the object are counted repeatedly at different scales. Then, the number of occupied boxes is plotted against the reciprocal of the scale on a log-log plot, and the box-counting dimension will be equal to the slope of the line connecting the data points (  
        
        #### Transform-based metrics
        
        Medical images comprise an immense number of pixel values distributed in the spatial domain. These images can be transformed into the frequency domain without losing any data as spatial- and frequency-domain representations of an image carry identical information. However, each emphasizes different aspects of an image; therefore, each enables different analytic options. In the frequency domain, the pattern and rate at which the pixel values change along spatial directions are used to represent the image instead of assigning gray-level values to spatial coordinates.  
        
        ##### Fourier and Gabor transforms
        
        Fourier transform decomposes the spatial-domain dataset into a fundamental sine wave and its harmonics along the two dimensions of an image. By converting the image into the frequency domain using this transform, spatial information is discarded. The Gabor transform, named after the Hungarian-born physicist Dénes Gábor, is a special case of the short-time Fourier transform, which enables the simultaneous evaluation of spatial and frequency information (  
        
        ##### Wavelet transforms
        
        Similar to the Fourier transform, wavelet transform also converts the image into the frequency domain, but spatial information is preserved (  
        
        ### Database building
        
        The power of predictive models heavily depends on having well-curated, sufficiently large datasets. Radiomics-based modeling can be performed with a few hundred patients as well; however, more extensive datasets would significantly enhance the predictive power and generalizability. Moreover, holistic models incorporating additional, nonradiomic features (e.g., clinical and genomic covariates) tend to be more robust; therefore, researchers should endeavor to capture several other domains of variables as well.  
        
        ### Modeling
        
        A detailed description of modeling goes beyond the focus of this chapter; however, a few aspects should be briefly discussed. The process of radiomic feature extraction will yield a virtually unlimited number of parameters, which often exceeds the sample size of the cohort used for modeling. Utilizing all features would inevitably result in overfitting; therefore, one needs to identify an optimal subset of input variables. Feature selection should be performed in a data-driven fashion and should be reported in a transparent manner. Various techniques (filtering, wrapper, and embedded methods) exist to pinpoint features that are robust, informative, and nonredundant ( Once the final set of input features is identified, one can proceed with building a specific predictive model. Different ML algorithms are associated with distinct inherent strengths and limitations; therefore, the choice of modeling definitely affects prediction performance ( Emphasis should also be placed on the thorough validation of models as nonvalidated predictive systems are of limited value ( Noting the high inconsistency in reporting of multivariate prediction tasks in medicine, researchers are advised to follow the recommendations set forth by the TRIPOD statement and the Radiomics Quality score (  
        
        ## Clinical implications
        
        The feasibility and potential utility of radiomics have been illustrated in various clinical scenarios. Significant success has been achieved in myocardial tissue characterization, coronary artery calcium quantification, coronary plaque phenotyping, and risk stratification of CV patients (  
        
        ### Characterization of myocardial texture
        
        A considerable number of proof-of-concept studies have demonstrated the capabilities of texture analysis to aid clinicians in various diagnostic dilemmas related to patients with suspected hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). In a small cohort,  In support of the presumptions above, radiomics seems to be capable of capturing subclinical changes in noncontrast cine cardiac MR images of hypertensive patients well beyond the efficiency of conventional image interpretation techniques ( The precise assessment of MI as well as myocardial viability are two other strengths of cardiac MR, and they account for a substantial proportion of referrals. Although late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) cardiac MR is a well-established and accurate method for the detection of ischemic myocardial scar ( With its unique capability for tissue characterization, cardiac MRI has become the primary tool for the noninvasive assessment of myocardial inflammation in patients with suspected myocarditis ( Despite being the most appropriate choice for myocardial tissue characterization, the availability of cardiac MR might be limited, and more accessible screening tools are warranted. Accordingly, Other investigators have attempted to detect infarcted myocardium from radiomics-based analysis of 2D echocardiograms as various radiomics descriptors such as first-order statistics ( If we are looking for alternatives to LGE MR for the detection of myocardial scar, late iodine enhancement CT scans might be an ideal choice as iodine contrast agents have similar wash-in and wash-out kinetics as gadolinium ( The detection of myocardial scars is fundamental to therapeutic decision-making, risk stratification, and therapeutic monitoring; however, the assessment of diffuse remodeling of the extracellular matrix is equally important. Multiple diagnostic strategies have been tested for the noninvasive assessment of diffuse extracellular matrix remodeling as an expanding body of evidence indicates that diffuse myocardial fibrosis is a causative factor of myocardial dysfunction and ventricular arrhythmias (  
        
        ### Automated coronary artery calcium scoring
        
        Coronary artery calcifications can be visualized and quantified with CT. The extent of coronary calcification is routinely expressed using the Agatston score, which has been shown to be an independent and robust predictor of adverse CV events (   
        
        ### Coronary plaque phenotyping
        
        Although the detection of coronary plaques relies on conventional coronary CT angiography-derived metrics, the comprehensive assessment of the plaque microenvironment, histology, and biology requires a more profound radiomic analysis. The radiomics-based phenotyping of a given plaque can identify high-risk plaque features—the radiological manifestations of complex pathological processes—as alterations in its attenuation histogram and texture. Out of the four main CT signatures of high-risk coronary atherosclerotic plaques, the napkin-ring sign (NRS)—a plaque cross-section with a central area of low CT attenuation apparently in contact with the lumen, surrounded by ring-shaped higher attenuation plaque tissue ( Visually detectable adverse plaque characteristics based on coronary CT angiography show only a modest correlation with intravascular ultrasound (IVUS), optical coherence tomography (OCT), or sodium-fluoride positron emission tomography (NaF18-PET)-derived features ( Advanced atherosclerotic lesions (early and late fibroatheroma or thin-cap atheroma) are associated with a higher risk of MI (   
        
        ### Radiomic phenotyping of perivascular fat
        
        There is an expanding body of evidence that perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) plays a pivotal role in the regulation of vascular function in both homeostasis and disease (  
        
        ### Valvular heart disease
        
        The assessment of mechanical prosthetic valve obstruction is challenging as the clinical and radiological signs are much alike, while the etiologies and the subsequent management are different. As part of a multimodality approach, cardiac CT has been suggested to facilitate the differentiation between thrombus, pannus, and vegetation ( Another interesting approach is the automated assessment of mitral regurgitation severity using radiomics-based ML classifiers. In a study, an SVM model utilizing texture features extracted from a rectangular ROI covering the regurgitant area of echocardiographic images exhibited an accuracy of over 95% in apical two-chamber, apical four-chamber, and parasternal long-axis views as well (  
        
        ### Intracardiac mass
        
        Echocardiography is the primary modality of choice for the differential diagnosis of intracardiac masses ( In patients with atrial fibrillation, transesophageal echocardiography is the gold standard imaging modality for the diagnosis and exclusion of left atrial (LA) and left atrial appendage (LAA) thrombi (  
        
        ### Risk stratification
        
        The accurate identification of high-risk patients who might benefit from more intensive therapeutic strategies represents a crucial mission in CV medicine. Radiomics can be helpful in such a scenario, as the extracted quantitative features can be supplied to ML-based predictive models to determine the risk of life-threatening cardiac events, hence providing a window of opportunity for treatment and prevention. Coronary artery calcium scoring only represents a small fraction of all information embedded in noncontrast cardiac CT scans. Therefore, a screening method that could integrate the assessment of coronary calcium and other phenotypic elements such as left ventricular hypertrophy would be highly desirable in preventive CV imaging. A study involving almost two thousand participants of the Dallas Heart Study has demonstrated that an automated pipeline using radiomic features extracted from noncontrast cardiac CT scans can achieve an AUC above 0.70 for detecting high-risk left ventricular hypertrophy ( Although numerous studies have attempted to explore the potentials of radiomics in plaque detection and phenotyping, there is only limited evidence of the prognostic value of coronary CT-derived quantitative intensity-based parameters. Nevertheless, it seems that the addition of quantitative plaque characteristics to clinical risk profile (as assessed by the Framingham risk score) and qualitative expert opinion increases the accuracy of predicting acute coronary syndrome (AUC: 0.64 vs. 0.79, P < .05) ( Both post-MI and HCM patients are susceptible to ventricular tachyarrhythmias that represent a well-established risk factor of sudden cardiac death. This unfavorable outcome can be prevented by the implantation of implantable cardioverter defibrillators ( It is a well-known fact that both the presence and the greater extent of LGE are associated with worse prognosis in HCM (  
        
        ## The future direction of radiomic research
        
        Radiomics is an appealing novel technology with the potential to expand medical knowledge and reform the field of CV imaging. It has achieved promising results in various clinical scenarios; nonetheless, there is still a long way to go before it transitions to routine clinical practice.  An inevitable step toward this aim would be the standardization of image acquisition, reconstruction, and postprocessing protocols, as it can be hard to determine whether differences in radiomic features reflect biological alterations or variations in the technical details of the imaging process ( It should also be highlighted that most of the published results were derived from proof-of-concept studies with relatively small sample size. Accordingly, for the verification of the proposed radiomics-based models and computer-aided diagnostic systems, multicenter and multivendor studies in larger cohorts are warranted. In addition, future investigations should also evaluate the clinical impact of radiomics analysis, as it is still unknown how much the utilization of such models improves patient care and outcomes. After proving the generalizability of the models, it should be ensured that radiomics-based decision support tools can be used conveniently without increasing clinical workload. In the CV imaging laboratory of the future, radiomics-based ML models will be directly linked to picture archiving and communication systems, and electronic medical records. Consequently, the extracted radiomic features can be easily compared with the results of previous visits and can be merged with information from different domains of clinical data to enable individualized decision-making.  
        
        ## Conclusions
        
        Radiomics represents an emerging image analysis technology with the potential to enhance the accuracy and precision of CV imaging. By unveiling imperceptible patterns in medical images, radiomics is capable of providing a detailed description of disease burden and linking distinct phenotypes to outcomes. In addition, radiomics offers a unique insight into tissue-level pathophysiology, which might facilitate the understanding of disease mechanisms. The utilization of radiomic features also holds the promise to objectify image interpretation, to tailor diagnostic and therapeutic strategies in a more individualized manner, and ultimately, to bring us one step closer to personalized patient management. If current efforts are able to resolve the existing technical challenges, radiomics will become a valuable tool in the clinical arena and will leave a permanent footprint in CV imaging.

        # Chapter 13: Automated interpretation of electrocardiographic tracings
        
        Mohammad Kachuee, and Majid Sarrafzadeh     Computer Science Department, University of California, Los Angeles, CA, United States  
        
        ## Abstract
        
        Electrocardiography (ECG) is frequently used to detect a wide variety of cardiac conditions. Historically, clinicians are trained to analyze ECG recordings and to make a diagnosis based on signal morphologies. However, due to the considerable monetary and nonmonetary costs associated with reliance on human experts as well as issues related to availability and continuous monitoring, there has been great attention toward the automated interpretation of ECG recordings. In this chapter, we present a brief background on ECG signals; then, we explain traditional and modern approaches to the automated analysis of ECG recordings, including methods based on feature engineering and automated end-to-end learning methods. Then, we conclude by discussing the evaluation of these systems and outlining research directions for future studies.
        
        ### Keywords
        
        Classification; Deep learning; Electrocardiography; Machine learning; Pattern recognition; Signal processing; Timeseries; Vital signals 
        
        1.  [Electrocardiography ](../B9780128202739000130/B9780128202739000130.xhtml#s0010)

        ## Electrocardiography
        
        Electrocardiogram (ECG or EKG) is a recording of the electrical activity of the heart measured using electrodes placed on the skin. Since its invention in the early 1900s, ECG has been widely used as a tool to diagnose various heart conditions, such as arrhythmias, ischemic heart disease, structural abnormalities, heart failure, and pacemaker dysfunction. A typical clinical ECG machine records from 12 leads based on 10 electrode contacts. Each lead provides a unique viewpoint to the electrical stimulation patterns across the heart ( [Fig. 13.1](#B9780128202739000130.xhtml#f0010) shows a typical ECG waveform with important key-points and cardiac cycles annotated. The P wave represents atrial depolarization where both atria contract simultaneously. The QRS complex marks the beginning of ventricular depolarization, initiating ventricular contraction. The pause after the QRS complex, the ST segment, marks repolarization of the ventricles. Lastly, the T wave corresponds to the end of ventricular repolarization and the end of ventricular contraction (systole). ECG recordings can be used to measure major electrophysiologic characteristics such as rate, rhythm, and axis. The heart rate is a measure of the time it takes for the heart to complete one cycle. The normal resting heart rate is within the range of 60–100 beats per minute. An irregular waveform pattern on the ECG signal can be indicative of different arrhythmias or pacemaker dysfunction. Usually, multiple leads are used to find the electrical axis of the heart. Any physical displacement or structural abnormality of the heart also results in the deviation of the electrical axis. Furthermore, the ECG can be used as a tool to diagnose important heart conditions such as hypertrophy in which myocardial tissue gets enlarged/thickened, causing disruption in ventricular systolic and diastolic function. Myocardial infarction is another important condition in which a part of myocardial tissue becomes ischemic and is replaced by akinetic scar tissue as a result of diminished blood flow, usually as a consequence of coronary artery disease. Further detail regarding ECG recordings and corresponding clinical cardiac conditions are outside the scope of this chapter, and are available in specialized textbooks ( ![Figure 13.1 A typical electrocardiogram (ECG) waveform with annotation of inflection points as well as important segments of the cardiac cycle.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000130/main.assets/f13-01-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 13.1 A typical electrocardiogram (ECG) waveform with annotation of inflection points as well as important segments of the cardiac cycle.
        
        ECG signals are susceptible to different types of noise and artifacts from various physiological, instrumental, and environmental sources. Baseline wander, powerline interference, muscular activity, and electrode motion are considered as major noise and artifacts impacting real-world ECG recordings. Usually, a preprocessing stage is included in an automated analysis system to enhance the quality of signals before any analysis is performed. For this purpose, different filtering and denoising approaches have been suggested in the literature, spanning from very simple moving average or median filters to complex deep learning models trained to recover the clean signal from noisy inputs ( 
        
        *   1\. Baseline wander is considered as very low-frequency artifact caused by breathing or slow body movements. A very simple high-pass filter can be used to filter signal components of less than 0.5 Hz. While it is straightforward to remove baseline wander, it is a very important step due to the often-large drifts it may cause to the signal baseline.
        *   2\. Powerline interference on ECG circuitry is another source of noise causing 50 or 60 Hz (and their harmonics) sinusoidal interference. Notch filters are usually designed to remove frequencies related to the powerline and its harmonics, and can be used to reduce the impact on signal quality. However, care must be taken as important signal components exist within the same frequency range, and excessive filtering may cause signal distortion especially to low-frequency waves such as P and T waves.
        *   3\. Muscular activity originating from the myocardium can cause significant interference with recorded electrical activity on the ECG tracing. From the frequency domain, it is very difficult to distinguish and remove this type of interference. One possible solution is to consider the periodic nature of ECG signals and to use longer signal windows since other muscular activities are not periodic.
        *   4\. Electrode motion artifacts are caused by skin impedance changes during physical activity. This artifact has frequency components within the range of 1–10 Hz strongly impacting major ECG signal components. Similar to muscular activity interferences, removing electrode motion artifacts requires more sophisticated filtering and analysis such as adaptive filters, estimating motion signals, wave averaging, and so forth.
        
         
        
        ## Traditional approach to automated ECG analysis
        
        Moving average (mean filtering) is frequently used to smooth ECG signals by removing high-frequency oscillations. Median filtering is often useful for removal of noisy samples captured by analog to digital converter (ADC) circuitry. While moving average and median filters are easy to implement and effective in practice, it should be noted that using these filters, especially in large window sizes, may result in oversmoothing or adverse nonlinear impacts for the case of median filters. Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters can be used to design different band-pass or band-rejection filters. However, designing a powerful FIR filter requires using large window lengths that may cause considerable latency and require extra memory to store a large signal segment during the process. Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) filters are usually much more compact and require very small filter windows; however, the phase response for IIR filters does not have a proper phase response as in FIR filters and may cause distortions to the original signals being processed. One solution to using the compactness of IIR filters without any adverse impact on the phase response is to use IIR filters in a bidirectional forward-backward fashion. A forward-backward filter simply applies an IIR filter on the signal window twice by inverting the signal window across the time axis after the first filtering and inverting again after the second filtering. One possible drawback of this approach is that bidirectional filters are not causal, which in practice is handled by using signal buffers causing a certain amount of latency. Time-Frequency domain methods such as discrete wavelet decomposition (DCT) can be used to extract different time and frequency components and to apply different filtering or denoising functions. Additionally, DCT can be used as an effective compression method as the decomposition of natural signals usually tends to be sparse having many zero components and a few large nonzero components. For a more detailed discussion of these methods, we refer interested readers to Recently, deep learning methods have been suggested as powerful tools for ECG denoising, imputation, and generation. Denoising autoencoders implemented as either a convolutional encoder-decoder pair or as sequence-to-sequence architectures are natural choices to make denoising models. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are suggested to generate synthesized data, applied to ECG inputs; one can use GANs for data augmentation or as a representation learning objective. Another use case would be to impute missing values which are in this case missing or noisy ECG samples based on partially observed data points ( [Fig. 13.2](#B9780128202739000130.xhtml#f0015) shows the general pipeline used in traditional automated ECG analysis systems consisting of delineation, feature extraction, and predictive analysis. In the delineation step, ECG key-points are detected for a signal window at hand, usually P, Q, R, S, and T waves for typical ECG signals. Note that based on certain clinical conditions it may not be always possible to detect all the typical key-points for all leads, or the morphology of waves can be drastically different from normal healthy signals. Afterward, based on the detected key-points, different features that are considered relevant to the final prediction task are extracted from the input window. It may include physiologically well-known features such as ST-segment length, the relative amplitude of key-points or any other expert-defined features such as frequency domain features, power spectrum, specific compression coefficient, and so forth ( ![Figure 13.2 Traditional pipeline for ECG classification consisting of signal delineation, feature extraction, and prediction.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000130/main.assets/f13-02-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 13.2 Traditional pipeline for ECG classification consisting of signal delineation, feature extraction, and prediction.
        
        ![Figure 13.3 An example of different hand-engineered features extracted from an ECG waveform.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000130/main.assets/f13-03-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 13.3 An example of different hand-engineered features extracted from an ECG waveform.
        
        As the final processing step, extracted feature vectors are fed to a predictor model. In the literature, various model families have been used to learn the target feature relationship including logistic, support vector machine, decision tree, and random forest classifiers. As introducing different machine learning models is not the focus of this chapter, we refer interested readers to recently published review work (  
        
        ## End-to-end automated ECG analysis
        
        As discussed in the previous section, traditional automated ECG processing techniques require finding important signal key-points within a certain processing window. However, due to different signal morphologies, it is not always straightforward to detect these key-points. For instance, based on specific clinical conditions, certain points may not appear in ECG signals or may appear in different forms as they usually appear in a normal population. As an example, a heart axis inversion may cause R waves to appear as minima in certain ECG channels, or an elevated ST segment may impose waveform changes that are far from normal morphologies ( From another perspective, recent advances in pattern recognition suggest that even a completely accurate delineation followed by hand-engineered feature extraction would lead to nonoptimal solutions ( Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are among the main drivers of advances in the field of deep learning. The convolutional layer outputs also can be interpreted as the results of different pattern detectors applied to a certain input. A typical CNN architecture consists of several convolution layers, each followed by nonlinearity, normalization, and pooling functions, as well as one or two classification layers. functions. The main drawback of RNNs stems from the limitations of gradient-based learning which effectively prevents RNNs from capturing representations from more than a dozen steps due to severe vanishing gradient issues. Note that to train an RNN, the computation graph of the recursive operations is unrolled, so the resulting networks are at least as deep as the number of time-steps. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) have been proposed in order to circumvent the issue by using gating mechanisms to help holding the internal state representation ( Architectures discussed earlier require a fix-sized input; however, ECG signals are usually recorded in varying lengths. Also, due to modeling and computational reasons applying learning models on very long signal sequences would be impractical. More specifically, it would cause massive memory usage and model complexity in CNNs or severe vanishing gradient in RNNs. In the literature, ECG records are commonly split into smaller fixed-size windows or segments. The size of processing windows usually spans from a single heartbeat to less than a minute based on the sampling rates, dataset sizes, and most importantly clinical conditions to be detected. It is well known that certain heart conditions may cause a consistent impact on ECG (e.g., myocardial infarction), while others only cause transient changes such as certain arrhythmia or pacemaker dysfunction. Also, each signal window can be aligned and preprocessed, or it can contain raw signals without any initial preparation. Certain models only permit a limited input length. For instance, LSTMs and GRUs are only effective in processing up to 50 time-steps and rapidly decline in performance for lengthier sequences. On the other hand, the size and distribution of the training dataset at hand determine how complex the trained prediction models can be. If only a relatively small set of data is available for the training, using a smaller window size and a more compact model would result in better final performances. Another factor to be considered is the sampling frequency. ECG signals are usually sampled at rates as low as 100 Hz to as high as 4 KHz. It is often very helpful to resample the raw signal to a reasonable sampling rate that provides the necessary signal features while minimizing the number of samples in each window. Lastly, the window size directly impacts the amount of memory and compute required to make predictions, as well as the classification latencies. To summarize, the following factors should be considered in selecting the proper window size: 
        
        1.  • Model architecture
        2.  • Dataset size
        3.  • Sampling frequency
        4.  • Cardiac conditions to be detected
        5.  • Computational, memory, and latency limitations
        
        It is worth noting that CNN and RNN models are often combined such that an initial CNN network summarizes the usually lengthy input sequence to a set of more compact features while an RNN takes in these compact features as input to make the final predictions. This architecture can be particularly useful for detecting certain conditions that require considering a large signal window that simple CNNs or RNNs would usually fail at. Such a network is trained in end-to-end error signal backpropagating from the classification layers to unfolded RNN layers as well as CNN layers.  
        
        ## Evaluation of ECG classifiers
        
        Evaluation of ECG analysis systems can be very challenging due to different factors such as limited quantity and quality of expert annotations, huge class imbalance, and coexisting health conditions to name a few. Another important aspect that is mostly unanswered in the current literature is considering the importance and severity of medical conditions in the evaluation of diagnostic systems. For instance, a system that is detecting several different diseases should be evaluated and compared based on the importance of weighted average of these disease types rather than simply using the average performance across all conditions ( In terms of the number of True Positive (TP), True Negative (TN), False Positive (FP), and False Negative (FN) predictions, typical evaluation measures ![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000130/main.stripin/si15.png)Intuitively speaking, Accuracy measures the ratio of correct predictions to the total number of predictions. Precision measures the ratio of positive predicted cases which are detected correctly to the number of all predicted positive cases, showing what percentage of samples predicted as positive are actually positive samples. Recall is the ratio of correctly detected cases to the number of actual positive cases, basically measuring how reliable a system is in detecting a less frequent positive condition. F1 score is reporting a harmonic mean of precision and recall values, which is quite helpful in comparing different systems using a single value rather than considering different measures at the same time ( Apart from these numeric measures, other more illustrative evaluation tools are often adopted in the literature. Confusion matrix is one of the most well-known evaluation measures that are frequently used in multiclass classification problems. In a confusion matrix, each row represents the number of actual samples in each class and each column represents the number of predicted samples for each class. Ideally, a perfect classifier would have zero elements for nondiagonal positions that are representing incorrectly classified samples. Furthermore, off-diagonal values can be used to investigate how different classes are being classified incorrectly with respect to other classes, i.e., confused or mixed-up with each other. Please refer to ( Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve demonstrates the rate of true positives (TPR) versus the rate of false positives (FPR) to visually evaluate the operation of a binary classifier at different decision threshold settings. Here: <mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:math> ![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000130/main.stripin/si16.png)<mml:math alttext="MathML" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:math> ![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000130/main.stripin/si17.png)Intuitively, the ROC curve shows the trade-off between the ability to detect positive samples versus the rate of samples detected as positive by error. Often area under the ROC (AU-ROC) curve is used to measure how close a certain model is to the ideal case, where high recall (or, TPR) is achieved without inducing any false positives, in which the AU-ROC approaches to one ([Fig. 13.6](#B9780128202739000130.xhtml#f0035)). Alternatively, the precision versus recall curve has been used to illustrate the precision-recall trade-off and the area under this curve is used as a quantitative performance measure to compare classifiers. There is evidence suggesting that the precision-recall curve is more informative in binary classification tasks with a considerable class imbalance (  
        
        ## Research directions
        
        In the previous sections, we presented different approaches for automated analysis of ECG recordings. Many of these approaches rely on machine learning models that require training based on a dataset. Practically, the training dataset determines the complexity of models to be trained which translates to the complexity of patterns to be detected and the final performance of the model. A common approach that is widely used in the deep learning literature is to augment a dataset with altered samples from the original dataset to effectively produce a larger training set. For instance, imaging data can be augmented by horizontal flipping, randomly cropping different parts of an image, changing pixel colors, etc. However, data augmentation for ECG signals is more challenging and most of the studies either use no data augmentation or use very basic augmentation such as adding a small Gaussian noise. A more comprehensive study on data augmentation for ECG signals can potentially unlock the use of more powerful and more complex architectures compared to the models being used today. ![Figure 13.5 An example of a confusion matrix used to evaluate a 5-class arrhythmia classifier. For instance, Physionet MIMIC III ( ![Figure 13.6 ROC curve can be used to evaluate classifiers at different decision thresholds.         Figure 13.6 ROC curve can be used to evaluate classifiers at different decision thresholds. The figure shows a few curves including a perfect classifier, a random classifier, and a typical case.
        
        Another avenue of research is using attention-based models for ECG analysis. Attention models are currently considered state-of-the-art for tasks that require detecting patterns within long intervals. Also, the attention mechanism can be used to reduce the computational load of processing signals. For example, Interpretability is considered one of the main challenges for any automated learning-based health analytic system. There are many legal and ethical concerns associated with block-box models that only provide statistically appealing performances but do not provide any reasoning based on each analyzed instance. There have been many recent endeavors to address this by either using models that provide insights about their operations or modeling dynamics of a black-box model. However, the case of timeseries input domain is more challenging than usual tabular data as explanations for a signal window should present visually appealing and yet accurate interpretations. This requires extensive research in the interpretation of timeseries models. A recent work by  
        
        ## Conclusions
        
        In this chapter, we presented an overview of the methods used for the automated interpretation of ECG records. We covered basic concepts about the ECG signal as well as different established signal processing, feature extraction, and recognition approaches. In the end, this chapter presents a few directions for future research that the authors believe to be promising avenues of extending the current literature.

        # Chapter 14: Machine learning in cardiovascular genomics, proteomics, and drug discovery
        
        Ming Wai Yeung[¹](#B9780128202739000142.xhtml#aff1), Jan-Walter Benjamins[¹](#B9780128202739000142.xhtml#aff1), Pim van der Harst[¹](#B9780128202739000142.xhtml#aff1)^,[²](#B9780128202739000142.xhtml#aff2)^,[³](#B9780128202739000142.xhtml#aff3), and Luis Eduardo Juarez-Orozco[¹](#B9780128202739000142.xhtml#aff1)^,[³](#B9780128202739000142.xhtml#aff3)     ¹University of Groningen, University Medical Center Groningen, Department of Cardiology, Groningen, The Netherlands     ²University of Groningen, University Medical Centre Groningen, Department of Genetics, Groningen, The Netherlands     ³Department of Cardiology, Division Heart and Lungs, University Medical Centre Utrecht, University of Utrecht, Utrecht, The Netherlands  
        
        ## Abstract
        
        This chapter discusses the current status and challenges in applying machine learning in three closely connected fields, namely genomics, proteomics, and drug discovery. Usage of machine learning methods are described and compared in the context of respective fields through selected literature. The current performance of implemented machine learning methods is described in comparison to traditional statistical methods. Finally, this chapter discusses potential future perspectives for implementation of machine learning in genomics, proteomics, and drug discovery.
        
        ### Keywords
        
        Cardiology; Cardiovascular disease; Drug discovery; Genomics; Machine learning; Proteomics

        ## Introduction
        
        Modern cardiovascular medicine and research have seen the development of novel state-of-the-art techniques and analytics. This convergence is currently helping unravel the mechanistic determinants, pathways, and potential therapeutic targets in cardiovascular diseases. On the one hand, three decades of refinements (including the completion of the Human Genome Project) in the study of genomics and its downstream influence into the study of proteomics have provided notions of the deterministic but also dynamic nature of this continuum (see [Fig. 14.1](#B9780128202739000142.xhtml#f0010)) in cardiac health and disease. On the other hand, the recent advent of modern machine learning (ML)-based artificial intelligence has provided the opportunity to explore, integrate, and analyze large amounts of data in terms of their inherent complex interrelations and nonlinear dependencies.   ![Figure 14.1 The continuum of -omics levels of analysis. Machine learning methods can be applied on the studies of different -omics levels such as genome, transcriptome, and proteome, which are major fields in molecular biology. Combination of evidence from different -omics levels contribute to new insights of our understanding of cardiovascular diseases.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000142/main.assets/f14-01-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 14.1 The continuum of -omics levels of analysis. Machine learning methods can be applied on the studies of different -omics levels such as genome, transcriptome, and proteome, which are major fields in molecular biology. Combination of evidence from different -omics levels contribute to new insights of our understanding of cardiovascular diseases.
        
        In essence, the very-high-throughput nature of -omics data at different analytical and mechanistic levels represents a suitable target for ML and is expected to boost our capacity to generate valuable insights in the study of cardiovascular disease. This chapter summarizes and interprets the current evidence on the application of ML in the genomic-proteomics horizon and in modern drug discovery initiatives.  
        
        ## Machine learning in genomics
        
        ML involves use of computational algorithms for a specific task, which is usually achieved through extracting characteristics/patterns from data. One key feature of ML is that the performance of the learner or model (also called classifier when the objective is data classification, i.e., a binary output) is expected to improve with exposure to more data (experience). Thanks to the increased availability of genomic data in recent years, various ML algorithms are being adopted to help identify “patterns” in the genome and to predict functional consequences of specific genetic variations.  
        
        ### Molecular genetics
        
        ML algorithms, using supervised and unsupervised learning methods (where the output label for the output is known or unknown, respectively), have yielded fruitful results in annotation of genomes ranging from identifying various genomic elements to predicting their functional consequences ( The choice of the algorithm should be made based on the task to be solved but also the characteristics of the data at hand. Importantly, data transformation (i.e., generation of features to represent the data) is also critical for the end-performance of the models. For example, Pertea et al. developed a decision tree-based model called GeneSplicer to classify splice sites in Arabidopsis thaliana and in the human genome ( While elaborate feature engineering incorporating extensive domain knowledge can improve performance, it may be not always efficient/feasible due to time constraints or limited understanding of the underlying mechanistic structures of the subject at hand. In recent years, ML methods with capability to learn features from data such as Deep Learning are gaining popularity (reviewed by Besides functional annotation of a specific genomic region, ML can also be applied to predict the biological effect of individual genomic variations. Pathogenicity prediction is highly relevant in cardiovascular clinical research, especially in rare genetic diseases. Annotations of the variation in different contexts including evolutionary conservation and location on genomic level, regulatory information on transcription level, and functional change on translation/protein level have served as input features for training ML methods ( Thus far, benchmarking studies have been carried out to compare the performance of different in-silico prediction tools for variants involved in different classes of diseases like cancer ( Conversely, studies have also been carried out to build specific prediction models with the aim of achieving a better performance than generic predictors. Unsupervised ML may be an alternative if a reasonable labeled training set is not available. In a recent paper by  
        
        ### Population and complex genetics
        
        The role of genetic markers in cardiovascular disease risk is an active area of research in population genetics. Multifactorial or complex diseases are those that are influenced by both genetic and environmental factors in contrast to Mendelian disorders whose cause can be attributed to single mutations with large detrimental effects. Complex diseases are often linked to multiple genetic variants, which are usually weaker in effect as compared with those discovered in Mendelian diseases. Associations between complex disease and genetic variants are discovered by genome-wide association study (GWAS) which look at the difference in allele frequency of variants between cases and controls. ![Figure 14.2 ML Targets in genomics. ML models have been developed to identify functional elements such as long-range regulatory elements and splicing sites on the genome. They can be further customized for specific disease associated genes and/or diseases. For instance, prioritization of a splicing variant among a large number of variants to be associated with a cardiovascular trait by comparing the clustering results between case and control.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000142/main.assets/f14-02-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 14.2 ML Targets in genomics. ML models have been developed to identify functional elements such as long-range regulatory elements and splicing sites on the genome. They can be further customized for specific disease associated genes and/or diseases. For instance, prioritization of a splicing variant among a large number of variants to be associated with a cardiovascular trait by comparing the clustering results between case and control.
        
        Many cardiovascular disorders such as coronary artery disease (CAD), atrial fibrillation (AF), hypertension (HTN), and stroke are complex diseases ( In recent years there has been interest in personal disease risk profiling using genetic information ( Since complex diseases are influenced by both genetic and environmental factors, it is sensible to combine information from all aspects such as genetic risk profile, clinical risk factors and lifestyle to maximize the predictive power of risk models ( Finally, ML can be used in genomic analysis beyond predictive purpose. Comparisons of diverse ML methods give new biological insights, such as the genetic architecture of complex diseases. Deep learning, for instance, is a method capable of abstracting nonlinear relationships that can be deployed to model gene-gene interactions (epistasis) (

        ## Machine learning in proteomics
        
        Following the line of modern system-levels approach to cardiovascular disease, emerging molecular profiling technologies such as proteomics could provide new insights into the pathophysiology of cardiovascular disease. However, implementations of ML in proteomic studies have not yet witnessed an accelerated advance comparable to the exploratory initiatives described in genomics. It is possible that this discrete (although steadily increasing) development relates to the position of proteomics within the continuum of translational research and medicine (genomics—proteomics—metabolomics—clinical implementation). In this sense, either from a bottom-up or top-bottom perspective, proteomics lies further down the line as ML optimization of data-driven tasks permeates into the analytical arsenal at our disposal. Clearly however, high-throughput molecular (protein) profiling data represents fertile ground for deep profiling of such varying molecular entities in relation to cardiovascular disease. Proteomics deals in multifaceted and dynamic profiles with complex signaling pathways and high levels of interconnectivity. In this sense, the potential of ML to explore nonlinear dependencies between large amounts of variables and to select, integrate, and interpret complex variable structures can ultimately refine classification and predictive performance, facilitating timely applicability in the evaluation of proteomic data. [Fig. 14.3](#B9780128202739000142.xhtml#f0020) depicts the continuum of applicability of ML in proteomics research. However, it is useful to contextualize that comprehensive data evaluation in this regard can benefit from a fair combination of statistical and ML approaches. Very early, ML implementation in cardiovascular proteomics research has predominantly utilized urinary proteomes, with a few reports dedicated to blood sampling.         Urine proteomic analysis though ML has also been conducted in a “discovery” study by Thereon, integration of numerous urinary protein biomarkers obtained from capillary electrophoresis and mass spectrometry has also been performed to identify patients with asymptomatic left ventricular diastolic dysfunction in patients with arterial HTN. Urinary proteomics has been also approached through ML for the identification of patients with heart failure (HF) with reduced ejection fraction. For instance, Aforementioned studies focusing on urinary proteomics have also underlined that coexistence of renal impairment may represent a major modifier of studied profiles (since excretion is by definition, hampered) and that results may not generalize to such subpopulations. Given the comorbid association of HF and chronic kidney disease, In parallel, Quite recently, Comparison of analytical approaches to characterize potential mechanistic profiles represents an interesting view in modern proteomics. In this sense, An emerging aspect within the horizon of ML application in proteomic analyses is that of method standardization and quality control. Previously in this chapter, it has been explained how a comprehensive ML workflow comprises organized sequential steps that guarantee the robustness of the resulting models as well as their generalizability. One of such stages is adequate feature selection, which allows the user to reduce the dimensionality of the data, focus on consequent variables, and reduce computational needs to optimize training times. Very-highly correlated input variables may represent redundancy and hamper optimal workflow and modeling unnecessarily, while very weak classifiers (variables) may increase the risk of overfitting unduly. Since this balance in the input structure tuning is crucial, efforts have begun to discuss, experiment, and converge in general recommendations that guarantee seamless flow in ML workflows dedicated to high-throughput omics data (i.e., genomics and proteomics). For instance, Deep Learning has recently become the sharpest end of ML analytics due to its success in image and complex signal recognition. Its performance, once constrained by computational and storage capabilities, is now unbound and has begun to permeate into proteomic research. In 2017, Furthermore, Interestingly, novel maneuvers to economize data utilization and needs such as transfer learning have begun to be used in explorative studies for mass spectrometry analysis results ( Furthermore, proteomics research also contemplates the analysis of a very large number of protein sequences for experimental functional characterization (e.g., using Gene Ontology), and ML-based approaches are expected to help in this multiclass and multilabel niche. In summary, the implementation of ML in the field of cardiovascular proteomics research has witnessed the progression between integration of high-dimensional classifiers (mostly through SVM) and modern deep learning approaches for high-throughput identification and function-prediction proteomic data. The suggested classifiers have been based on established software that could improve the identification of patients with cardiovascular disease (including CAD, DVT, HF, and cardiomyopathies), cardiovascular risk factors (dyslipidemia), or risk of adverse cardiovascular events, including death. However, such studies have been restricted in sample size and novel interest in analytical standardization and quality control for adequate ML model training and validation is only recently reemerging. On the other hand, Deep Learning-based approaches to proteomics are being explored as tools to optimize pattern recognition and functional identification/prediction, but only marginally in cardiovascular research. Considering the advancing technologies of molecular profiling, proteomics is eventually expected to consolidate as a standard component of our approach to cardiovascular disease characterization that could be routinely generated from patient samples processed and integrated into, for example, biomarker signatures that convey clinically relevant insights through ML analytics.         ## Machine learning in drug discovery
        
        Over the past century, drug discovery has evolved in multiple phases from the coincidental discovery of disease-treating substances—extracted from plants or found otherwise in biological organisms such as fungi—through a knowledge based, but manual approach to a fully automated industry. Following the initial extraction of active substances from plants, a first step in biochemical synthesis was taken to create the active molecular structures, isolated from their native organisms of origin. In the following decennia, wide ranges of chemical compounds were screened for activity in cells, without a prior chosen biological target, such as an amino-acid or protein. After discovery of a compound, a proper target playing a role in disease was then searched. This is what is known as phenotypic drug discovery or “classical” pharmacology. More recently, drug discovery has shifted toward a target-based approach, in which the disease modifying biological targets are first identified, followed by the search for chemical compounds with the required effect on the given targets. Based on available chemical property databases a preselection of chemical compounds can be made for inclusion in multiple screening rounds in which slight molecular modifications are made to optimize target modification and to minimize effect on closely related structures. In de novo drug design, “in-silico” virtual prescreening is performed with computer models. Chemical properties of molecular substructures are thereby tested against the intended target, aiming for optimally targeting synthesized models. Most of these computer models are based on chemical compound descriptors, such as quantitative structure-activity relations (QSARs), giving an indication of how a synthesized molecule will alter biological targets. Despite tremendous developments as seen in drug discovery over the past century, including the migration to a more target focused design process, the rate of positive treatment of disease is still relatively low. For example, Drug discovery also entails minimizing activity of synthesized substances in nonrelated biological targets, meaning to maximally reduce side-effects. In currently prescribed drugs, side-effects are numerous, and in some cases, serious adverse events (AEs) occur. An example is given by Schmidt et al. investigating side-effects in PCSK9 inhibitors. The investigators report that lipid lowering PCSK9 inhibitors are more effective than statin in lowering short- and mid-term LDL-C levels, as well in reducing long-term risk for CVD, showing no significant effect on mortality ( Warfarin is an anticoagulation drug, known for its increased risk for bleeding and hemorrhage ( Additionally, Spironolactone is a diuretic that prevents dropping potassium-levels while facilitating excretion of water from the body. Overall, the one-size-fits-all nature of most commonly used drugs lays the primary basis for reduced effects in parts of the addressed patient population, and for undesired, adverse side-effects reported frequently in literature. Individual biological structures in humans differ due to individuals’ genetic makeups and their dependent protein profiles. This not only affects their individual risk to develop cardiovascular diseases, but also their individual drug metabolisms, thereby determining the way they respond to their treatments, and what complications or side effects they face. Therefore, a more patient-tailored and better disease targeting approach is required in the development of new cardiovascular drugs to solve issues seen in current drug therapy. As described before, software models are currently used to perform a prescreening of components with potential disease target modifying chemical properties, with none or minimal activity toward non-targeted biological structures at the same time. Expert coded rules and traditionally simplistic regression or classification QSARs are used to predict chemical properties of newly synthesized substances in relation to their activity toward a drug target. Research into the application of expert coded rules by ML and particularly deep learning techniques have the ability to “see” patterns in complex data structures, allowing humans to uncover information from complex data that would be otherwise hidden to the human eye. Thereby deep learning models may represent a powerful extension to traditional statistical models, such as linear and logistic regression models that perform well on one or a handful of independent variables, but gracefully fail to uncover dependencies in high-dimensional data. Following the successes of advanced ML techniques in other fields such as image processing, the first examples of ML models have already been recently developed in the field of drug discovery. A first example that aims for increased drug target effectiveness, is shown by  Following more traditional feature selection strategies to infer QSAR models, ML techniques assist in the approach of feature learning on chemical compounds. It was reported by To overcome the poor predictive power of most rule-based systems and traditional QSARs, An example of research undertaken to diminish undesired side-effects in newly synthesized drugs can be found in the work of Most examples so far focus largely on better targeting biological structures that require modification in disease. However, except for It should be noted that, even with more precisely targeted drugs, identification of a patient’s genetic profile in relation to the targeted disease will remain crucial in administering drugs in a personalized way. Presently, the only part of a total solution seems to be to identify patient groups that are most likely to respond to a drug, and that are most unlikely to have any AEs in any of the non-disease-related, nontargeted biological structures, based on their genetic profiles. Applying ML techniques may help to both improve patient selection and patient specific targeting of the disease, by development of personalized medications, improving overall patient outcomes, and preventing side-effects and adverse events induced by pharmacological treatment. Additionally, these models could assist to minimize adverse side-effects on nonrelated biological structures.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000142/main.assets/f14-05-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 14.5 ML-supported cardiovascular drug development horizon. ML models have shown to be of increased predictive value compared to rule-based QSARs, by better inferring and matching the required biochemical properties of potentially useful chemical components in relation to the treated disease. Additionally, these models could assist to minimize adverse side-effects on nonrelated biological structures.
        
        Where the first steps have been taken to improve gene-based patient selection for certain drug treatment, and the first ML models have been used for biochemical feature learning as well as feature selection, huge improvements are to be expected, if ML models will be applied further on integral multiomics data, to gain knowledge of mechanisms underlying disease, and to improve identification of disease-related biological drug targets. Finally, combined improvement of disease-targeting medications and selection of responders should not only improve patient outcomes but also positively affect the economic burden of healthcare costs on society, by lowering unnecessary hospital admissions as well as readmissions.  
        
        ## Summary
        
        Adaption of ML varies in the field of genomics, proteomics, and drug discovery in cardiovascular research. Drug Discovery. ML is widely used in the study of genomics in cardiovascular research for various purposes from variant annotation to disease risk prediction. It is less popular in proteomic analyses due to current limits in performance. ML has been used for QSAR analyses with a generally superior performance over simple rule-based and statistical methods, such as linear/logistic regression. While traditional ML methods namely SVM and random forest remain the most popular methods, emergence of deep learning in this field is expected with increasing data availability in the field. Efforts of developing better prediction/classification models with ML for disease status/risk have been seen in all three fields. An integral workflow/framework combining these data could be a promising approach to further enhance the predictive performance of ML models.

        # Chapter 15: Wearable devices and machine learning algorithms for cardiovascular health assessment
        
        Abdallah Elshafeey, Omar Mhaimeed, Jamal Al Ani, and Mohamed B. Elshazly     Department of Medicine and Medical Education, Weill Cornell Medicine-Qatar, Doha, Qatar  
        
        ## Abstract
        
        The rapid improvement in wearable technology and its increasing sophistication is providing endless opportunities for progress in societal wellbeing and healthcare institution. Chapter 15 discusses the evolving field of digital medicine, specifically smart wearables, and its application to both cardiovascular health and disease. It begins by first introducing some of the currently used sensors and detailing their underlying mechanisms of action. Thereafter, it explores the concept of machine learning and how it allows for the rapid and meaningful analysis of the millions of bytes of data collected by these sensors on a daily basis. Further, we delve into some of the ways wearables are being used to monitor cardiac health and disease, including: disease prevention through lifestyle management, screening for disease, and disease management. Lastly, this chapter provides a discussion of some of the challenges facing this rapidly evolving field.
        
        ### Keywords
        
        Cardiovascular health; Digital medicine; Machine learning; Smart wearables; Technology

        ## Introduction
        
        Smart wearables are smart, consumer-grade devices that can be worn on the body either as an accessory or part of clothing. They include clothing, ear-wear, watches, headbands, rings, sociometric badges, and wristbands. Smart wearables incorporate high processing power, advanced software, sophisticated sensors that can track activity, Global Positioning System (GPS), and biometric data. In the rapidly proliferating technological world of our modern day, the plethora of smart wearables in the market has made it rather difficult for one to keep up with this field. However, recent advancements in technology have begun to have implications on smart wearables and their role on human health, and investing in the pursuit of the virtues of smart wearables may very well be a worthwhile endeavor. Medical wearables date back to around 1286, when the first wearable eyeglasses were made by Salvino D’Armate ( In the past few years, the smart wearables industry has been centered around the wrist, particularly in the form of smart watches, which have contributed to its massive growth ( Another major driver for the smart wearables market is healthcare. Wearables are significantly improving in their ability to capture and record real-time user activity and biometric data, and have an appeal in the healthcare sector as they allow for daily monitoring of activity and a number of clinical parameters ( Smart wearables also allow for remote patient monitoring of biometric data by measuring an individual’s pulse throughout the day across a number of various activities. Additionally, some can monitor the blood pressure and may even record a patient’s heart rhythm through a single-lead electrocardiograph (ECG). Although this is not as accurate as the typical 12-lead ECG used in the clinical workplace, it can still provide invaluable information of a patient’s heart rhythm ( A systematic review of 22 subjects conducted in June of 2019 by a team in Germany concluded that mobile health devices can aid in the early diagnosis and treatment of atrial fibrillation (AF), and that successful application of mobile health technologies could significantly contribute to reducing the cost of illness associated with AF (  Smart wearables can also aid in the issue of medication adherence. In case of adults with chronic illnesses who are prescribed medications, 30%–50% of the medications are not taken as prescribed (  
        
        ## Types of data collected
        
        Smart wearables have evolved over the years and have become capable of monitoring a multitude of organs, thereby providing real-time information about the various functions of the human body. These include devices that collect epidermal, ocular, intracochlear, dental, biochemical, and physiological parameters that can subsequently be processed and analyzed by complex algorithms and artificial intelligence (AI) software ( There are many different types of sensors, each of which can collect unique data about the human body such as heart rate, blood pressure, activity levels and much more. Some examples of such sensors include: 
        
        1.  • Accelerometers, altimeters, and GPS systems that can determine characteristics such as acceleration, speed, pace, and altitude. This information can then be combined with age, sex, weight, and height to give an indication of activity levels at any point in time. This is done through complex machine learning algorithms that can determine parameters such as the number of calories burned, number of steps taken, distance walked, and others.
        2.  • Heart rate sensors that can continuously measure heart rate at rest and during exercise. Most devices use a technology known as photoplethysmography (PPG), which consists of a light-emitting diode that emits green photons toward the skin. The light interacts with blood and gets absorbed at various degrees based on the blood flow, and the reflected light is then received by a photodiode and interpreted by the receiver. Again, machine learning algorithms that detect time from pulse peak to peak are able to determine heart rate (
        3.  • ECG sensors that can provide single lead ECG recordings whenever needed, or on a regular basis. Most sensors like the one used by the Apple Watch do this through utilization of a vector between the left and right arms when the patient places a finger on the watch.
        4.  • Sensors that can measure blood pressure when prompted. These include devices that utilize PPG technology. Some other watches (Omron Heart Guide) use an inflatable cuff around the wrist to measure blood pressure.
        
          These are only a few of the multitude of sensors currently available. Others include oxygen saturation sensors, respiratory rate sensors, and many more ([Table 15.1](#B9780128202739000154.xhtml#t0010)) (
