        ## Machine learning (ML)
        
        The collection of data is the first part in this process. Technology and progress have permitted the gathering of enormous amounts of data while simultaneously allowing for the safe storage. The challenge, however, lies with the effective utilization of the data and turning it into clinically meaningful parameters to consumers and patients. This is where the implementation of machine learning comes into play. ML is the complex interplay between computer science and mathematics, more specifically statistics ( Supervised learning is the type of learning a computer does to which the outcome is already known and well established. They are all tasks that a trained person can do well, and the computer simply tries to replicate the same outcome reached by humans. These can range from simple to complex tasks, and mostly involve recognition and classification. Examples of these include classifying documents based on their content, or even just recognizing whether an image shows a cat or a dog ( On the other hand, unsupervised ML is much more open-ended and has limitless possibilities. In this type of learning, there is no specific outcome being measured. The computer simply aims to manipulate the data in limitless ways, in hopes of identifying patterns or specific groupings that can later be tested using a supervised algorithm in order to determine its clinical use, if any (  
        
        ## Uses of smart wearable data
        
        Now that we have discussed the multitude of different types of data that can be collected by smart wearables, as well as the different ways in which they can be manipulated and interpreted, we can delve into how smart wearables can be useful for cardiovascular health. The uses of wearable data can be broadly split into three different groups: lifestyle management in the general population, screening for cardiovascular disease, and disease management in patients suffering from cardiovascular diseases.  
        
        ### Lifestyle management in the general population
        
        Several modifiable causes of cardiovascular disease (CVD) have long been identified. These include hypertension, obesity, smoking, and diabetes mellitus among many others ( The field of smart wearables and machine learning is relatively young, and there has only been a small amount of research into it. However, there is one study that has looked at exercise data and attempted to link it to several diseases including diabetes and hypertension. This study is known as the Henry Ford Exercise Testing (FIT) project ( One challenge that arises when considering wearable technology as a primary tool for lifestyle management in the general population is the notion that many individuals may not be motivated enough to actively keep track of their fitness level on a daily basis. Behavioral change in general is extremely difficult to instigate. The Framingham Heart Study could provide some insight on how this issue can be tackled (  ![Figure 15.1 AUC (Area Under the Curve) for six different supervised machine learning models (FIT Study). The RTF (Random Tree Forest) method reached the highest accuracy at 91%. Abbreviations: ANN, Artificial Neural Network; BN, Bayesian Network classifier; LB, LogitBoost; LWB, Locally Weighted Naive Bayes; RTF, Random Tree Forest; SVM, Support Vector Machine.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000154/main.assets/f15-01-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 15.1 AUC (Area Under the Curve) for six different supervised machine learning models (FIT Study). The RTF (Random Tree Forest) method reached the highest accuracy at 91%. Abbreviations: ANN, Artificial Neural Network; BN, Bayesian Network classifier; LB, LogitBoost; LWB, Locally Weighted Naive Bayes; RTF, Random Tree Forest; SVM, Support Vector Machine.
        
         This goes to show that individuals get increasingly motivated when a competitive component is included. This notion could be further exploited to encourage members of the population to actually use smart wearables, and in doing so, increase physical activity. In fact, this is already implemented by Apple in their Apple Watches. The activity app in the Apple Watch allows users to challenge friends or family, and whoever has the most steps by the end of the week earns a virtual trophy. Users can also work their way to different trophies by meeting their daily step goals. Lifestyle management in the general population to prevent the incidence of CVD has been a constant challenge facing the healthcare system. However, as was demonstrated, wearable technology can play a vital role in how the healthcare community approaches such an important undertaking of disease prevention. Precision behavioral change may be difficult to accomplish; however, future endeavors must focus on identifying the most suitable, evidence-based, and personalized primordial prevention strategies to implement as early as possible in childhood, when behaviors are more pliable, and likely to last a lifetime.  
        
        ### Screening for CVD
        
        With the prevalence of smart wearables across the general population, and the intrinsic feature of continuous data collection of those smart wearables, there is a wealth of data being acquired by these electronics that could prove instrumental at identifying certain diseases and pathologies. Continuous heart rate monitoring can allow these devices to screen their users for cardiac arrhythmias, and when asked to conduct an ECG, they can additionally screen for atrial fibrillation (AF) or long QT syndrome, for example. Asymptomatic AF presents with the same risks and complications as symptomatic AF, such as heart failure, kidney disease, stroke, coronary artery disease, and death. Using their smartwatches, Apple launched the prospective Apple Heart Study in 2017, which aims to investigate the concordance of recorded pulse irregularities with simultaneous ECG recordings, and to assess the time it takes for the user to contact a healthcare provider within 3 months of pulse irregularity detection. The data collected by the Apple Watch, using a combination of LED (light-emitting diode) lights and light-sensitive photodiodes, measured the changes in blood flow to generate a photoplethysmogram that is subsequently used to estimate the pulse by recording intervals between photoplethysmography signal peaks (PSP) and producing a tachogram. The photoplethysmogram waveforms are then fed to an algorithm developed by Apple, the Irregular Pulse Notification Algorithm, to identify irregular pulses possibly indicative of AF. In the case of an irregularity that meets inclusion criteria, the algorithm will prospectively and opportunistically scan for photoplethysmography irregularities when there is minimal arm movement. Upon 4 serial conformations of an irregular photoplethysmography, the participant is informed of the irregular pulse. Out of a study population of 419,093 participants, an irregular pulse was detected in 0.52% of smartwatch wearers. About 34% of those with an irregular pulse were diagnosed with AF after wearing an ECG patch for up to 7 days. The results of this study showed a positive predictive value of 84% (participants who received a notification of an irregular pulse and also had an ECG showing AF) ( Devices that screen for hypertension, such as the Omron HeartGuide, present numerous benefits, given the high rates of hypertension among the general population. The value of such devices lies in their function of conducting serial blood pressure measurements during the course of the day, and hence developing an extensive record of a user’s blood pressure. This record can be used by a user’s primary care physician with the assistance of ML algorithms to patients at risk for developing hypertension, and possibly predict cardiovascular events in patients with an established diagnosis of hypertension.  
        
        ### Disease management in CVD patients
        
        Beyond the multitude of opportunities that data gathered by smart wearables have in lifestyle management within the general population, the data being collected also has the potential to be utilized in the management of patients with preexisting cardiovascular diseases. Examples of such opportunities that will be discussed in this section are monitoring for cardiac arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, detection of myocardial infarctions, and guiding postinfarction care, and monitoring as well as managing heart failure.  
        
        #### Management of atrial fibrillation
        
        AF is one of the most common cardiac arrhythmias, particularly in older patients, and is characterized by an irregular heartbeat and loss of atrial contraction, consequently resulting in blood clots, stroke, and heart failure. There are several risk factors that predispose individuals to developing AF, such as increasing age, hypertension, obesity, and other underlying cardiovascular diseases. In the United States, it is predicted that the number of individuals expected to be diagnosed with this arrhythmia will reach up to 6 million by 2050, posing a significant pecuniary burden on the healthcare system ( There has been significant progress recently in the development of wearable cardiac rhythm recorders that can record rhythm strips using smartphone technology. After the initial success of AliveCor’s single lead Kardia Mobile device in 2017, the company introduced the Kardia Band (KB), the first FDA-cleared Apple Watch accessory that patients can use to record 30 s rhythm strips. The KB operates synchronously with an application that uses machine learning ECG-recognition algorithms to provide an instant diagnosis of AF, informing the patient of the diagnosis, and providing them with the option of sending the results to their physician ([Fig. 15.2](#B9780128202739000154.xhtml#f0015)). Further, this technology has numerous applications in patients with previously established AF. A promising use to this technology in AF patients is confirming their AF status prior to a scheduled electrical cardioversion appointment, allowing them to make an informed decision on whether they should come to the hospital or not. On its own, the application’s ML algorithm is able to accurately identify cases of AF up to 93% of the time, and electrophysiologists using the KB recording were able to accurately identify in up to 99% of AF cases. Not only does this help patients determine whether or not they should go to the hospital, but it can also help the hospital save valuable time and resources if a scheduled procedure such as direct current cardioversion is no longer necessary ( ![Figure 15.2 Illustration depicting the integration of the Kardia Band with the smartphone application, and the accuracy of AF (Atrial Fibrillation) diagnosis compared to 12-lead ECG (electrocardiogram) across different methods. Abbreviations: right (VnR) and left (VnL) limb leads.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000154/main.assets/f15-02-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 15.2 Illustration depicting the integration of the Kardia Band with the smartphone application, and the accuracy of AF (Atrial Fibrillation) diagnosis compared to 12-lead ECG (electrocardiogram) across different methods. Abbreviations: right (VnR) and left (VnL) limb leads.
        
        Other beneficial applications of this technology is ECG monitoring in patients postcardioversion and ablation procedures that are common in AF, as there is an estimated recurrence rate of up to 50% within the first year following these treatments (  
        
        #### Detection of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)
        
        Another significant application of smart wearable technology is the detection of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), a possibly life-threatening cardiac event that requires urgent revascularization and is diagnosed largely using an ECG. In the United States, the occurrence of a coronary event in 2019 is expected to occur in about 1,055,000 individuals ( Smart wearable technology, such as the Kardia Mobile, allows at-risk individuals to obtain an ECG earlier when presenting with STEMI, reducing their time for diagnosis and receiving critical intervention. The ST LEUIS pilot study used an adapted version of the Kardia Mobile device consisting of two wire leads, allowing the device to reconstruct a 12-lead ECG from serial lead measurements. The study showed excellent concordance of the reconstructed 12-lead ECGs with standard 12-lead ECGs for detecting an STEMI as well as non-ST elevation myocardial infarctions (NSTEMI), as seen in table 2 (  
        
        #### Postmyocardial infarction management and recovery
        
        A significant factor in recovery of any cardiovascular event is education and compliance after hospital discharge. Unfortunately, most of this often occurs hastily during the discharge process, and considering the pervasiveness of technology in our lives, it seems intuitive to integrate technology in this process, and capitalize on the advantages artificial intelligence has to offer. The application Corrie Health, developed by a group at Johns Hopkins, is an example of how technology and smart wearables can be integrated into the hospital discharge process, and transform it into a patient-centered approach. The target age group of Corrie Health are individuals between the ages of 40 and 85 years who are recovering from a myocardial infarction in the acute setting. The application accounts for this target cohort by working with Apple to create an optimal user interface. Some of the features of the Corrie Health application include informing users of their daily tasks, such as taking their prescribed medications and measuring their heart rate, blood pressure, and weight ( Importantly, Corrie Health integrates with smart wearable devices and uses wearable data such as daily step or stairs count to provide personalized guidance to each patient. This information can be very valuable in structuring home-based cardiac rehabilitation programs that push patients to gradually increase their submaximal exercise capacity. Biometric wearable data, particularly heart rate, may even be used to optimize beta-blocker dosing in patients with chronic coronary artery disease, and correlate this data with their angina symptoms.  
        
        #### Detection of hyperkalemia in heart failure patients
        
        Another innovative application of smart wearables is the detection of hyperkalemia from smartphone ECGs. Hyperkalemia is prevalent in multiple pathologies, including congestive heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and as an effect of several medications used to treat these conditions. Normally, the detection of hyperkalemia requires an invasive blood test, since only relatively severe hyperkalemia causes evident changes on an ECG. At mild to moderate levels, the PR interval is prolonged, and there is the development of peaked T waves ( In a recent 2018 study, Mayo Clinic developed an algorithm utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) that was trained to detect hyperkalemia using ECG leads I and II from a training group of 484,310 patients admitted between 1994 and 2017 with a serum potassium collected within 12 h of their ECG. After an extensive learning phase, its performance was evaluated on an initial testing group of 224,690 patients. In the initial test group, the AUC was 0.87 (sensitivity 85%, specificity 72%). A secondary performance evaluation was conducted prospectively on 10 patients undergoing hemodialysis wearing the portable AliveCor smartphone ECG device. The sensitivity was 94% and specificity 74% across 5.4 h of ECG data in the hyperkalemic state and 44.1 h in a nonhyperkalemic state ( ![Figure 15.3 Electrocardiographic changes associated with progressive hyperkalemia. These include peaking of the T wave, flattening of the P wave, prolongation of the PR interval, ST-segment depression, and, eventually, progressing to a sine wave pattern.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000154/main.assets/f15-03-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 15.3 Electrocardiographic changes associated with progressive hyperkalemia. These include peaking of the T wave, flattening of the P wave, prolongation of the PR interval, ST-segment depression, and, eventually, progressing to a sine wave pattern.
        
         
        
        #### Monitoring chronic heart failure prognosis using physical activity
        
        Similarly to how cardiac rehabilitation significantly improves recovery in post-MI patients, patients with chronic heart failure are seen to have low tolerance to physical activity, preventing them from engaging in daily tasks. Moreover, decreased physical capacity in heart failure patients portends a worse prognosis, with increased rehospitalization and mortality risk ( These functional capacity tests, however, only occur in a hospital setting by scheduled appointments, and thus cannot pick up on health deteriorations that may occur between appointments. Smart wearables can close this gap by utilizing in-built accelerometer to calculate a patient’s 6MWT score, and additionally, send the results to the patient’s providers to monitor their progress. The benefit is that many smartphones currently have accelerometers built into their devices, making it even easier to collect and use the data necessary to assess a patient’s functional capacity. Accelerometers were found to have high accuracy in detecting physical activity in heart failure patients, demonstrating their clinical applicability in performing out-of-clinic 6MWT that would allow for continuous patient monitoring and early detection of health deterioration. These results have instigated a multicenter trial to assess whether a smart wearable-based intervention improves functional capacity in patients with chronic heart failure with reduced (HFrEF) and preserved (HFpEF) ejection fractions (  
        
        ## Current challenges
        
        As with any novel medical advancement, the principle of using smart wearables and artificial intelligence processed data to prevent, detect, and manage CVD is not without limitations. The first limitation that comes into play is the feasibility of collecting all this data for millions of people. The data for one person could exceed thousands of gigabytes, so how feasible would it be to collect and store all this data for an entire population? This would require lots of new data infrastructure that could accommodate these massive amounts of data. This is not something beyond reach but does need a lot of prospective planning before anything is implemented nationwide. This brings us to the second challenge we face which is confidentiality and privacy. With so much personal data being collected every second, patients deserve to know where that data goes and who has access to it. These are issues that companies need to be fully transparent about in order to maintain the everlasting trust between patients and the healthcare community. Another important challenge will be deciding which types of data will be actually useful to collect and use in algorithms to predict CVD. Not all data is actionable and some of it may be redundant and the key to improving population health is generating clinically meaningful data. For example, is 24/7 monitoring of heart rate for the entirety of life meaningful? ML algorithms work more effectively when data is preoptimized. This can only be achieved through trial and error, as is the case with any development throughout human history. A lot more focus is shifting toward this novel field and more information will come to light in the coming years regarding which types of data are most useful and which types of algorithms work best. This also ties in with the next challenge, which is the need for extensive validation studies into the findings that preliminary studies report. These studies will come with time and will allow to further refine the methodology to achieve the most efficient data collection and analysis. The final challenge is the economic aspect of an endeavor of such a scale. Studies and trials would need significant funding, since it is plausible to assume that individuals would require smart wearables in order to collect data, which is an expensive task. This will require a lot of reconsideration of national research funding allocation. It might also take time to convince health administrators and policy makers that this is a worthwhile national endeavor to pursue. To consider an example, the recently published Apple Heart Study recruited approximately 400,000 Apple Watch users over 2  years. Although this trial was the first of its kind and proved that such large-scale and rapid recruitment is possible, it had significant problems with retaining patients wherein 79% dropped out in the first few months. One has to be creative regarding improving such potentially revolutionary trials through integration of various clinical platforms and encouragement of patient involvement. After that comes the huge challenge of applying what is discovered through research and trials to clinical practice and healthcare in general, especially disease prevention. Providing everyone in a population of 300 million with a smart wearable is not cheap. The research phase will be important in providing strong evidence as to whether or not a large-scale investment could potentially save healthcare providers’ costs over the long term by lowering the incidence of CVD and lowering readmission rates for CVD patients.  
        
        ## Conclusion and future directions
        
        The advent of smart wearables constitutes the latest trend in health technology. With improvements in computation and technology allowing for the incorporation of AI and ML, their clinical utility is only expected to rise. The design and implementation of sensors such as glucose, sleep, and breathing sensors would provide new and clinically significant health-related data. Parameters measured using different modalities can be used to expand already existing datasets in order to make ML algorithms more accurate in the detection of disease. These datasets can then be used in large studies in order to assess their effectiveness and their utility. Once the virtual infrastructure containing these parameters is built, physicians and healthcare professionals should be trained to retrieve and interpret the data from smart wearables. It is also imperative that cheaper, smart wearables are manufactured in order to be accessible by those of lower socioeconomic status. Smart wearables undoubtedly add a new dimension to healthcare, and when utilized properly, have the potential to be extremely beneficial in a healthcare setting. They allow patients to take charge of their own health, be more engaged in the pursuit of good health, and build healthy habits. This can be achieved in numerous ways such as simply ensuring medication adherence and physical activity. With the extremely high rates of obesity and associated noncommunicable diseases such as CVD and cancer, physical activity would undoubtedly be a worthwhile endeavor, and help curtail the significant morbidity and mortality associated with such diseases. Their implementation in the clinical space would result in a paradigm shift, as the focus of disease can be aimed more toward prevention. Smart wearable technology is also ready for prime-time integration in the management of many cardiovascular diseases; however, we still need to improvise ways to streamline big data analysis, while making result visualization meaningful and seamless to both the physicians and patients.

        # Chapter 16: The future of artificial intelligence in healthcare
        
        Nathan Radakovich[¹](#B9780128202739000166.xhtml#aff1), and Aziz Nazha[²](#B9780128202739000166.xhtml#aff2)     ¹Cleveland Clinic Lerner College of Medicine, Cleveland, OH, United States     ²Cleveland Clinic Taussig Cancer Center, Leukemia Department, Cleveland, OH, United States  
        
        ## Abstract
        
        The field of artificial intelligence (AI) has witnessed significant advances in the last decade in terms of computational power and the ease of implementing AI in domain-specific settings. The medical field, in particular, contains many prominent examples of these advances. AI has already taken a foothold in some specialties such as radiology, and is likely to continue expanding into other clinical realms, altering established approaches for disease diagnosis, research conduct, and patients interaction. This chapter provides an historical perspective and background on recent computing advances that have set the stage for the emergence of AI in healthcare, describes the burgeoning trends in AI’s clinical implementation, and considers some of the challenges that will face healthcare providers as AI makes its way into day-to-day clinical practice.
        
        ### Keywords
        
        Artificial intelligence; Computer vision; Electronic health records; Interpretability; Machine learning; Neural network; Time series analysis

        ## Introduction and historical perspective
        
        Intelligence is a difficult to encapsulate concept, one for which scientists and philosophers have proposed myriad definitions and metrics over the years. It is unsurprising, given the difficulty of reaching a consensus regarding our own intelligence, that a firm definition of artificial intelligence (AI), a term first coined by the pioneering AI researcher John McCarthy in the 1950s ( Modern applications of AI fulfill previous definitions to various degrees. Autonomously driving cars, for instance, have debuted with some success, and have featured software both programmed a priori to understand and obey the rules of the road, as well as software whose driving abilities and decision-making is derived from observing hours of human driving. In these two different approaches to the same task, we see two data-processing and judgment-making faculties that we deem as signs of intelligence: the ability to learn the rules governing a task and then implement those rules; and the ability to learn from experience, thereby coming to an inductive understanding of a previously unknown task. Turing’s definition of AI required a computer to match human abilities, but in certain realms AI has begun not only to match human abilities, but to surpass them. Computational power, which has increased exponentially since the advent of microprocessors in the 1960s ( With the diverse and rapid developments in AI, it is unsurprising that healthcare, which comprises one-fifth of the United States’ economy and has data repositories measuring in the petabytes, has been a recent hotbed for AI research. The notion of computers as powerful tools—or rivals—for physicians is by no means recent, however. In a 1970 commentary, “Medicine and the Computer: The Promise and Problems of Change,” in the New England Journal of Medicine, Dr. William Schwartz, an early advocate of AI in healthcare, envisioned not only the “housekeeping” role that computers would play in the form of electronic health records (EHRs), but the more direct role they would play in the intellectual work of medicine (  
        
        ## Supervised and unsupervised learning
        
        AI tasks can be described as “supervised” or “unsupervised” according to the output desired by the user. In supervised learning tasks, an algorithm is given input data to make a prediction, which can be categorical (e.g., “does this biopsy contain malignant tissue?”) or numerical (e.g., “what is the predicted survival of this patient, given their disease status and comorbidities?”). Source data are used to generate initial predictions by the algorithm. Predictions are then compared to actual outcomes, and the algorithm is iteratively refined based on the discrepancies between the two, yielding successively more accurate predictions (  
        
        ## Neural networks: a brief overview
        
        Neural networks are amongst the most widely used and successful tools in contemporary AI. Neural networks’ namesake and inspiration come from biologic neurons, and in particular from the way that action potentials between neurons are used as the basic unit of communication in the nervous system. Neural networks process information by propagating data along a series of interconnected nodes, or “neurons,” starting with some external input and generating an output after relaying the data through many layers of neurons ( Because of their ability to create more abstract representations of data in hidden layers, neural networks are also capable of integrating several different types of data into a single model. Distinct types of data are fed into separate inputs, processed through several parallel hidden layers, and then connected by subsequent layers prior to yielding an output. This is of particular utility in medicine, where images, laboratory values, and free text reports all play a role in decision-making and patient care; rather than considering different data types in isolation, interactions between data can be captured.  
        
        ## The pace of change in AI research
        
        The pace of innovation in healthcare-related AI is accelerating, and is on pace to continue doing so. A PubMed search of terms “deep learning,” “machine learning,” “artificial intelligence,” or “neural network” reveals a consistent increase in both the absolute volume of AI-related research, and in the proportion of the medical literature that it constitutes. In the year 2000, 1838 articles (0.38% of all articles published in 2000) met the aforementioned search criteria. In 2010, there were 5491 such articles (0.74% of all articles), and in 2018 there were 15,240 (5.20% of all articles) ([Fig. 16.2](#B9780128202739000166.xhtml#f0015)). ![Figure 16.1 Schematic of neural networks. Data (pixels, words, etc.) are formatted and fed into neurons in an input layer. Subsequent hidden layers of neurons allow the network to capture nonlinearity and higher-level representations of source data. The network’s output can be used for classification or regression tasks or to generate novel data.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000166/main.assets/f16-01-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 16.1 Schematic of neural networks. Data (pixels, words, etc.) are formatted and fed into neurons in an input layer. Subsequent hidden layers of neurons allow the network to capture nonlinearity and higher-level representations of source data. The network’s output can be used for classification or regression tasks or to generate novel data.
        
        These trends reflect the increasing recognition of AI’s utility and promise in healthcare, as well as ongoing improvements in the hardware and software that facilitate increasingly sophisticated AI algorithms. They also reflect the democratization of the tools used to implement AI. Most industry-standard AI packages are freely available online, and cheap online computing power can be accessed for computationally demanding projects, eliminating the need for costly upfront capital investments. The convergence of these factors has lowered the threshold for successfully using AI, thereby allowing clinician experts to begin implementing AI across a wide array of domain-specific applications.  
        
        ## Computer vision
        
        Computer vision is the use of AI to interpret and extract data from images. No medical application of AI has seen as much recent progress, or garnered as much popular attention, as medical image processing, especially in the fields of pathology and radiology. This progress has been facilitated by the advent of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), a subtype of neural network designed to process images in a manner similar to human sight. CNNs begin with basic patterns and textures such as horizontal and vertical lines, then build successively more complex and abstract representations based on those initial steps, thereby learning a more generalizable version of the object in question (3,5). This allows CNNs to learn from training data, and to effectively apply what they have learned to previously unseen examples. The advent of transfer learning, which uses models that have already been trained to recognize basic shapes and contours, allows powerful models to be trained efficiently and effectively on novel tasks, facilitating the expansion of computer vision to increasing numbers of novel applications ( ![Figure 16.2 Healthcare-related AI publications’ increase in absolute numbers and proportion.In 2018, 15,240 articles were published related to AI in healthcare, or 5.20% of all articles in 2018. Publication numbers were generated via a Boolean PubMed search of the terms “deep learning,” “machine learning,” “artificial intelligence,” or “neural network.”](IMAGES/B9780128202739000166/main.assets/f16-02-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 16.2 Healthcare-related AI publications’ increase in absolute numbers and proportion.In 2018, 15,240 articles were published related to AI in healthcare, or 5.20% of all articles in 2018. Publication numbers were generated via a Boolean PubMed search of the terms “deep learning,” “machine learning,” “artificial intelligence,” or “neural network.”
        
         
        
        ### AI in radiology
        
        CNNs are approaching the point of clinical usefulness in several tasks in radiology, and in some cases have already passed that threshold. Routine screening mammography, detection of abnormalities on chest radiographs, bone age assessment, pulmonary nodule detection, and tuberculosis screening have all been successfully performed by CNNs, to name a few notable applications ( Image segmentation, a tedious but important task used to identify areas of interest in images such as individual organs, tumors, fluid collections, or injured tissue, can also increasingly be performed by AI ([Fig. 16.3](#B9780128202739000166.xhtml#f0020)) ( Beyond achieving remarkable performance on existing tasks in radiology, AI has demonstrated the potential to extract novel, clinically meaningful information from images. In lung cancer, AI has shown promise in using CT images to predict the invasiveness of tumors, assess tumors’ response to chemotherapy, and distinguish between indolent and aggressive tumors ( ![Figure 16.3 Automated cardiac segmentation by deep neural networks (24).Myocardium, atria, and ventricles are distinguished from one another and highlighted by a neural network, facilitating automated measurement of cardiac dimensions.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000166/main.assets/f16-03-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 16.3 Automated cardiac segmentation by deep neural networks (24).Myocardium, atria, and ventricles are distinguished from one another and highlighted by a neural network, facilitating automated measurement of cardiac dimensions.
        
        Generative adversarial networks (GANs), a type of neural network designed to generate de novo data that resemble real data, have also found a foothold in radiology ([Fig. 16.4](#B9780128202739000166.xhtml#f0025)). GANs have shown promise in several realms: reducing noise artifact in images, thereby making them more interpretable for human observers; synthesizing images across modalities, such as different MRI sequences; and creating synthetic instances of training data that can be used to improve the generalizability of image classifiers ([Fig. 16.5](#B9780128202739000166.xhtml#f0030)) (<miss\_match refids="bib6" ref\_cout="1"/>Armanious et al.; ![Figure 16.4 Style transfer with generative adversarial networks for cross-platform image generation.Source data are processed by a generator, which attempts to transform the source data to resemble template data. A discriminator attempts to determine which data are original and which are transformed, allowing the generator’s performance to be iteratively improved.](IMAGES/B9780128202739000166/main.assets/f16-04-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 16.4 Style transfer with generative adversarial networks for cross-platform image generation.Source data are processed by a generator, which attempts to transform the source data to resemble template data. A discriminator attempts to determine which data are original and which are transformed, allowing the generator’s performance to be iteratively improved.
        
         
        
        ### AI in pathology
        
        Pathology has seen similar improvements as radiology in the use of AI for common tasks. While efforts to apply AI to tasks such as routine pap smears date to the early 1990s, contemporary work has yielded highly accurate and specific models capable of detecting abnormalities on routine smears ( ![Figure 16.5 Applications of generative adversarial networks (GANs).GANs can be trained to reduce motion artifacts and reduce noise in CT/PET images (36), or to alter images to resemble other modalities (MRI to CT translation is shown) (37).](IMAGES/B9780128202739000166/main.assets/f16-05-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 16.5 Applications of generative adversarial networks (GANs).GANs can be trained to reduce motion artifacts and reduce noise in CT/PET images (36), or to alter images to resemble other modalities (MRI to CT translation is shown) (37).
        
         
        
        ### Dermatology and ophthalmology
        
        AI has also taken a foothold in clinical specialties, namely in ophthalmology, where AI is increasingly used to interpret fundoscopic images, and dermatology, where it is employed in classifying skin lesions. Importantly, recent work in these fields has also included implementation of AI into regular practice. In a 2018 trial, an AI-based diabetic retinopathy detection tool achieved 87.5% sensitivity and 90.7% specificity in a primary care setting, subsequently becoming the first AI-based system to gain U.S. Food and Drug Administration authorization ( Prospective, implementation-oriented studies in ophthalmology demonstrate the potential for AI’s generalizability and practical integration into clinical workflow, two factors that represent barriers to more widespread utilization of AI in medicine. Crucially, they also address an unmet healthcare need. Time, expense, and provider scarcity are barriers to success in any form of preventative care, and the patients affected by those barriers experience poorer health as a consequence ( AI has made similar strides in dermatology, namely in classifying skin lesions. CNNs have continually improved over the last decade, with the latest generation of algorithms achieving parity with dermatologists in melanoma and multilabel lesion classification tasks ( Beyond single pictures of lesions, a logical next step in lesion imaging is longitudinal monitoring, since change over time is a consideration when evaluating potentially cancerous skin lesions. Dermatologists’ sensitivity is only 80% for detecting melanomas when viewing a lesion at a single point in time, so even models that outperform humans will likely miss a significant number of melanomas, and interval monitoring may be required to improve screening (35). Prospective data are needed in order to create the datasets necessary to develop such a tool (  
        
        ## Time-series analysis
        
        Understanding the chronology of patients’ diseases is an integral part of the practice of medicine. Time-series analysis, which employs AI to process sequences of events, has seen significant strides in recent years. Time-series problems abound in medicine, from single variable tasks such as interpreting the pattern of voltages recorded in an electrocardiogram to complex multivariable predictions, such as determining whether an ICU patient is improving or deteriorating based on trends in vital signs, labs, written notes, and day-to-day physical exam findings. Much of the recent research in time-series analysis has to do with event prediction. In the ICU setting this includes risk-stratifying patients by likelihood of mortality and promptly identifying sepsis (   
        
        ## Mobile device applications
        
        Medical data are traditionally collected either in clinics or the inpatient setting, but for most patients this represents a small fraction of their lives. When we observe a tremor or assess a patient’s gait in the clinic, it is with the assumption that we are seeing a representative sample of their daily lives, but this may not always be true, such as in patients with masked hypertension, or in Parkinson disease patients who experience fluctuations in symptoms throughout the day. With the advent of inexpensive and accurate portable monitoring devices, it is now feasible to directly gather information about patients’ day-to-day activity outside of a medical setting, thereby greatly expanding the pool of potentially useful data about patients ( This wealth of data has been studied in many settings, such as monitoring for fall risk in the elderly (  
        
        ## AI in medical research
        
        ### Classification of disease
        
         While much popular attention is directed toward AI’s applications in clinical practice, it also promises to alter how physicians research disease. For example, unsupervised clustering of asthma patients was able to group patients into distinct clinically meaningful cohorts that varied based on asthma severity, resource utilization, responsiveness to bronchodilators, and biologic variables such as eosinophilia, circulating inflammatory markers, and exhaled nitric oxide ( Not only do such clusters, which are generated without any a priori designation of outcomes or patient phenotypes, identify clinically relevant subpopulations of patients, they have clear diagnostic and therapeutic ramifications. Clustering approaches could be used in clinical practice to fine-tune aggressiveness of therapy, avoid ineffective treatments, and to identify those most likely to respond to novel targeted therapies. AI-based clustering may also inform future clinical trial design. In fields like oncology, where many new agents are designed with disease-specific biology in mind, AI may facilitate more targeted selection criteria. In cases where there is a strong biologic rationale for those selection criteria, this may allow for smaller trials to be conducted while still achieving statistical power, thereby reducing trial costs and sparing unnecessary interventions for those unlikely to benefit.  
        
        ### AI as a tool in data gathering
        
        One of the challenges in clinical research that draws from EHRs is accurately sifting through disorganized data. Important information about patient outcomes often comes in the form of unstructured text in pathology reports or clinician notes, and such data need to be extracted manually in order to be incorporated into outcomes research. Obtaining information through manual review of EHR is time-consuming, and may place practical constraints on sample size. Conversely, methodologically convenient but less granular methods of chart review, such as querying International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes without manual review of individual charts, facilitate larger sample sizes at the expense of detail. Natural language processing (NLP), another field where AI has yielded important strides, could be used in the future as a means of collecting data with the speed and throughput of computerized queries. Traditional rule-based methods of natural language processing require explicit programming on how to extract information. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), a type of network designed to take previous inputs into account, are capable of more flexible, context-sensitive performance, and can be applied to NLP; CNNs have also been used effectively in this setting (  
        
        ## Future challenges in implementation
        
        Much of the focus on AI in healthcare has been on the development of AI models themselves: how to more accurately identify objects, classify sequences, or deal with the subtleties and inconsistencies of interpreting written language. However, as progress continues in each of these realms, thought also needs to be given to other factors that will impact the clinical utilization of AI.  
        
        ### Practical considerations
        
        Broadly speaking, the enthusiasm for AI in healthcare is driven by two hopes: that AI will improve the quality of care that physicians deliver, and that it will do so in a way that improves patient and physician experiences. Thus, in arenas where AI achieves or surpasses human performance, the question turns from one of theoretical usefulness to one of practical implementation. Even if an AI-based model performs exceedingly well, it will not provide any clinical benefit unless it can reasonably be integrated into physicians’ workflows. For many applications this likely means integration into existing EHR systems, which carries the attendant requirements of securely handling patient data, reliably standardizing the input data used by AI systems, and likely the ability to interface with other EHR-based AI programs (  
        
        ### Interpretability
        
        Any AI that plays a significant role in guiding patient care will have to include mechanisms for making its predictions explicable to clinicians and patients. Simple models such as logistic regression are easy to interpret because each variable is considered in isolation, making interpretation straightforward. However, simplistic models are rarely adequate, and medicine provides many examples of the adage that “for every complex problem there is an answer that is clear, simple, and wrong.” Medical data are never considered in isolation, and medical decision-making is almost never simple. For example, the same heart rate could have very different implications depending on patient comorbidities, other vital signs, and numerous other factors, all of which are implicitly or explicitly considered by human clinicians when delivering care and choosing a course of action. Moreover, clinicians are able to describe how they interpret complex sets of data and why they draw certain conclusions. If AI is to gain widespread acceptance by clinicians and patients, it will have to manage to be sophisticated while remaining similarly accountable.  
        
        ### Testing and overdiagnosis
        
        The risk of overdiagnosis needs to be considered as AI-based diagnostic tools become increasingly sensitive. Overdiagnosis occurs when a test correctly identifies the presence of disease, but there is no benefit from intervening on the disease (  Outside of the scope of existing screening, overdiagnosis also needs to be considered as new sources of health information, such as wearable devices, become increasingly common. In some cases, such as atrial fibrillation or atrial high rate episodes in ambulatory patients, even asymptomatic events have unfavorable prognostic implications and require intervention (  
        
        ### Barriers to implementation
        
        Beyond practical barriers, the impact of AI on physicians themselves must be considered. It is often assumed that better technology necessarily improves the lives of its users, but studies of physician satisfaction with EHR and computerized order entry belie this assumption. Indeed, the use of computerized records and orders is an independent predictor of physician burnout, and if EHR-integrated AI increases the time spent interacting with EHR and detracts from physician-patient interactions, it could in turn become a contributor to the burnout problem ( Precautions about burnout aside, fluid and user-friendly EHR integration is also crucial to the successful uptake of AI. Numerous best practice alerts (BPAs) to warn clinicians about drug-drug interactions, adherence to guidelines, or health maintenance are already incorporated into EHR systems, with varying degrees of success and uptake, which in turn determines how much patients ultimately benefit from such tools. In cases where BPAs do not provide benefit, a major contributor is physician alert fatigue, which is driven in part by the sheer volume of BPAs encountered ( Despite posing potential problems, clinical AI may also offer solutions for physicians’ struggles with burnout and burdensome EHR. The use of human scribes is known to ameliorate burnout and increase physician job satisfaction without detracting from patients’ experiences, but their widespread use is limited by cost and scarcity ( NLP in medicine currently functions as a dictation tool, and while dictation may be more efficient than typing, it does not substantially alter the current workflow for physicians; with or without dictation, a sizable amount of physician time is spent on documentation rather than actual patient care. This may change with the advent of increasingly sophisticated language-processing technologies. A system that can summarize physician-patient discussions and generate summary statements about patients problems would be able to capture the unique aspects of an individual visit, thereby freeing physicians from having to recapitulate an entire visit when writing or dictating a note (  
        
        ### The challenge of accurate source data
        
        AI models’ performance will only be as good as their source data, and if flawed data are used, flawed predictions should be expected. For instance in cases such as pulmonary nodule classification where intraobserver variability is high, it is difficult to assign accurate labels to training data without a tissue diagnosis, limiting the ceiling of an algorithm’s usefulness ( Beyond the accuracy of source data, the same precautions about external validity need to be taken as with any other form of research. Many AI models achieve exquisite accuracy on internal datasets, but fail to recapitulate that accuracy when validated externally, meaning that stellar performance in one setting could be unacceptably, even dangerously, flawed in another ( Beyond the prospect of inaccurate data, AI has the potential to unintentionally adopt human bias and prejudices. Photo recognition software, including some models developed for medical use, performs more accurately on light-skinned individuals than on dark-skinned ones due to underrepresentation in datasets; more troublingly, minority individuals are more likely to be viewed unfavorably by AI systems such as crime-prediction or loan-approval algorithms (  
        
        ### Will AI make physicians obsolete?
        
        The emergence of increasingly useful, clinically viable AI brings with it uncertainty about the future role of human physicians, including fears of being displaced or even replaced. This has been especially true in radiology, where much of the recent progress in medical AI has occurred. The majority of medical trainees anticipate that AI will reduce the workload required of radiologists, and in one study half of students contemplating careers in radiology cited this as a source of trepidation ( Practicing radiologists have expressed similar views in commentaries, acknowledging AI’s incorporation into clinical practice as inevitable while simultaneously predicting that AI will support radiologists and augment their skills but not supplant them ( Meanwhile, complex decision-making remains the purview of human physicians, and AI systems capable of taking an active role in clinical decision-making have had decidedly mixed success. IBM’s Watson, which attracted widespread attention for its ability to interpret semantically nuanced questions and compete on the TV quiz show Jeopardy, underwent several years of pilot testing as a decision support system in clinical oncology. However, after a period of use at select major cancer centers in the United States, Watson for Oncology (WFO) was discontinued, although it continues to be studied in several East Asian countries ( Retrospective comparisons between WFO’s recommendations and those of a multidisciplinary tumor board show that WFO’s missteps occur more commonly in elderly patients, intermediate-staged disease, or in malignancies where there are significant regional or national variations in standards of care (  Nonetheless, the prospect of AI as a partner in clinical decision-making remains appealing, especially when considering the gaps in care provided by human clinicians. Medical error incurs billions of dollars in costs annually, and is estimated by some to be the third-leading cause of death in the United States, a sobering reminder of our own limitations (  
        
        ### AI in medical education
        
        As AI becomes integrated into clinical practice, medical school and residency curricula will need to adapt in order to ensure that clinicians approach it in an informed manner. Since the reforms in medical education prompted by the Flexner report, one of the cornerstones of medical education has been literacy in research methods and statistics, as well as careful review of scientific literature ( A knowledge gap likely already exists in the medical community. When surveyed about their understanding of AI, medical students’ self-assessment of their level of knowledge outstrips their ability to actually answer questions about the basics of AI, suggesting that awareness and popular coverage of the topic alone does not confer a deeper understanding or the ability to critically appraise AI-based research (  
        
        ## Conclusion
        
        The degree of computing power available in the modern era and the sophistication and diversity of artificial intelligence that has followed would have been unthinkable in prior decades. Modern AI has already made significant inroads in the fields of pathology and radiology, and is poised to become a routine part of clinical practice within the decade, with other branches of medicine likely to follow suit as the technology continues to mature. Beyond automating and improving on many existing tasks that physicians perform, AI also holds the promise of yielding new insights from the vast amount of medical data now available. As AI becomes more widespread, care needs to be taken to ensure that it is implemented thoughtfully, with an eye to unintended consequences, and to ensure that medical education promotes a basic working knowledge of AI for future physicians.

        # Chapter 17: Ethical and legal challenges
        
        Emily Tat[¹](#B9780128202739000178.xhtml#aff1), and Mark Rabbat[²](#B9780128202739000178.xhtml#aff2)     ¹Department of Internal Medicine, Columbia University Medical Center, New York, NY, United States     ²Medicine and Radiology, Division of Cardiology, Loyola University Chicago, Chicago, IL, United States  
        
        ## Abstract
        
        As the technology of artificial intelligence (AI) grows in cardiovascular medicine, so do the ethical and legal challenges that come with it. Currently, the medical community is ill-informed of what these challenges entail, and policy and ethical guidelines are lacking. Physicians and policy makers should be informed of these issues to minimize harm and promote patient care. Three overarching themes relating to the data, the algorithms, and the results comprise the foundation of these challenges and will be discussed in this chapter. The introduction of big data raises concern for patient privacy and security, with issues of data quality and inconsistent medical records. There is also risk for biases in the algorithms that could worsen health disparities or skew results for financial gain. Finally, the archetypal “black box” algorithm, questions of legal liability, and what happens when humans and machine disagree are discussed in depth. Ultimately, a code of ethics in the coming integration of AI is needed to ensure the preservation of human rights.
        
        ### Keywords
        
        Artificial intelligence; Autonomy; Big data; Black box; Ethics; Informed consent; Liability; Privacy; Safety

        ## Introduction
        
        Artificial intelligence (AI) has significant potential to transform the field of cardiovascular medicine. Major advancements are seen throughout all subsets of AI from machine learning algorithms and neural networks, natural language processing, and robotics to cognitive computing computer vision. There is promise for these advancements to improve the morbidity and mortality associated with cardiovascular disease, from better disease surveillance, improved diagnostics, novel treatments, and an era of truly personalized medicine ( The contents within this chapter will examine some of the most pressing ethical and legal challenges that healthcare providers must be informed of in this new era of medicine. One major theme that will be addressed is big data and the issues involving its integration. This includes threat to patient privacy and safety, the limits of inconsistent electronic health records, and the catch-22 of balancing reductionism and holism, that is, which and how many input variables are required to ensure accurate results. A second theme that will be discussed is the potential for biases within the algorithms. In particular, bias that can worsen health disparities and bias by way of an algorithm’s intent to either improve patient care or for financial gain. The final theme of the chapter discusses the algorithm’s accuracy and the consequences of decisions made from its results. Specifically, the dilemma of the archetypal “black box” algorithm, liability in the face of adverse events, and the question of what to do when humans and machines disagree will be elucidated. Underlying each theme is the emphasis for transparency in the algorithm and a need for a code of ethics and clear guidelines to promote patient safety and minimize harm. Most importantly, there is a large fear of AI’s potential to replace the human physician and disrupt the physician-patient relationship (  
        
        ## Big data
        
        ### The current state of big data
        
         From whole-genome sequencing to wearable biometrics, physicians are now tasked with making sense of an enormous amount of data in an increasingly limited amount of time. Enter AI systems, well-oiled algorithms that are designed to interpret and operationalize larger volumes of health information in a fraction of the time it would take for a human physician.  Using a machine learning based model, a personalized effect of health behavior on blood pressure can be derived ( 
        
        1.  • “Don’t collect data unless it has a non-zero chance of changing your actions.”
        2.  • “Before you seek to collect data, consider the costs of processing that data.”
        3.  • “Acknowledge that data collected isn’t always accurate and consider the costs of acting on data that isn’t correct.”
        
        These principles translate well to the use of artificial intelligence in healthcare. In the face of big data, information is of low utility unless it can improve clinical outcomes. To collect data for the sake of collecting data skews the balance of enormous costs outweighing the benefit of clinical outcomes. The distinction for accurate data should also be emphasized. Incorrect results and predictions in the realm of healthcare can lead to severe consequences, and meticulous quality reporting must be protocolized into AI development to ensure reproducible results. However, professional associations, government agencies, and AI developers may be unaware of how to proceed in this new era of uncharted AI territory.  
        
        ### The effect of AI on healthcare expenditure
        
        The logistics of how AI can be integrated into medicine require a discussion of cost. Healthcare costs in the United States currently surpass all other countries. The United States spends over $10,000 per capita or 18% of its Gross Domestic Product (GDP) on healthcare with costs projected to increase at an annual rate of 4.1% from 2017 to 2021 (  
        
        ### Privacy and security
        
        In the transference of such large amounts of data, questions of confidentiality and security arise. An efficient and accurate AI system cannot be built in solidarity confined to a single hospital network. This is reminiscent of current electronic medical records that are limited to the institution’s hospital network, which greatly impact the efficiency of outside hospital transfers and the like. Given how extensively patient data would be shared across an AI system, existing practices of obtaining consent would be unrealistic. The alternative option also proves difficult. The privacy rule in the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) of 1996 allows the use of deidentified patient-level data without consent ( An incident involving Google DeepMind and the Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust occurred in which identifiable patient records were transferred across the entire Trust without explicit patient consent ( Google introduced Federated Learning in 2017, a “distributed machine learning approach which trains machine learning models using decentralized data residing on end devices such as mobile phones” ( ![image](IMAGES/B9780128202739000178/main.assets/f17-01-9780128202739.jpg)
        
        Figure 17.1 Federated Learning Protocol.The communication protocol enables institutions (devices) to contribute to a single global machine learning model through successive computational rounds. Each round consists of three phases of data selection, configuration, and reporting which underlies constant communication between the model and the institution (  
        
        ### The issue with electronic health records
        
        The issues with electronic health record (EHR) integration into AI systems should be discussed. Currently, EHRs are designed for billing, not clinical knowledge. Regulatory and billing requirements in the United States not only dampen EHR usability but also burden physicians with more administrative duties and contribute to physician burnout. In addition, EHRs are incomplete and ridden with errors. Data collection is highly variable, from vitals collected every 4–12 h, labs scheduled at inconsistent intervals, and chest X-rays and electrocardiograms (ECGs) ordered as needed to outdated medication and demographic data. Even worse, clinical notes are written in unstructured free-form text, awry with acronyms and misspelt words, and copy and pasting used in abundance to meet documentation requirements ( In order to effectively be used in AI systems, data derived from EHRs should ideally be streamlined and rid of inaccurate data, designed to be utilized as clinical knowledge, and kept up to date. If this can be accomplished, EHR data will serve as a rich source of information that can provide significant depth to our current medical knowledge. Given such paramount tasks, existing systems are integrating third-party AI vendors or installing in-house AI capabilities. Firms such as Epic, Cerner, Allscripts, and Athena have begun to add “natural language processing and machine learning capabilities for clinician decision support, integration with telehealth technologies, and automated imaging analysis” (  
        
        ### Data sharing
        
        Advancements in data sharing allow for the creation of data repositories on a global scale. International data harmonization initiatives such as the Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics (OHDSI) program have shown success in aggregating individual datasets into large population-based analytics ( Nonetheless, initial studies utilizing harmonization processes in healthcare are promising. The Biobank Standardisation and Harmonisation for Research Excellence in the European Union (BioSHaRE) project is an example of successful synchronization of data across eight databases that used both data harmonization and federated learning in evaluating healthy, obese individuals (  
        
        ### Data quality and quantity
        
        Reductionist thinking in medicine was dispelled around 20 years ago when genome sequencing was thought to be the best method for predicting disease. It was assumed that the presence of a gene or genetic mutation was the key to finding disease. This reduction of a pathologic state to a molecular entity obviated environmental, developmental, and epigenetic factors that as we now know are large contributors to disease. The complexity of the natural world relies not only on these additional factors, but also the relationships between them. Holism, the antagonist to reductionism, is the concept that all variables matter. In the development of AI for cardiovascular application, it is easy to see how difficult it is to find the right balance of reductionism and holism—which variables matter? The accuracy of an AI algorithm to predict clinical outcomes is highly dependent on the data quality and quantity being inputted. A study using roughly 250 variables showed that three separate machine learning algorithms were not able to predict 30-day remission better than traditional logistic regression (  
        
        ## The algorithm
        
        ### Risk to worsen health disparities
        
         Predictive AI models should be reflective of the entire population to create representative models of disease presentation and response to intervention or medical therapy ( The overarching problem is in the dataset training the algorithm. Not only is the data incomplete, with little representation from women and minority groups, but it is also well-ingrained with real-world biases. Historically, women, minority groups, and obese patients are underrepresented in research trials and as a result have worse health outcomes ( AI algorithms should be validated on various minority and low-income groups to ensure accurate outcomes. Yet, to get access to this type of data is no easy task. To do so raises the concern of data protection and safety for vulnerable populations. Medical data is sensitive, and “information such as HIV status could be used to discriminate against certain populations” (  
        
        ### The Algorithm’s intent
        
        An additional source of bias is in the intent of the algorithm. An algorithm designed to reduce costs will yield far different results than an algorithm designed to reduce mortality. Conflicts of interest are apparent in this coined approach to either generate profit as opposed to improving health outcomes in this very delicate relationship between the algorithm’s architects, the purchasers of the machine, and the users of the machine. There is a clear need for transparency in the algorithm’s design for all involved parties. At present, cardiovascular disease is the number one cause of death worldwide, with care especially lacking in lower-income countries (  
        
        ## The results
        
        ### The black box of AI
        
         The “black box” of AI represents the lack of explanation regarding the machine’s diagnostic and therapeutic conclusions. Whereas first-generation algorithms were unable to adapt beyond the strict parameters defined by the human programmer, advancements in deep learning allow for machines to create their own internal rules and patterns to provide predictions. Preliminary machine models used in ECG analysis, for instance, were once limited to discrete ST segment changes or degree of PR prolongation. Now, deep neural networks use ECGs to predict risk for developing arrhythmia and even risk of death within 1 year, as demonstrated in a recent study by Given the complexity of these algorithms, the exact programming and methodology of how such results arise and what these minute details within an ECG are are difficult to extract. Without “the knowledge within the machine,” it would be inherently difficult for a clinician and the patient to carry forth with a therapy without an explanation as to why or how the particular therapy was chosen by the algorithm (  
        
        ### Autonomy and informed consent
        
        While the AI designer understands the architecture of a deep learning system as it is being developed, what happens after the algorithm is developed is unpredictable. To receive a decision from this “black box” begs the question of both patient autonomy and liability in the case of an adverse event. In contrast to the physician describing the risks and benefits of each medical treatment option that the patient has, a single decision arises out of a black box without explanation. In this manner, the patient is left incompletely informed and almost psychologically obliged to follow suit an algorithm’s command. This then begs the question of patient autonomy. As we know, autonomy is one of the four basic principles of medical ethics. It is the patient’s right to thought, intention, and action when making decisions regarding their own health, and must be free of coercion or coaxing ( The black box archetype combined with threat to patient autonomy complicates the informed consent process. In addition to the traditional aspects enclosed in an informed consent—purpose of treatment, potential risks and benefits, alternative treatments—the technical sophistication of AI has to be explained by the physician who fully understands the risks, possible biases, and error rates of the machine. In essence, the patient is asked to trust a new element of the unknown. Specifically, to trust a new technology that cannot explain its reasoning and lacks years of trusted use to support its use in making critical health decisions. AI users must have full transparency of the algorithm’s capabilities and limits to close the gap of the black box phenomenon. In the progression of AI technologies, it is essential to regard patient care at the center of its development.  
        
        ### Medical malpractice and product liability
        
        In the face of possible medical malpractice and product liability that results during the use of AI technology, who is then responsible? Currently, liability, as described by Yavar Bathaee “is built on legal doctrines that are focused on human conduct, which when applied to AI, may not function” ( Critical factors that the court or jury would consider in determining physician liability include: familiarity with the benefits and limitations of AI’s use as well as the data used to train the algorithm, and if the algorithm’s decision was substituted for their own clinical judgment. Extending beyond the physician using the technology is the hospital or network that could potentially be responsible for the integration of the AI software without proper investigation of its usability. Likely, rigorous screening and strict guidelines for safety and efficacy will become a part of their integration as AI further develops. Lastly, the AI company could be liable on multiple fronts, from design flaws, false advertising, negligent training, and lack of supervision ( 
        
        1.  • Transparency (operations visible to user)
        2.  • Credibility (outcomes are acceptable)
        3.  • Auditability (efficiency can be easily measured)
        4.  • Reliability (AI systems perform as intended)
        5.  • Recoverability (manual control can be assumed if required)
        
        There is an imminent call for legal structure to better assign responsibility for medical errors. At present, irrespective of the remarkable potential shown thus far in AI technology, our current systems are limited to translational applicability due to the enigma of the “black box,” questions of autonomy, safety, and liability.  
        
        ### When humans and machines disagree
        
        An interesting dilemma arises when humans and machines disagree. Who can ultimately make better decisions? Human errors in judgment and decision-making can be broadly understood as either errors of bias or errors of noise ( With AI systems already surpassing human performance in several domains, there is great fear in their potential to replace the human physician. Ultimately, the best results occur when humans and machines work together as advocated for by AI proponent Eric  
        
        ## Conclusions
        
        The role of AI is thus not to replace the cardiologist, but to augment the cardiologist’s role as an advocate for patient care through time- and cost-saving benefits. Simple, repetitive tasks from electronic medical record documentation to the analysis of large quantities of data currently make up the majority of a physician’s day to day. If physicians can be alleviated of these automated tasks with the integration of AI, more time can be spent enjoying the thrills of complex problem-solving with a return of meaning and purpose to the practice of medicine. With its ability to process massive datasets quickly, accurately, and inexpensively, AI holds potential to not replace, but to enhance the patient-physician relationship. Of course, clear guidelines and a code of ethics must be placed to ensure there is no loss of patient integrity with maximal preservation of human rights. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has already issued a statement on a proposed regulatory framework that would allow “the FDA and manufacturers to evaluate and monitor a software product from its premarket development to postmarket performance” ( While significant progress has been made, there are still many details to figure out as AI enters the realm of cardiovascular medicine. These questions of safety and efficacy—who is at fault in the event of medical error, its defined role in the physician’s practice—have to be fully addressed before AI’s integration into the practice of medicine. In the use of these new technologies, the most fundamental question that must be asked is—how will this benefit patient care? Ultimately, the core principles of medical ethics, including respect for persons, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice must be prioritized in the integration of AI technologies in the future of cardiovascular medicine.
