        # Glossary
        
        A ACC/AHA   American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association. Accelerometer   A device that measures proper acceleration. Adjunctive therapy   One or more secondary interventions used concurrently with a primary intervention to enhance treatment effectiveness. Algorithm   A process or set of rules to be followed for calculations or other problem-solving operations, especially by a computer. Altimeter   An instrument used to measure the altitude of an object above a fixed level. Amyloidosis   The buildup of amyloid proteins in the heart, kidneys, liver, or other organs. Angiography   A medical imaging technique used to visualize the inside, or lumen, of blood vessels and organs of the body, with a particular interest in the arteries, veins, and the heart chambers. Annotations   A note of explanation or comment added to a text or diagram. Anomalies   Something that deviates from what is standard, normal, or expected. Armamentarium   A collection of resources available for a certain purpose. Arrhythmia   Improper beating of the heart, whether irregular, too fast, or too slow. Artificial intelligence   The theory and development of computer systems that are able to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as visual perception, speech recognition, decision-making, and translation between languages. Artificial neural networks (ANN)   Computing systems vaguely inspired by the biological neural networks that constitute human brains. ASCVD   Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. ASCVD risk score   A calculation of 10-year risk of having a cardiovascular event, such as a heart attack or stroke. Atrial fibrillation   An irregular, often rapid heart rate that commonly occurs as a result of disruption of organized atrial activation. Attenuation   The reduction of the amplitude of a signal, electric current, or other oscillation. B Bayesian learning   A particular set of approaches to probabilistic machine learning. Biomarker   A measurable indicator of the severity or presence of some disease state. Boltzmann machines   A type of stochastic recurrent neural network. Boosted trees   A machine learning technique for regression and classification problems. Bootstrapping   Any test or metric that uses random sampling with replacement, and falls under the broader class of resampling methods. C Calibration   A procedure in statistical classification performed to determine class membership probabilities that assess the uncertainty of a given new observation belonging to each of the already established classes. Cardiac decompensation   A combination of symptoms and signs that indicate that the heart because of its abnormal condition no longer is able to maintain an efficient circulation. Cardiomyopathy   An acquired or hereditary disease of the heart muscle that makes it harder for the heart to pump blood to the rest of the body. Cardiovascular medicine   The branch of medicine that deals with the diagnosis and treatment of diseases and disorders of the heart and blood vessels. Caveat   A warning or proviso of specific stipulations, conditions, or limitations. Chromosome   A threadlike structure of nucleic acids and protein found in the nucleus of most living cells, carrying genetic information in the form of genes. Cine images   Short movies that are able to show heart motion throughout the cardiac cycle. Consensus label   Labeling training data multiple times and only using that data if all the labelers agree on the label of the data. Creatinine   A breakdown product of creatine phosphate from muscle and protein metabolism. It is usually measured in clinical practice to determine kidney function. Curating   (Curate) Select, organize, and look after the items in (a collection or exhibition). D Data augmentation   A strategy that enables practitioners to significantly increase the diversity of data available for training models, without actually collecting new data. Decision trees   A flowchart-like structure in which each internal node represents a “test” on an attribute (e.g., whether a coin flip comes up heads or tails), each branch represents the outcome of the test, and each leaf node represents a class label. Deep learning   A subset of machine learning where artificial neural networks, algorithms inspired by the human brain, learn from large amounts of data. Denoising   The process of removing noise from a signal. Dermoscopic   Refers to the examination of the skin using skin surface microscopy. DICE coefficient   A statistic used to gauge the similarity of two samples. Dimensionality   The minimum number of coordinates needed to specify a point. Downsampling   The process of reducing the sampling rate of a signal, or the sample size of a cohort. E ECG   Electrocardiogram, a test that measures the electrical activity of the heart. Echocardiography   The use of ultrasound waves to investigate the action of the heart. Edema   A condition characterized by an excess of watery fluid collecting in the cavities or tissues of the body. Ejection fraction   A measurement, expressed as a percentage, of how much blood the left ventricle pumps out with each contraction. Electrophysiology   The study of the electrical properties of biological cells and tissues. Embeddings   An embedding is a mapping of a discrete, categorical variable to a vector of continuous numbers. En masse   In a group; altogether. Endocarditis   An infection of the heart's inner lining, usually involving the heart valves. Ensemble models   A process where multiple diverse models are created to predict an outcome, either by using many different modeling algorithms or using different training data sets. Eosinophilia   A high level of disease-fighting white blood cells known as eosinophils in the blood. Epigenomics   The study of the complete set of epigenetic modifications on the genetic material of a cell, known as the epigenome. F F1 score   A measure of a test's accuracy in statistical analysis. Fourier transform   A function derived from a given function and representing it by a series of sinusoidal functions. Fragility   The quality of being easily broken or damaged. Framingham risk score   A gender-specific algorithm used to estimate the 10-year cardiovascular risk of an individual. G Gabor transform   A special case of the short-time Fourier transform. It is used to determine the sinusoidal frequency and phase content of local sections of a signal as it changes over time. Gamification   The application of game-design elements and game principles in nongame contexts. Gaussian kernel   A weighted linear combination of the kernel function computed between a data point and each of the support vectors. Gaussian model   A stochastic process (a collection of random variables indexed by time or space), such that every finite collection of those random variables has a multivariate normal distribution. Genomics   The branch of molecular biology concerned with the structure, function, evolution, and mapping of genomes. Gradient boosting   A machine learning technique for regression and classification problems, which produces a prediction model in the form of an ensemble of weak prediction models. H Heart failure (HF)   A condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs. Hemodynamics   The dynamics of blood flow. Hemoglobin   A red protein responsible for transporting oxygen in the blood of vertebrates. Its molecule comprises four subunits, each containing an iron atom bound to a heme group. Heterogeneous   Diverse in character or content. Heuristics   Any approach to problem solving or self-discovery that employs a practical method that is not guaranteed to be optimal, perfect, or rational, but which is nevertheless enough for reaching an immediate, short-term goal. Hidden Markov models   A finite set of states, each of which is associated with a (generally multidimensional) probability distribution. Hierarchical clustering   An algorithm that groups similar objects into groups called clusters. High-dimensional data   The number of dimensions is staggeringly high, so high that calculations become extremely difficult. Histopathology   Refers to the microscopic examination of tissue to study the manifestations of a disease. HITECH   Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act. HITECH Act   An act was created to motivate the implementation of electronic health records (EHR) and supporting technology in the United States. Holism   The idea that various systems should be viewed as wholes, not merely as a collection of parts. Hyperkalemia   A high level of the electrolyte potassium in the blood. Hypertension   Elevated blood pressure. Hypertrophy   The increase in the volume of an organ or tissue due to the enlargement of its component cells. Hypoechoic   A hypoechoic mass is a tissue in the body that is more dense or solid than usual. I Image texture   A set of metrics calculated in image processing designed to quantify the perceived texture of an image. Image texture gives information about the spatial arrangement of color or intensities in an image or selected region of interest. Incidence rate   It is a measure of the frequency with which some event, such as a disease or accident, occurs over a specified time period. Inference time   Inference times are often expressed as “X + Y,” in which X is the time taken in reasonably well-optimized GPU code and Y is the time taken in unoptimized CPU code. Infrastructure   The fundamental facilities and systems serving a country, city, or other area, including the services and facilities necessary for its economy to function. Interpretability   A relation between formal theories that expresses the possibility of interpreting or translating one into the other. Intervention   Action taken to improve a situation, especially a medical disorder. Interventional cardiology   A branch of cardiology that deals specifically with the catheter-based treatment of structural heart diseases. Intravascular   Situated or occurring within a vessel or vessels of an animal or plant, especially within a blood vessel or blood vascular system. Iterative   The repetition of a process to generate a sequence of outcomes. J Jaccard index   A statistic used for gauging the similarity and diversity of sample sets. Jensen-Shannon divergence   A method of measuring the similarity between two probability distributions. K K-space   An extension of the concept of Fourier space; well known in MR imaging. Kullbach–Liebler divergence   A measure of how one probability distribution is different from a second, reference probability distribution. L Lasso models   A regression analysis method that performs both variable selection and regularization to enhance the prediction accuracy and interpretability of the statistical model it produces. Late gadolinium enhancement   A useful tool for scar detection, based on differences in the volume of distribution of gadolinium, an extracellular agent. Latent Dirichlet allocation   A generative statistical model that allows sets of observations to be explained by unobserved groups that explain why some parts of the data are similar. Logistic regression   A statistical model that in its basic form uses a logistic function to model a binary dependent variable, although many more complex extensions exist. M Machine learning   The study of computer algorithms that improve automatically through experience. It is seen as a subset of artificial intelligence. Mathew's correlation coefficient   (MCC) It is used in machine learning as a measure of the quality of binary (two-class) classifications. Matrices   A rectangular array of numbers, symbols, or expressions, arranged in rows and columns (singular- matrix). Melanoma   A serious form of skin cancer that begins in cells known as melanocytes. Meta-analysis   A quantitative, formal, epidemiological study design used to systematically assess the results of previous research to derive conclusions about that body of research. Methylation   A form of alkylation, with a methyl group, rather than a larger carbon chain, replacing a hydrogen atom. Modalities   A mode in which something exists or is experienced or expressed. Mutually exclusive   Two or more events that cannot coincide. Myocardial infarction   A blockage of blood flow to the heart muscle. N Naive Bayes   An algorithm that uses Bayes' theorem to classify objects. Nash equilibrium   A proposed solution of a noncooperative game involving two or more players in which each player is assumed to know the equilibrium strategies of the other players, and no player has anything to gain by changing only their own strategy. Neural networks   A set of algorithms, modeled loosely after the human brain, that are designed to recognize patterns. NEWS score   National Early Warning Score determines the degree of illness of a patient and prompts critical care intervention P Paradigm   A typical example or pattern of something; a model. Parameter   A numerical or other measurable factor forming one of a set that defines a system or sets the conditions of its operation. Parasternal   Situated beside the sternum. Parkinson's disease   A progressive nervous system disorder that affects movement. Pathogenicity   Refers to the ability of an organism to cause disease (i.e., harm the host). Perceptron   An algorithm for supervised learning of binary classifiers. Perfusion   The passage of blood, a blood substitute, or other fluid through the blood vessels or other natural channels in an organ or tissue. PET   Positron emission tomography is a nuclear medicine functional imaging technique that is used to observe metabolic processes in the body as an aid to the diagnosis of disease. Phantom model   A body of material resembling a body or bodily part in mass, composition, and dimensions and used to measure a particular effect. Phenomapping   To classify a group of patients with one disease into separate “phenotypes” within that category. Phenotype   The set of observable characteristics of an individual resulting from the interaction of its genotype with the environment. Piezoelectricity   The electric charge that accumulates in certain solid materials in response to applied mechanical stress. Pixel   The smallest controllable element of a picture represented on a screen. Polar maps   Maps that provide a two-dimensional view of the entire three-dimensional left ventricular myocardium, and are used to show abnormal left ventricular myocardial perfusion when coronary artery disease is suspected. Polymorphism   The occurrence of different forms among the members of a population or colony, or in the life cycle of an individual organism. Predictive analytics   A variety of statistical techniques from data mining, predictive modeling, and machine learning, that analyze current and historical facts to make predictions about future or otherwise unknown events. Probabilistic model   Model incorporating random variables and probability distributions of an event or phenomenon. Probability   A numerical description of how likely an event is to occur or how likely it is that a proposition is true. Prognosis   Predicting the likely or expected development of a disease. Prognostication   The action of foretelling or prophesying future events. Propensity   An inclination or natural tendency to behave in a particular way. Proteomics   The large-scale study of proteins. Pseudoaneurysm   A collection of blood that forms between the two outer layers of an artery, the tunica media, and the tunica adventitia. R Radiomics   A method that extracts a large number of quantitative features from medical images using data characterization algorithms. Random forest   An ensemble learning method for classification, regression and other tasks that operate by constructing a multitude of decision trees at training time and outputting the class that is the mode of the classes (classification) or mean prediction (regression) of the individual trees. Recurrent neural networks (RNN)   A class of artificial neural networks where connections between nodes form a directed graph along a temporal sequence. Reductionism   The practice of analyzing and describing a complex phenomenon in terms of phenomena that are held to represent a simpler or more fundamental level, especially when this is said to provide a sufficient explanation. Regression problem   A problem where the output variable is a real or continuous value, such as “salary” or “weight.” Retinopathy   A disease of the retina that results in impairment or loss of vision. Risk stratification   The process of assigning a risk status to patients, then using this information to direct care and improve overall health outcomes. Robustness   The quality or condition of being strong and in good condition. S Sarcoidosis   An inflammatory disease that affects multiple organs in the body, but mostly the lungs and lymph glands. Schizophrenia   A serious mental disorder that affects a person's ability to think, feel, and behave clearly. Sensitivity   Sensitivity (also called the true positive rate) measures the proportion of actual positives that are correctly identified as such (e.g., the percentage of sick people who are correctly identified as having the condition) Single-photon emission computerized tomography (SPECT)   Nuclear medicine tomographic imaging technique that uses gamma rays to image myocardial tissue perfusion at rest and stress conditions. Sinogram   A set of many projections under different angles organized in 2D. Sociometry   A qualitative method for measuring social relationships. Specificity   Specificity (also called the true negative rate) measures the proportion of actual negatives that are correctly identified as such (e.g., the percentage of healthy people who are correctly identified as not having the condition). Stochastic   A randomly determined process. T ^(201)Thallium   A radiopharmaceutical used in myocardial perfusion imaging. Technetium-99m   A metastable nuclear isomer used in a number of medical diagnostic imaging scans. Thrombectomy   The interventional procedure of removing a blood clot (thrombus) from a blood vessel. Thrombosis   The formation of a blood clot, known as a thrombus, within a blood vessel. Topological properties   Properties of a geometric object that are preserved under continuous deformations, such as stretching, twisting, crumpling, and bending, but not tearing or gluing. U U-Net   A convolutional neural network that was developed for biomedical image segmentation. V Vectors   An object that has both a magnitude and a direction. W Wasserstein GAN   An extension to the generative adversarial network that both improves the stability when training the model and provides a loss function that correlates with the quality of generated images.
